articles.title: ECB Moves to Expand Euro’s Global Reach as Over 30 Central Banks Show Interest - Brand Icon Image
articles.summary: ECB Moves to Expand Euro’s Global Reach as Over 30 Central Banks Show Interest  Brand Icon Image
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank (ECB) is seeking to strengthen the euro’s position in the global financial system by expanding access to emergency liquidity facilities for foreign central banks, as policymakers reassess the dominance of the US dollar amid uncertainty surrounding Washington’s economic policies.
Philip Lane, the ECB’s chief economist, said on Wednesday that demand for the bank’s recently expanded euro liquidity facilities had been strong, with more than 30 central banks expressing interest in accessing the arrangements.
Speaking at a closed-door event in Shanghai titled Monetary System Beyond the Dollar, Lane argued that providing foreign central banks with access to euros could increase confidence in the currency, encourage its international use and extend the influence of euro area monetary policy beyond the 21-nation currency bloc.
"Liquidity lines bolster confidence in the currency and reduce the associated risks, supporting its wider usage," Lane said in prepared remarks at the event, held as part of the annual Bund summit.
The initiative comes at a time when policymakers and financial market participants are examining whether the US dollar’s longstanding dominance in international trade, investment and central bank reserves could face greater competition.
Uncertainty surrounding US President Donald Trump’s economic policies has added to those discussions, prompting renewed interest in the role other major currencies could play in the international monetary system.
Lane said broader international use of the euro would not only strengthen its standing in global markets but also improve the ECB’s ability to deliver on its mandate of maintaining price stability.
Greater use of the currency internationally could increase the reach of monetary policy decisions taken in the euro area, while potentially creating additional demand for euro-denominated financial assets.
LIQUIDITY FACILITIES TO SUPPORT EURO DEMAND
A central component of the ECB’s strategy is its EUREP facility, which allows foreign central banks to obtain euros by providing collateral denominated in the single currency.
Such arrangements can help foreign monetary authorities manage liquidity pressures and maintain access to euros during periods of financial market stress.
By reducing the risk that overseas institutions will struggle to obtain the currency when needed, the ECB hopes to make the euro more attractive for international transactions, financial contracts and reserve management.
Lane said the facilities could also support bond markets across the euro area, particularly by encouraging official reserve managers to purchase more euro-denominated securities.
Stronger demand from foreign central banks could increase the international investor base for European government bonds and other eligible assets, potentially supporting market liquidity and reinforcing the euro’s role as a reserve currency.
The ECB’s approach reflects a broader recognition that international currency use depends not only on economic size but also on the availability of reliable funding arrangements, liquid financial markets and confidence in the institutions supporting the currency.
ECB REVIEWS CURRENCY SWAP NETWORK
The liquidity initiative is also linked to the ECB’s review of its network of currency swap lines, which allow participating central banks to exchange their currencies for euros under agreed conditions.
ECB President Christine Lagarde recently said the bank was reviewing the arrangements, which form part of its wider efforts to strengthen the euro’s international role.
Currency swap lines can provide an additional source of funding during periods of market disruption, allowing central banks to obtain foreign currency liquidity and, where appropriate, make it available to financial institutions in their jurisdictions.
The arrangements are particularly important during periods of heightened uncertainty, when demand for major currencies can rise sharply and access to international funding markets may become more difficult.
The ECB maintains swap arrangements with selected central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and the People’s Bank of China, reflecting the importance of cooperation among major monetary authorities in managing global financial risks.
However, Lane indicated that access to such arrangements should remain selective rather than being extended indiscriminately to all central banks.
He said swap lines could encourage borrowing in euros but should be reserved for central banks in economies with close financial links to the euro area and a clear ability to repay their euro liabilities.
The approach suggests that the ECB is seeking to balance the benefits of wider international currency use with the need to manage financial and credit risks associated with providing liquidity abroad.
EURO’S GLOBAL AMBITIONS FACE STRUCTURAL CHALLENGES
Although the ECB’s initiative could strengthen the euro’s appeal, expanding its international role would require more than access to liquidity facilities.
The US dollar remains deeply embedded in global trade, commodity pricing, cross-border lending and international financial markets. Its widespread use is supported by the scale of the US economy, the depth of its capital markets and the extensive availability of dollar-denominated financial assets.
For the euro to gain a larger share of international transactions and official reserves, foreign investors and institutions would also need confidence in the accessibility, liquidity and stability of European financial markets.
The ECB’s liquidity arrangements could help address one aspect of that challenge by reducing funding risks and making euros more readily available to participating central banks.
At the same time, the arrangements are intended to support the transmission of euro area monetary policy, ensuring that developments in European financial conditions can be reflected more effectively in international markets.
The interest expressed by more than 30 central banks indicates that the expanded facilities have attracted considerable attention, although it does not necessarily mean that all interested institutions will qualify for access or ultimately use the arrangements.
For the ECB, the immediate objective is to strengthen the infrastructure supporting the euro’s international use while preserving safeguards against financial risks.
As debate over the future of the global monetary system continues, the bank’s efforts highlight Europe’s ambition to increase the euro’s influence without compromising the stability and credibility underpinning the currency.

articles.title: Pound Sterling Today: UK Inflation At 3.5% Sharpens BoE Rate Debate - Exchange Rates UK
articles.summary: Pound Sterling Today: UK Inflation At 3.5% Sharpens BoE Rate Debate  Exchange Rates UK
articles.full_text:
Two BoE Hikes, Then What? The Debate Facing Pound Sterling
Pound Sterling edges higher against the Euro and US Dollar as Pantheon weighs a third BoE hike, while ING sees scope for rate cuts later in 2027.
Pound Sterling held modest gains against the Euro and US Dollar on Wednesday as economists offered sharply different readings of the latest UK inflation figures.
The Pound-to-Dollar exchange rate was trading at $1.3384, up 0.09%, while GBP/EUR stood at €1.1921.
Pound Sterling was weaker against the Australian and New Zealand Dollars, leaving the day's performance mixed despite inflation exceeding expectations.
The 21 October release showed annual CPI rising to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, above the 3.4% consensus.
Pantheon Macroeconomics expects increases in November 2026 and February 2027 and is close to adding a third, while ING anticipates the same first two moves but a return to cuts by November 2027 if wider inflation pressures remain contained.
Airfares divide the reading of services inflation
Motor fuels supplied the largest upward contribution to the headline acceleration, but services inflation also rose to 3.7% from 3.4%.
Lloyds senior UK economist Nikesh Sawjani notes that headline inflation is half a percentage point above the Bank of England's July projection, whereas core and services inflation are each only 0.1 percentage point higher.
He writes: “To us, the much larger overshoot in headline inflation therefore continues to look predominantly like an energy story rather than evidence, at this stage, of a similarly large broadening in underlying inflation pressures.”
Airfares fell as the summer holiday season ended, but by less than a year earlier, lifting their contribution to annual inflation.
Pantheon thinks that smaller decline follows logically from the unusually weak summer increase:
“But July and August airfares increases combined were also the weakest since 2003. Less summer strength meant less to unwind in September.”
It therefore expects the correction to carry forward, rather than disappear as a temporary statistical disturbance.
ING puts more weight on measures that remove volatile components from services inflation:
“Remove these jumpy categories, as well as those that are indexed, and the Bank of England’s preferred measure of ‘core services’ inflation is still relatively contained – albeit up slightly over the past few months.”
Pantheon reports: “Underlying services inflation accelerated to 3.9% year-over-year in September, from 3.7%, its highest since March.”
ING also points to food prices, where it had expected the energy shock to be more visible by now.
It writes: “Partly as a result, our calculation of ‘energy intensive’ inflation has actually fallen this year and shows little-to-no sign of picking up.”
“This remains the case even after stripping out last year's increases in water bills and car taxes, which would otherwise distort the picture.”
The BoE is trying to prevent higher energy costs becoming embedded in wages and other prices, prolonging inflation beyond the original shock.
Two precautionary hikes or a longer cycle?
The policy divide has sharpened since Tuesday's jobs figures strengthened the case for a November increase.
Pantheon now forecasts headline inflation peaking at 4.8% in February 2027 and remaining above 4% until July, a prolonged period in which it believes wage and price-setting risks would grow.
The consultancy says: “Strong growth, stable or falling labour market slack and surging inflation mean the MPC will hike in November. We expect another hike in February and are very close to adding a third in May, or earlier.”
Pantheon has not yet adopted that third hike.
ING instead expects inflation to peak briefly around 4% this winter and regards its anticipated hikes as precautionary.
“We expect hikes in both November and February, but by the spring, we think the Bank will be more confident in calling the ‘all clear’ on second-round effects.”
“If we’re right, then we think the Bank can start cutting rates again by next November and into 2028.”
The next BoE decision is on 5 November, with Bank Rate at 3.75%.
Lloyds recorded roughly four quarter-point increases priced by July 2027 in its post-release assessment, a more aggressive path than either ING's forecast or Pantheon's current two-hike call.
Sawjani writes: “Against that backdrop, the latest data continue to argue for the MPC to remain patient rather than respond mechanically to higher headline CPI, although the combination of rising inflation and resilient activity means that patience is likely to be tested increasingly over coming months.”
TLDR: What This Means for the Pound
With a November increase already heavily anticipated, support for further GBP/USD and GBP/EUR gains depends partly on how much tightening investors expect after it. Pantheon's evidence of persistent domestic pressure could help sustain those expectations, although it has yet to endorse the full path priced into markets.
ING's scenario would leave less lasting interest-rate support for Pound Sterling: two precautionary increases would eventually give way to cuts. If incoming data favour that view, investors could reduce the returns they expect from UK assets before the first cut arrives.
The next CPI release is due on 18 November, after the BoE's decision. Whether food prices and less volatile services begin to show stronger pressure will help determine whether a November hike starts a longer cycle or proves one of a limited number of precautionary moves.

articles.title: Inflation at 3.5% Puts These UK ETFs in Focus as BOE Hike Bets Mount - Yahoo Finance UK
articles.summary: Inflation at 3.5% Puts These UK ETFs in Focus as BOE Hike Bets Mount  Yahoo Finance UK
articles.full_text:
UK inflation has climbed to an 11-month high, reinforcing expectations that the Bank of England will deliver its first interest rate hike next month, in more than three years. Notably, consumer prices rose 3.5% in the 12 months through September 2026, up from 3.1% in August and above economists' forecasts of 3.4%, according to the Office for National Statistics.
The acceleration was driven largely by motor fuel costs, which surged 29.8% year over year — the fastest pace since August 2022 — as Britain's status as a net energy importer left it exposed to external shocks. To this end, markets are now pricing a 98% probability of a 25-basis-point hike to 4% next month, with traders also betting on a further increase at the central bank's final meeting of the year in December.
A rate hike reshapes the return calculus across UK equities, lifting bank margins, pressuring rate-sensitive sectors like real estate and consumer discretionary, and shifting gilt yields. The latest inflation hike puts UK stocks and by extension exchange-traded funds (ETFs) holding them squarely in the spotlight.
Before diving into those ETFs, it is worth understanding which industries stand to gain or lose from tighter policy (and why) so investors can make an informed decision.
Industries Stand to Gain or Lose
The UK's inflation rebound to 3.5%, combined with mounting expectations of a November rate hike, creates a sharply divergent picture across industries.
Direct beneficiaries of the rate hike will be banks and financial institutions. A hike widens net interest margins, which should act as a tailwind for major UK lenders such as HSBC, Lloyds, and NatWest. Near-term sentiment, however, may still be choppy, as expectations of higher interest rates have weighed on bank stocks amid concerns that tighter monetary policy could slow economic growth and increase credit losses. Investor anxiety over a potential increase in the bank tax surcharge in the upcoming Autumn Budget has added to the pressure.
Rate-sensitive industries like real estate and REITs are first in the firing line, as higher borrowing costs compress valuations. Retail and consumer discretionary face a tougher backdrop too; as unemployment at 4.7% and slowing real wage growth may push consumers to cut non-essential spending, leaving supermarkets and value retailers relatively more defensive.
As far as the Energy sector is concerned, the result is expected to be mixed. This is because while high oil prices lift energy earnings expectations, fuel inflation is itself the core driver of this hike, and eventual policy tightening could weigh on demand. As investors weigh both sides, BP and Shell's share price movement will be in focus.

articles.title: BoE’s Dhingra Flags Wage Disinflation Need as Traders Brace for Higher UK Rates - VT Markets
articles.summary: BoE’s Dhingra Flags Wage Disinflation Need as Traders Brace for Higher UK Rates  VT Markets
articles.full_text:
A Bank of England Monetary Policy Committee member said the Bank has concerns about its estimate of target-consistent pay growth and argued that further wage disinflation is required to return Consumer Price Index inflation to target. She set out a benchmark in which wage growth of 3% is consistent with 2% inflation, while adding that households tend to notice inflation once it is above 3%. She also said supply shocks are likely to remain a recurring feature of the outlook.
The policymaker warned that the current monetary policy stance may not be restrictive enough and said inflation expectations are anchored above norms. The remarks sit within a framework where central banks focus on core measures that strip out volatile food and fuel components, and typically respond to above-target inflation with higher interest rates. Such moves can support a currency through higher yields and, through the opportunity cost channel, can weigh on gold.
Currency, Bond, and Equity Market Implications
We believe derivative traders should prepare for prolonged higher interest rates in the UK as sticky wage growth threatens the Bank of England’s 2% target. With UK average earnings growth still hovering near 4.5%—well above the target-consistent 3% benchmark—monetary policy will likely remain tighter for longer. We suggest positioning for a stronger Pound Sterling by taking long currency derivative positions against lower-yielding peers like the Euro.
In the rates market, we expect short-term UK government bond yields to push higher as traders reprice the probability of persistent restrictive policy. Historical data from previous inflationary cycles shows that unanchored inflation expectations usually cause severe pullbacks in short-duration debt instruments. Derivative traders can take advantage of this setup by shorting short-term interest rate futures or using put options on gilt contracts.
Prolonged high rates will also weigh heavily on domestic equities, particularly mid-cap stocks that depend on resilient consumer spending. When borrowing costs remain high and core inflation stays elevated above 3%, corporate profit margins face immediate pressure. We recommend hedging domestic equity portfolios using index put derivatives or setting up short positions on consumer discretionary sectors.
Commodity Market Implications
For commodity markets, we expect gold to face renewed pressure as elevated real yields raise the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets. Historically, precious metal rallies stall when central banks signal that monetary policy is not restrictive enough to cool wage growth. We advise derivative traders to limit unhedged long gold exposures and instead consider defined-risk spread strategies to manage short-term downside risks.

articles.title: U.K. CPI Goes Off the Rails Ahead of BOE Meeting - Haver Analytics
articles.summary: U.K. CPI Goes Off the Rails Ahead of BOE Meeting  Haver Analytics
articles.full_text:
Inflation in the United Kingdom is back to misbehaving in September. The HICP rendition of inflation posted a 0.5% increase, its second in a row, following a 0.6% increase in July. The CPIH, however, performed exactly the same, with a 0.5% increase in September and August, after a 0.6% gain in July. This is going to put the Bank of England's back up against the wall when it comes to making its next interest rate decision.
Hot, hot, hot: Inflation runs hot in the United Kingdom. The CPIH version shows a 6.6% annual rate over three months, a 4.2% pace over six months, and 3.6% over 12 months. This is a clear accelerating profile with inflation clearly over the 2% mark over each one of those horizons. A year ago, inflation was rising 4.1% year-over-year. There's very little here to provide any escape from the conclusion that interest rates need to go up and inflation is a problem that needs some strict attention.
Core inflation is rising as well: Core inflation in the U.K. under the CPIH measure rose 0.4% in September after rising 0.2% in August and 0.4% in July. The sequence of core inflation rates from 12 months inward shows a 12-month pace of 3.1%, a six-month pace of 3.2%, and a three-month pace of 4.1%. These increases are faster-paced step by step as horizons shorten. However, like the headline, all three of these metrics are above 2% and once again there is this accelerating trend in place, even for the core, and that has to be an even more difficult pill for the Bank of England to swallow.
Inflation acceleration: If we look at the tendency to accelerate, acceleration occurred in 58.3% of the categories in July; that proportion fell to 41.7% in August, and it was back up to 50% in September. So, as of September, the proportion of these categories showing acceleration is split pretty much 50/50, making it less of a clear acceleration imperative on volatile monthly data. However, over three months compared to six months, 75% of the categories are accelerating; over six months compared to 12 months, again 75% of the categories are accelerating; over 12 months compared to 12 months ago, that proportion drops to 41.7%. But the drop in the breadth of inflation is also related to the fact that the 12-month inflation rate had dropped from a year ago at 3.8% to 3.5%; it dropped more, from 4% to 3.1%, in the case of the core CPIH. In other words, inflation has fallen from a very excessive pace to a still excessive pace, and that drop is ‘endorsed’ by a drop in breadth. Breadth can reinforce direction. And now inflation and breadth both are rising – a bad sign.
Inflation ranking: We also can look at how inflation ranks compared to where it's been and on this basis that we wind up with another troubling finding. The HICP version of inflation has an 82nd percentile standing; the CPIH version also has an 82nd percentile standing and the CPIH core measure has a slightly higher 82.7 percentile standing. So, inflation is high even by historic experience; that compares current year-over-year inflation in September to inflation rates back to the year 2000. On that timeline, in fact, the median for inflation has a 77th percentile standing and the average pace for inflation has a 72nd percentile standing across categories. Now both of these are slightly lower than the actual CPIH version at a ranking of 82%. What that tells us is that inflation has been even more virulent in those categories that have a higher weight in the CPI.
Summing up On balance, this is a poor report; it will probably put the Bank of England's back up against the wall to enforce another rate hike. It's hard to see how the central bank can look at these various measures of inflation and their path and decide to pass on a rate hike at its next meeting, so brace yourself.
- Robert A. Brusca is Chief Economist of Fact and Opinion Economics, a consulting firm he founded in Manhattan. He has been an economist on Wall Street for over 25 years. articles.title: UK Treasury chief vows to give families 'some breathing space' as inflation runs hot, highest in a year - Fortune
articles.summary: UK Treasury chief vows to give families 'some breathing space' as inflation runs hot, highest in a year  Fortune
articles.full_text:
Inflation in the U.K. rose to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to ratchet up fuel prices, official figures showed Wednesday, cementing market expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month.
The Office for National Statistics said consumer prices rose by 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August. That’s the highest reading since October last year, and above the 3.4% that most economists had been expecting for the month.
The increase takes inflation further above the Bank of England’s target rate of 2%.
Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly at the pump. Overall, motor fuels soared by 30% in the year to September, up from a 23% annual rise in August.
Fuel costs have been soaring because of the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz, which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies.
Treasury chief John Healey said his budget statement next week will aim to give businesses and families “some breathing space” from the upward march in the cost of living.
Whatever measures he comes up with to keep a lid on rising prices, economists expect the Bank of England to increase interest rates at its next meeting on Nov. 5. Last month, rate-setters held the bank’s main rate at 3.75% but gave a big hint that they were ready to hike soon.
“With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise,” said Suren Thiru, chief economist at ICAEW.
Most economists expect an increase in the bank’s main rate to 4%. Other central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, have raised rates recently.
Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

articles.title: ECB's Kazaks says that some more policy tightening might be necessary if inflation continues to reside above target; recent rise in yields has already tightened financing conditions, Econostream reports - Newsquawk
articles.summary: ECB's Kazaks says that some more policy tightening might be necessary if inflation continues to reside above target; recent rise in yields has already tightened financing conditions, Econostream reports  Newsquawk
articles.full_text:
- Monetary policy cannot cure the French situation.
What it means
Kazaks sits on the hawkish wing of the Governing Council, so conditional tightening talk from him reads as a lower-bound signal rather than the committee median; in past episodes, remarks from this flank have tended to matter only when doves begin echoing the conditionality. The two-part framing is the useful structure: an explicit link between above-target inflation persistence and possible further tightening on one side, and an acknowledgment that higher yields have already done some of the work on the other. That second clause is the established pattern through tightening cycles, where officials have used the rise in term premia and sovereign spreads to argue that market pricing is substituting for policy action, a framing that historically caps how much further hawkish rhetoric pushes the front end. The aside that monetary policy cannot cure the French situation fits the recurring Council distinction between cyclical inflation, which rates address, and country-specific fiscal slippage, which they do not; in comparable episodes officials have used that line to resist pressure to smooth sovereign spread widening, leaving OAT-Bund dynamics to fiscal and political developments. Worth noting is whether other officials repeat the conditional tightening formulation or treat the financing-conditions point as grounds for staying on hold. As commentary rather than a decision, the signal is directional.

articles.title: Dollar index steady as markets await central bank rate decision - IDNFinancials
articles.summary: Dollar index steady as markets await central bank rate decision  IDNFinancials
articles.full_text:
NEW YORK - The US dollar index, which measures the greenback against six major currencies, remained steady at 101.78 after falling 0.2% on Tuesday.
Investors had previously turned to the US dollar as a safe-haven asset amid market volatility driven by the war in the Middle East and a surge in artificial intelligence (AI) investment.
According to Reuters, one factor supporting the dollar was the United States' relative energy independence. However, oil prices fell in overnight trading after briefly reaching a five-month high.
Meanwhile, the Australian dollar strengthened after Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook had deteriorated significantly.
Speaking at a Citi conference, Hauser said the situation had left him uncertain about whether the central bank would need to raise its benchmark interest rate again next month.
The Australian dollar rose 0.1% to US$0.7013, slightly below the previous session's high of US$0.7017.
Markets are monitoring a meeting between Iran's president and Pakistan's army chief, who has been acting as a mediator in US-Iran relations, amid continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabian infrastructure and reports of attacks on vessels in the Gulf region.
In equity markets, Wall Street advanced as the technology sector's corporate earnings season got under way.
Japanese and South Korean stock markets also rose on Wednesday.
Carol Kong, an economist and currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said the performance of major technology companies could have a significant influence on the US dollar, as stock market sentiment and economic growth prospects are closely linked to these companies' results.
According to Kong, the US dollar has been the most prominent safe-haven asset compared with other traditional alternatives so far this year.
Demand for the dollar as a safe-haven asset is expected to ease if the Middle East conflict ends and energy prices decline.
Nevertheless, Kong expects the US dollar to strengthen moderately over the coming months as foreign capital flows into US markets increase.
Euro Faces Pressure from French Political Unrest
Elsewhere in the foreign exchange market, the US dollar was steady at 158.33 Japanese yen. The euro was also little changed at US$1.1229, while the pound sterling held at US$1.33735.
Investors remain cautious about the euro amid expanding anti-government demonstrations in France and the country's deteriorating fiscal position.
On Tuesday, the French government announced plans to strengthen security by deploying police and military personnel ahead of further demonstrations scheduled for Saturday.
The move came after the government acknowledged shortcomings in its handling of violence over the previous weekend.
Investors are now turning their attention to monetary policy decisions by several major central banks.
The US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank (ECB) and Bank of Japan (BOJ) are scheduled to announce their interest rate decisions consecutively, beginning next Wednesday.
Market participants currently expect all three central banks to leave interest rates unchanged.
Meanwhile, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Bank of Canada are scheduled to announce their policy decisions on the same day as the Federal Reserve.
Markets expect both central banks to raise interest rates by 25 basis points.
The New Zealand dollar fell 0.1% to US$0.5677 on Wednesday, while the Canadian dollar was steady at 1.4064 per US dollar.
Currency movements over the coming days are expected to remain influenced by developments in the Middle East conflict, fluctuations in energy prices, technology company earnings and the direction of global monetary policy.
(DK/LM)

articles.title: PBOC Nudges Yuan Fix Slightly Stronger Against the Dollar - TradingPedia
articles.summary: PBOC Nudges Yuan Fix Slightly Stronger Against the Dollar  TradingPedia
articles.full_text:
Key Moments
- The People’s Bank of China set the USD/CNY central parity at 6.7192 for Wednesday’s session, marginally stronger than the prior fix of 6.7200.
- The new fixing contrasted with a 6.6779 estimate from Reuters for the same session.
- The PBoC continues to use multiple policy tools – including the Loan Prime Rate and foreign exchange operations – to pursue price and exchange-rate stability while supporting growth.
Latest USD/CNY Central Parity Fix
The People’s Bank of China (PBoC) set the USD/CNY central reference rate for the upcoming Wednesday trading session at 6.7192. This represents a slight adjustment from the previous day’s central parity of 6.7200.
The newly announced fixing diverged from a 6.6779 projection reported by Reuters for the same session.
| Parameter | Value | 
|---|---|
| Current USD/CNY central rate | 6.7192 | 
| Previous day’s fix | 6.7200 | 
| Reuters estimate | 6.6779 | 
PBoC’s Mandate and Policy Role
The PBoC’s main monetary policy goals are to maintain price stability, which includes stabilizing the exchange rate, and to support economic growth. The central bank also focuses on advancing financial sector reforms, such as the opening and further development of China’s financial markets.
Ownership and Governance Structure
The PBoC is wholly owned by the state of the People’s Republic of China and is not treated as an independent institution. A Chinese Communist Party (CCP) Committee Secretary, nominated by the Chairman of the State Council, plays a central role in shaping the central bank’s management and strategic direction, rather than the governor alone. According to the article, Mr. Pan Gongsheng currently holds both positions.
Monetary Policy Toolkit
Compared with central banks in Western economies, the PBoC employs a wider array of monetary policy instruments to achieve its objectives. Key tools include:
- Seven-day Reverse Repo Rate (RRR)
- Medium-term Lending Facility (MLF)
- Foreign exchange interventions
- Reserve Requirement Ratio (RRR)
China’s benchmark interest rate is the Loan Prime Rate (LPR). Adjustments to the LPR directly affect loan and mortgage costs as well as returns on savings. Through changes in the LPR, the central bank can also influence the exchange rate of the Chinese renminbi.
Private Banking in China
The article notes that private banks operate within China’s financial system, though they represent only a small share, with a total of 19 such institutions. The largest private lenders are WeBank and MYbank, both digital banks backed by major technology firms Tencent and Ant Group, as cited from The Straits Times.
In 2014, authorities allowed domestically funded lenders, fully capitalized by private capital, to enter and operate in the state-dominated banking sector.

articles.title: Americans are struggling to buy homes amid rising costs - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.summary: Americans are struggling to buy homes amid rising costs  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosHousing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes  CNBCPending home sales sink to 25-year low as buyers flee high mortgage rates  Yahoo FinanceWhy Americans have stopped buying new homes  The EconomistHomebuilder sentiment is at a 14-year low  Axios

source_detail.name: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

articles.full_text:
September was the worst month for pending home sales since they’ve been tracked.
There has never been a worse month for pending home sales than September 2026.
Data released Tuesday shows the housing market weakening sharply, squeezed by rising mortgage rates and elevated home prices.
Pending home sales fell 7.3% in September from the previous month, according to the National Association of Realtors (NAR). It was the lowest reading in the history of the Pending Home Sales Index, which began in 2001.
Mortgage rates have also moved higher. Mortgage News Daily put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 7.43% on Monday, up from 7.37% on Friday.
The spike in mortgage rates over the past eight weeks -- and the even bigger increase since the start of the Iran war -- has priced out millions of aspiring homebuyers.
When rates increase from 6% to 7%, nearly 6 million fewer Americans can afford the monthly payment on the median-priced home in the U.S. with a 10% down payment, according to data provided to ABC News by NAR. The median single-family home was around $435,000 as of September 2026.
A separate estimate out Wednesday from Pantheon Macroeconomics found the typical monthly payment on the median-priced home will climb to 40% of average after-tax income this month, up from 35% at the start of the year.
In other words: to buy a typical single-family home in the U.S. right now, at around a $435,000 list price, your monthly mortgage will cost you 40% of your take-home pay.
"Affordability is too stretched, despite the near-stagnation in home prices for the last three years, for the rise in mortgage rates to leave no mark," said Pantheon Chief U.S. Economist Samuel Tombs in a research note.
Economists say many families -- especially first-time buyers -- are waiting on the sidelines to buy, while other families who locked in low mortgage rates are reluctant to move. The latest ABC News-Washington Post-Ipsos poll found half of adults say their mortgage or rent is unaffordable.
The West posted the largest drop in pending home sales, followed by the South, Midwest and Northeast. NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun attributed the decline to rapidly rising mortgage rates and said higher energy prices are adding to uncertainty.
A separate report released this morning by the Commerce Department's Census Bureau showed homebuilding also slowing sharply. Housing starts -- a measure of how many new homes builders begin constructing -- fell 5.2% in September from August and 7.4% from a year earlier, to an annualized rate of 1.221 million units.

articles.full_text:
The Pound to US Dollar (GBP/USD) exchange rate gained ground on Wednesday after stronger-than-expected UK inflation figures reinforced expectations of further Bank of England (BoE) interest rate increases.
At the time of writing, GBP/USD was trading at approximately $1.3394, edging higher during the session and approaching the $1.3400 level.
Sterling found support after the latest UK consumer price index (CPI) revealed that inflation accelerated more sharply than economists had anticipated in September.
Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed annual headline inflation climbing from 3.1% to 3.5%, exceeding forecasts for an increase to 3.4%.
The reading marked the highest inflation rate in almost a year, with higher energy tariffs contributing significantly to the acceleration.
Core inflation also increased, suggesting that price pressures were not confined to energy costs.
The figures strengthened expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates at its November meeting, while encouraging speculation that further tightening could follow during the coming months.

Combined with Tuesday's unexpectedly strong employment figures, the inflation report has reinforced the argument that policymakers may need to maintain a more restrictive stance to bring price growth under control.
However, Sterling's advance was restrained by renewed concerns over the UK's public finances.
Government borrowing exceeded expectations in September, adding to the challenges facing Chancellor John Healey ahead of next week's Autumn Budget.
Higher debt-servicing costs and persistent inflation could further restrict the Treasury's fiscal headroom, leaving investors cautious about the sustainability of Sterling's recent recovery.
The US Dollar (USD), meanwhile, remained under pressure as continued weakness in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks unsettled investors and reinforced doubts about further Federal Reserve monetary tightening.
Concerns have grown over whether the substantial investment being directed towards AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns.
Investors are also increasingly questioning the financial resilience of companies involved in the sector's rapid expansion, particularly those relying heavily on borrowed capital.
The possibility that financial difficulties could spread beyond technology companies has added to concerns about the wider US economic outlook.
Against this backdrop, expectations for another Federal Reserve interest rate increase have weakened considerably.
Markets now broadly anticipate that policymakers will leave borrowing costs unchanged at next week's meeting, reducing support for the Dollar.
Near-Term GBP/USD Forecast: UK Retail Sales and PMIs Could Test $1.34
The Pound to US Dollar exchange rate is approaching the important $1.3400 level, but further gains may depend on whether upcoming UK economic releases reinforce the recent improvement in Sterling sentiment.
Attention will turn to September's retail sales figures and October's preliminary purchasing managers' index (PMI) surveys.
Economists expect consumer spending to have softened, while growth across the UK's dominant services sector is also forecast to have slowed.
Disappointing readings could raise concerns that higher borrowing costs and persistent inflation are beginning to weigh more heavily on economic activity.
Such an outcome could temper expectations for further Bank of England tightening and make it harder for GBP/USD to establish a sustained move above $1.3400.
Conversely, stronger-than-expected figures would provide further evidence of UK economic resilience and could allow Sterling to extend its recovery.
For the US Dollar, Thursday's initial jobless claims figures will provide another indication of labour-market conditions.
A larger-than-expected increase in unemployment benefit applications could reinforce expectations that the Federal Reserve will remain on hold, potentially weakening the Dollar further.
A sustained break above $1.3400 would strengthen the near-term outlook for Sterling, while renewed selling pressure could see GBP/USD retreat towards the $1.3350 area.

articles.title: ‘Indonesia fears no one!’ Prabowo blasts ‘bully’ MSCI over downgrade threat, record stock market rout - Bilyonaryo Business
articles.summary: ‘Indonesia fears no one!’ Prabowo blasts ‘bully’ MSCI over downgrade threat, record stock market rout  Bilyonaryo Business
articles.full_text:
By Reuters
Reuters – Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has accused global stock index provider MSCI of trying to intimidate his country after its threat to downgrade Indonesia’s stock market triggered a record two-day selloff and raised fears of massive foreign capital flight.
“The MSCI…intended to intimidate us,” Prabowo told his Cabinet on Wednesday, October 21, in remarks broadcast on the Indonesian government’s official YouTube channel.
“I simply say to the MSCI: the Indonesian nation fears no one and will not be cowed,” he declared.
“We possess strength, we have courage, we are willing to make sacrifices, and we refuse to surrender.”
Prabowo’s defiant response came after MSCI warned that Indonesia could be downgraded to standalone market status, a classification that could significantly reduce its exposure to international investment funds tracking major emerging-market stock indexes.
MSCI, whose indexes are widely followed by global fund managers, raised concerns that Indonesian authorities had not done enough to curb coordinated stock trading practices.
The warning sparked a record two-day rout in Indonesian equities, putting additional pressure on Southeast Asia’s largest economy, valued at approximately $1.5 trillion.
For Filipino investors, the controversy highlights the influence of international index providers over emerging stock markets, including the Philippines.
MSCI classifications matter because major investment funds use its indexes to determine where to allocate money. A downgrade can prompt funds tracking those indexes to reduce their holdings, potentially triggering foreign selling and putting pressure on share prices.
Indonesia’s dispute with MSCI has also fueled accusations of foreign interference.
Former Indonesian trade minister M. Lutfi alleged that Singapore’s sovereign wealth funds Temasek and GIC were involved in pressuring MSCI to issue the downgrade warning.
Both Singapore investment institutions rejected the allegations. A Temasek official described Lutfi’s claims as “patently untrue,” while GIC also denied the accusation, according to DealStreetAsia.
MSCI defended its procedures, saying its decisions are based on transparent, established rules rather than political pressure.
“MSCI will continue to monitor developments in the Indonesian market and engage with market participants and authorities,” the index provider said in an emailed response to Reuters.
Senior Indonesian economic minister Airlangga Hartarto also questioned why MSCI had not raised the possibility of a downgrade during meetings with Indonesian officials in Bangkok just days before its announcement.
Other lawmakers called for closer scrutiny of MSCI’s assessments while acknowledging the need to address weaknesses in Indonesia’s stock market.
“We should not be defensive in the face of criticism, but neither should we accept judgements without examining their basis and objectivity,” said Hanif Dhakiri, a lawmaker from the National Awakening Party.
Opposition legislator Said Abdullah was more pointed.
“MSCI’s executives are not prophets delivering divine revelations, like apostles writing sacred texts, who can claim a monopoly on flawless truth,” he said.
Prabowo, a former special forces commander who became president in 2024, has frequently invoked Indonesian sovereignty in responding to perceived foreign pressure.
His latest confrontation with MSCI comes as Jakarta faces the challenge of reassuring international investors while defending the credibility of its financial markets.—Reuters

articles.title: AI boom ‘overhyped’ as copper demand driver: LME Week - Fastmarkets
articles.summary: AI boom ‘overhyped’ as copper demand driver: LME Week  Fastmarkets
articles.full_text:
Copper prices have been driven by US policy and constrained supply rather than by demand, panellists said at the “Unlocking new supply: is the answer higher prices or more capital?” session of Bloomberg’s “2026 Base Metals: Tonnes, Tariffs and Terawatts” event.
The panel included Alice Fox, commodities strategist for base metals at Macquarie, Gregory Shearer, head of base and precious metals strategy at JPMorgan, and Nicholas Snowdon, head of metals and mining research at Mercuria. It was moderated by Kwasi Ampofo, metals and mining specialist at BloombergNEF.
“We’re not at current price levels in base metals because of demand conditions,” Snowdon said.
He said copper was at $14,500 per tonne because of US policy, while aluminium and zinc prices had been supported by supply “going backwards” for long periods this year.
The London Metal Exchange three-month copper price closed at $14,420.50 per tonne at 5pm on Tuesday October 20, up by 0.57% from Monday’s 5pm close.
“In today’s commodity market environment, aggregate metal demand conditions are quite modest in terms of growth rate,” Snowdon added.
AI not as metals-intensive
Snowdon described the AI capital expenditure cycle as “immense”, comparable in investment terms to another US or China. He said it had boosted global industrial production and manufacturing purchasing managers’ indices (PMIs), but metals demand had underperformed its traditional relationship with those indicators.
“AI is not as metals-intensive as the headline capex numbers suggest,” he said. “That’s not to say it doesn’t provide metals demand, but [warehouses and chips are] the main area where the capital’s been spent. It’s not on copper.”
Fox said she thought the AI boom was “overhyped”.
“Personally, I think it’s overhyped, just in terms of the sheer scale of it,” she said, citing the equipment, power and capital required.
She added that US investment in data centres was “really small” in the grand scheme of things. It was, however, one of the few areas still growing compared with the rest of the construction sector.
Shearer did not expect data centres to transform the copper balance. “We actually don’t think that AI data centres are this game changer for copper that’s going to send us into a million-tonne deficit,” he said. “But policies… are being made on a premise that whoever wins this race in AI controls the next 30 years geopolitically – and at the moment, copper is tied into that race.”
Snowdon said AI and data centres, along with the grid, remained clearly positive parts of the demand picture. He described them as long-cycle capital investments. He added that AI would provide “a very significant uplift in US copper demand over the course of the next three to five years”.
Cyclical demand subdued
Snowdon said the parts of demand tied to cyclical factors were under pressure. These included household-linked sectors in China and Europe such as construction, housing and autos.
He said a recovery in those sectors would probably need interest rates to ease, which in turn would likely require a lower oil price.
Shearer said copper demand had been resilient despite double-digit declines in Chinese construction demand for the metal. He said growth sectors such as battery energy storage systems (BESS), solar, wind and grid upgrades were helping to insulate copper from cyclical downturns.
200,000 tonnes of copper demand lost to substitution in China
Snowdon said around 200,000 tonnes of copper demand had been lost to substitution in China this year, but added that high aluminium prices had limited further switching.
“The bigger picture is less about substitution and thrifting,” he said. “It’s more about the subdued nature of cyclical demand sectors.”
A source at an Indian smelter told Fastmarkets on Monday that aluminium was already replacing copper in air conditioners, but that this would not significantly change the market because copper could not be entirely replaced.
Copper was trading at nearly five times the price of aluminium on Tuesday, with LME three-month aluminium closing at $3,002.50 per tonne.
US stockpile estimated at 1.6 million tonnes
Fox estimated that there were about 1.6 million tonnes of copper in the US, worth about $23 billion at current prices, and said it was owned by traders.
Fox added that the copper held in the US was currently free to leave the country, but that could change because export restrictions on domestically produced copper could come into force next year.
US exchange stocks were out of proportion to the country’s consumption. Comex stocks accounted for 69% of world exchange stocks, in a country that consumed about 6% of the world’s copper, Fastmarkets principal analyst Andy Cole said. By contrast, Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE) stocks accounted for 4% of world exchange stocks, in a country that consumed about 60% of the world’s copper, he added.
SHFE copper stocks ended September below 40,000 tonnes, while LME stocks outside the US were about 120,000 tonnes, Cole noted.
If the US increased the tariff, Fox said, prices “will just go up and up” because the market outside the US would become very tight. That would cause problems for demand and inflation more generally.
The US has imposed a 50% tariff on semi-finished copper products since August 1, 2025, but refined copper remains exempt. A presidential proclamation dated July 30, 2025 outlined a phased duty on refined copper of 15% from January 1, 2027, rising to 30% from January 1, 2028.
The US Department of Commerce was due to give the president an updated report on the US copper market by June 30, 2026. That deadline passed without a public decision, and no refined copper tariff had been announced as of early October.
Three-month copper on the LME hit an intraday all-time high of $14,875 per tonne on September 10, 2026, as metal flowed into US warehouses ahead of a possible refined copper tariff.
Snowdon said the US now had about two years of inventory cover. He described the influence of US tariff risk on the market as “one of the greatest feats of policy support for a price in commodity market history”.
He said the only way for the US to protect its inventory while keeping imports coming was to announce an escalation in the tariff rate from 2027 to 2028. Anything else, he said, would put the stockpile at risk and put import volumes under “immense pressure”.
He said he would be bullish on copper if the US adopted the “15/30” tariff outcome, referring to the phased duty outlined in the 2025 proclamation.
Shearer said the US stockpile reflected supply security concerns rather than end-use demand.
“I can’t stand here and say I know what the end game or the ultimate destination of this 1.6 million tonnes is,” he said. “In that environment, what I think you do is buy time to figure that out.”
Who smelts the concentrate?
Shearer said US supply chain security was not only about where mines were built. If a new US mine produced concentrate rather than solvent extraction-electrowinning (SX-EW) cathode, he asked, “who’s going to smelt that?” He said there was strong local community resistance to smelting operations.
He contrasted Chinese-built smelters in Indonesia, which he said could ramp up in under nine months, with the US “going in circles” over projects at home.
Fastmarkets’ copper concentrates TC implied smelters purchase, cif Asia Pacific, was calculated at $(242.00) per tonne on October 16, down by $4.05 per tonne from $(237.95) per tonne on October 9.
Fastmarkets’ copper concentrates TC implied traders purchase, cif Asia Pacific, was calculated at $(314.00) per tonne on October 16, down by $7.55 per tonne from $(306.45) per tonne on October 9.
Snowdon said it took 16 years on average to bring a copper deposit from discovery into production. That made greenfield mines a harder sell for capital than a smelter or an SX-EW plant in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which could produce within a year.

articles.title: ECB Finds Euro Zone Oil Dependence Halved as AI and Fiscal Spending Support Growth - ESG News
articles.summary: ECB Finds Euro Zone Oil Dependence Halved as AI and Fiscal Spending Support Growth  ESG News
articles.full_text:
- Lower oil exposure: The euro zone economy is about half as reliant on oil as in the early 1990s, ECB economists estimate.
- Stronger fiscal support: Fiscal stimulus reached 0.5% of GDP, twice the level expected at the end of last year.
- Temporary growth drivers: ECB economists warn that AI investment, global demand and government spending may fade.
The euro zone economy has proved more resilient to this year’s energy shock than expected, according to European Central Bank (ECB) economists. Lower fossil fuel dependence, artificial intelligence investment and stronger government spending have helped sustain growth despite higher oil and gas prices.
Energy Dependence and Economic Resilience
ECB economists Oscar Arce, Gerrit Koester and Beatrice Pierluigi published the assessment in an ECB blog on Wednesday. They estimated that the euro area now relies on oil about half as much as in the early 1990s. This reduction has limited the economic impact of rising energy prices.
The Iran war disrupted energy markets, pushing oil and gas prices higher and renewing inflation concerns. However, the currency bloc has continued expanding, with business surveys showing that economic activity remains positive. Higher renewable and nuclear electricity generation has also weakened the connection between gas prices and electricity costs in several countries.
AI Investment and Fiscal Support
The ECB economists identified AI-related trade as an “important tailwind” for the euro area. Technology-related export orders and sectors linked to AI have outperformed, supporting economic activity during the energy shock.
Government spending has also exceeded earlier expectations. The fiscal impulse reached 0.5% of gross domestic product, twice the level projected at the end of last year. German government spending on defence and infrastructure accounted for much of the additional support.
However, the economists cautioned that several growth drivers could prove temporary. Global demand, fiscal stimulus and AI investment may weaken, particularly if geopolitical tensions intensify or energy markets face further disruption.
Monetary Policy Implications
The findings arrive as the ECB considers further interest rate increases to contain energy-driven inflation. A third rate increase this year is expected in December, following renewed inflation pressures and a global bond selloff.
The ECB assessment identifies reduced oil exposure as a structural source of resilience, alongside shorter-term support from investment and fiscal policy. However, its economists warn that fresh energy disruptions could leave the euro area vulnerable if those temporary sources of growth weaken.
RELATED ARTICLE: ECB Publishes Climate-Related Disclosures Showing Decarbonization Path
Who It Affects
- Euro zone businesses: Lower oil dependence and stronger electricity generation diversity have reduced exposure to energy price shocks in several countries.
- Technology exporters: AI-related investment and trade have supported stronger export orders and activity in AI-linked sectors.
- European policymakers: Energy-led inflation and the possibility of fading fiscal support complicate decisions on further interest rate increases.

articles.title: Bank of England set to overshadow Healey’s Budget with interest rate hike - City AM
articles.summary: Bank of England set to overshadow Healey’s Budget with interest rate hike  City AM
articles.full_text:
The Bank of England is expected to overshadow John Healey’s maiden Budget with a “done deal” interest rate hike aiming to tame soaring inflation while risking economic growth.
Top City economists predict the central bank’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) will raise the base rate at its November meeting, just one week after the Autumn Budget.
The Bank has left rates unchanged at 3.75 per cent since its last 25 basis point cut at the end of 2025. But hawks on the committee have called for rates to increase in response to the energy crisis triggered by the ongoing US-Iran conflict.
Following a blowout inflation print on Wednesday, all barriers to a rate hike are expected to be removed.
Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM, said the inflation news, coming after stronger economic growth and a lower unemployment rate, “almost guarantees an interest rate hike next month”.
“With inflation likely to significantly exceed four per cent in the new year, a second rate hike looks likely in 2027,” he added.
Increased fuel prices drove September’s inflation spike, with diesel costs hitting their highest since July 2022. While the US-Iran war, which is stretching into its eighth month, has triggered a sharp rise in oil prices following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial shipping route.
Cathal Kennedy, senior UK economist at RBC, said there was “limited evidence of broader inflationary pressures” outside of fuel pressures. But added this was “unlikely to stand in the way of the MPC raising rates”.
The Bank voted in a 6-3 split in favour of holding rates in September, with Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill the three dissenters.
Healey to contend with interest rates restricting growth
A rate hike would deal a major blow to Chancellor John Healey as he seeks to put the economy on a stable footing in the Budget.
“If the Chancellor didn’t have enough on his plate ahead of the budget, now he will likely have to contend with higher interest rates further constricting economic growth,” George Lagarias, chief economist at Forvis Mazars, said.
Any limits on growth would follow a better-than-expected period for UK GDP. In August, the economy grew 0.1 per cent, despite expectations of a contraction. The International Monetary Fund upgraded its growth forecast for the UK in 2026 to 1.3 per cent, from one per cent.
But it warned growth would slow to 1.2 per cent next year as long-term interest rates hit households as prices rise. The inflation spike is a major setback for Healey, due to it stemming from imported energy, which will raise household bills and state benefit costs without giving the same boost to domestic wages and tax revenues that home-grown inflation would.
Schroders’ head of global economics David Rees said the UK economy faced a “perfect storm of imported inflation pressures”.
He added the latest figures around growth and unemployment “means a November rate hike now looks like a done deal.”
In a speech in September, Healey said fiscal credibility was “indivisible from growth” and promised his central purpose as Chancellor would be to change Britain’s “weak” growth trajectory.
“With a week to go until John Healey’s eagerly anticipated first Budget, inflation figures provide a stark reminder of the UK’s difficult economic position,” Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, said.
“Economic growth has remained resilient to date this year, but should rates rise, these are likely to bite in 2027 and hold the economy back as the Bank continues its inflationary battle.”
Responding to the inflation surge, Healey said: “We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide.”
He said he would use the Budget to maintain “fiscal discipline and drive for growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space.”

articles.title: JAMIE MCGEEVER | Fed sneezes, but emerging markets haven’t caught a cold yet - Business Day
articles.summary: JAMIE MCGEEVER | Fed sneezes, but emerging markets haven’t caught a cold yet  Business Day
articles.full_text:
Emerging markets have developed stronger immune systems. US debt dynamics are deteriorating, and the Federal Reserve has started hiking interest rates, yet emerging markets appear under no pressure to follow suit. The US has sneezed, but they aren’t catching the proverbial cold.
Historically, when the Fed starts tightening policy, emerging economies are forced to hike as well, even if their domestic economies aren’t strong enough to warrant it, due to currency concerns and debt dynamics. This has given rise to another market cliche: the Fed is the central banker to the world.
But surprisingly resilient economic growth across emerging economies this year, sturdier fiscal fundamentals, and relatively high interest rates and bond yields are giving central banks of emerging markets a degree of flexibility. That could allow them to start cutting rates in the next year or, at the very least, enable them not to follow the Fed in lockstep as it tightens.
Credibility restored
Emerging markets — like their developed peers — are beset by a host of risks stemming from geopolitical strife, trade frictions, the energy price shock, and AI bubble fears. But even though some emerging market countries are particularly vulnerable, either to persistently high energy prices or a sudden, disorderly unwind of the AI trade, the threat of rapidly tightening monetary policy is mostly absent.
This is largely because policy rates are already elevated across many emerging markets. The weighted average 10-year emerging bond yield at the end of September was around its highest point in five years at nearly 6.45%, according to State Street, the US-based financial services group. Average inflation-adjusted emerging market yields, meanwhile, are also historically high, close to 3%.
Lofty policy rates have helped restore the credibility of emerging market central banks, support exchange rates, and create a real rate buffer. Bank of America strategists say emerging market rates at the front end of the curve have “materially” overshot to such an extent that implied policy rates next year will be in restrictive territory in all major emerging economies except China.
“Widespread tightening seems unlikely,” State Street strategists wrote earlier this month.
While emerging markets look surprisingly calm, robust, and attractive — Indonesia being a notable exception, though — the same cannot be said of their developed-market peers.
While many emerging countries appear to be strengthening their economic fundamentals, investors’ concern about the fiscal trajectory in the US, Japan, much of the eurozone, and the UK has sent yields across the industrialised world to the highest in decades.
Positioned accordingly
Investors are positioning accordingly. A JPMorgan survey of investors at the IMF/World Bank meetings in Bangkok last week showed that 33% favour emerging market stocks, compared with 26% who prefer developed market equities.
Bank of America’s (BofA) latest fund manager survey shows that a net 34% of those polled are overweight in emerging market stocks, down slightly from 38% in September, but hardly bearish.
Could investors be too optimistic about emerging markets? Perhaps. The long emerging markets equities position is one of the most crowded trades in BofA’s survey, suggesting there is still plenty of room for it to be trimmed further.
Of course, emerging market bond yields are higher because debt there is still a riskier proposition than developed market offerings, especially traditionally “risk-free” US treasuries. But it is notable that realised volatility in emerging market bonds has been lower than that of Treasuries for a few years, according to iShares benchmark emerging market bond and treasuries exchange traded funds.
To be sure, emerging economies’ debt burden is rising, narrowing the gap with highly indebted advanced economies. But the average emerging market debt-to-GDP ratio still appears manageable. The IMF projects an overall emerging market debt-to-GDP ratio this year of 77.2%, rising to 86.2% in five years, compared with forecasts for advanced economies of 108.2% this year, rising to 114.8%.
While the debt-to-GDP risk threshold in emerging market countries is lower because these economies are typically less resilient, few alarm bells are being rung. Indeed, the rise in emerging market debt has been quite gradual, suggesting policymakers are determined to keep it under control.
Idiosyncrasies
Rising Fed rates and US market turbulence will always affect emerging market economies, especially those carrying more dollar-denominated debt. And there will always be idiosyncratic emerging market distress stories, as is the case now in Indonesia. But events like this typically bear little relation to the broader emerging market narrative. Removing Indonesia could actually make emerging market equity indices more attractive to investors.
It’s also important to remember that the emerging market universe is wide, and the differences between economies are vast. Policymakers in some emerging market countries where core inflation is relatively low and expectations are anchored, like Brazil and Mexico, are cutting rates, and some, like South Africa and South Korea, are raising them to offset currency weakness or inflation. Others may prefer to keep their options open.
But the Fed doesn’t appear to be calling the EM tune like it used to, and if the record attendance at Barclays’ emerging markets conference in Bangkok last week is any guide, that’s music to investors’ ears.

articles.title: Euro-to-Dollar Forecast: ECB Rate Upgrade Tests EUR/USD Recovery - Exchange Rates UK
articles.summary: Euro-to-Dollar Forecast: ECB Rate Upgrade Tests EUR/USD Recovery  Exchange Rates UK
articles.full_text:
The Euro-Dollar Rate Edges Higher as Crédit Agricole Raises Its ECB Rate Forecast
The Euro is recovering against the US Dollar, but Crédit Agricole's higher ECB rate forecast still leaves it cautious about market tightening bets.
The Euro-to-Dollar exchange rate recovered to $1.1230 on Tuesday morning, up 0.15% from Monday's close.
Crédit Agricole has raised its forecast for the European Central Bank's peak deposit rate to 3% in March 2027, adding another increase to its previous outlook.
Yet its new forecast remains below the eventual peak markets were pricing when the bank made the revision.
UBS separately expects EUR/USD to recover to $1.16 by end-2026 and $1.20 by June 2027, provided European risks become less damaging than investors fear.
The latest French unrest is an immediate test of that confidence.
More ECB tightening, but less than markets expect
Crédit Agricole's Louis Harreau expects quarter-point increases in December and March, with an October rise still possible but unlikely.
Higher oil and gas prices have pushed the bank's inflation forecasts upwards, leaving underlying price growth uncomfortably high through next year.
Harreau writes: "In our view, our new inflation forecasts warrant deposit rate hikes until 3.0%. But as things stand currently, we see no reason for the ECB to hike to 3.25%."
"Of course, if gas prices continue increasing, then our core inflation forecasts would change and accordingly our ECB scenario."
The bank expects core inflation to peak in the first quarter of 2027 before easing, weakening the case for extending the hiking cycle beyond March.
Harreau writes: "Until March 2027, we are more or less aligned with the current market pricing (as we have upwardly revised our call and the market has de-priced some hawkishness)."
"Beyond March 2027, markets expect one more hike-by around July 2027. Again, we see this pricing as too high, but 3.25% is still within the limits of what is possible."
Harreau also identifies a larger disagreement further ahead, with markets not pricing the eventual cuts Crédit Agricole expects as inflation declines.
An upward revision to one bank's forecast therefore need not lift the Euro if investors are already assuming a stronger tightening cycle.
The ECB itself remains cautious about how widely expensive energy is spreading through the economy.
In her latest statement to the IMF's policy committee, Christine Lagarde said wage growth had shown no material response to the energy shock and that underlying inflation measures remained broadly stable in September.
She also noted that financing conditions had tightened as long-term interest rates rose.
French bond stress complicates the recovery
That tightening can occur without another ECB decision.
Investors demanding a higher premium to lend to France can also raise funding costs for private borrowers, restraining activity and reducing the amount of additional monetary tightening required.
Crédit Agricole warns that either a sovereign crisis or the fiscal retrenchment needed to repair France's finances would hurt growth.
On Monday, French bonds sold off following weekend riots, with MarketWatch reporting that the 10-year yield rose nearly six basis points to 4.845% early in trading as investors questioned the government's ability to reduce its deficit.
UBS's recovery forecast, published before that unrest, depends partly on a budget agreement restoring confidence.
Its strategists Constantin Bolz and Clémence Dumoncel write: "Although the fiscal situation in France remains challenging and is unlikely to improve materially in the near term, we do not expect a broader European debt crisis."
"Instead, we believe some form of budget agreement is likely to be passed, potentially through the use of Article 49.3."
The bank expects an agreement to narrow France's borrowing premium over Germany and help the Euro recover.
A budget agreement could give the recovery more lasting support than the oversold conditions Scotiabank identified near $1.11.
UBS's longer-term currency forecast also relies on relief from Europe's energy bill.
The UBS strategists write: "With the situation in the Middle East unresolved and the Northern Hemisphere entering the winter season, it is difficult to envisage a significant near-term decline in energy prices. However, in our base case, we expect energy prices to moderate during 2027, particularly after the winter period with Brent oil prices approaching 80 USD/bbl next summer."
Oil and US yields could still pull the Euro lower
Standard Chartered's Steve Englander cautions against treating the Euro's difficulties as exclusively French.
His analysis links the recent decline to higher US yields relative to Germany, widening borrowing premiums within the Eurozone and rising oil prices, while acknowledging that their separate effects are difficult to isolate.
Those risks are related: stronger US growth can lift Treasury yields while increasing concern about Europe's capacity to cope with higher borrowing costs.
Englander writes: "Alternatively, if the driver of higher yields is higher oil prices, all three EUR negatives could be pushing in the same direction simultaneously, as has been the case over the last seven weeks."
"Even having two of three factors pushing in the same direction is likely to be enough to put some downward pressure on the EUR. So while the market may pause to absorb recent moves, we could easily see a resumption of EUR depreciation down the road."
EUR/USD Exchange Rate FAQ
What is UBS's EUR/USD exchange rate forecast?
UBS expects $1.16 by end-2026 and $1.20 by June 2027. Its recovery case includes lower energy prices and reduced French political uncertainty.
Does Crédit Agricole expect more ECB rate rises?
Yes. It forecasts quarter-point increases in December and March, taking the deposit rate to 3% in March 2027. That is an interest-rate projection, not an exchange-rate target.
Why might higher European rates fail to lift the Euro?
Some tightening is already priced in. Expensive energy and widening government borrowing premiums can also weaken growth and confidence in European assets.
