articles.title: USD/JPY Price Forecast — USD/JPY (158.18) Capped Below 159 as Tokyo Guards 160 — BoJ Holds Oct 30, December Hike Decides 155 - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: USD/JPY Price Forecast — USD/JPY (158.18) Capped Below 159 as Tokyo Guards 160 — BoJ Holds Oct 30, December Hike Decides 155  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- USD/JPY trades at 158.18, inside an October range of 156.95 to 158.95.
- The BoJ holds its policy rate at 1.25%, with swaps pricing an 80% chance of a hike by December.
- Japan spent ¥11.7 trillion on yen intervention and joined the U.S. in a coordinated operation in July.
USD/JPY traded at 158.18 on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, slightly lower on the session after the dollar touched 158.35 in Asian trading. The pair opened near 158.29 to 158.35, held a tight early range of 158.27 to 158.39, and eased through the European and U.S. sessions as Treasury yields and oil reversed part of their morning gains. Tuesday’s session ran from 157.82 to 158.61 before closing at 158.29, and Monday’s ran from 157.70 to 158.56 with a close at 158.50.
The defining feature of USD/JPY this month is how little it has moved. Over the past 30 days, the pair has traded between 156.82 and 158.85, averaging 157.89. October’s daily closes have stayed between 157.86 and 158.64. The October intraday range runs from 156.95 on October 2 to 158.95 on October 14, the day hot U.S. inflation data pushed the yen to its weakest level of the month. A 200-pip range across a month of Iran war headlines, oil above $100, a hawkish Fed and an AI-stock selloff is an unusually quiet market.
That quiet reflects a standoff. The interest rate gap between the U.S. and Japan, with the Fed’s upper bound at 4.00% and the Bank of Japan’s policy rate at 1.25%, pulls the dollar higher against the yen. Tokyo’s demonstrated willingness to intervene, including a coordinated yen-buying operation with the U.S. Treasury at the end of July, caps the pair below 160. Both central banks are priced to hike in December, which keeps the rate gap stable and removes the main source of directional pressure.
This forecast runs on a single thesis. USD/JPY is trapped between a carry trade that favors the dollar and an intervention line at 160 that Tokyo and Washington have jointly defended, and neither force can break the other before the Fed decides on October 28 and the BoJ decides on October 30. The pair is likely to hold between 156.80 and 159.00 into those meetings. A Fed that signals December as its final hike while the BoJ confirms a December move would narrow the policy gap and send USD/JPY toward 155.50. A Fed that leaves hikes open into 2027 would push the pair toward 160, where intervention risk becomes acute.
Over longer horizons, the yen has weakened. It is down 0.44% over the past month and 4.01% over the past 12 months against the dollar. The 2026 low for the yen sits near 164 per dollar, which means the yen is 3.7% stronger now than at its weakest point of the year. Over the past 90 days, USD/JPY has ranged from 153.54 to 163.87.
The Intervention Line: 160 in Neon
Japan’s currency authorities have made 160 the line the market respects. The yen weakened past 160 per dollar in late March and early April, then again at the end of April, when it hit 160.72. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama issued what was described as a final warning on April 30, saying the time for bold steps was nearing, a phrase Japanese officials use for intervention. Suspected intervention followed, and the yen firmed to 159.23 that day.
Tokyo then intervened on a record scale. Japan spent 11.7 trillion yen, equal to $73.14 billion, supporting its currency in the round that began in late April, the largest monthly intervention ever recorded. Yen-buying intervention requires selling foreign assets, and Japan held about $1 trillion in reserves at the end of April. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi echoed Katayama’s warnings that authorities stood ready to respond.
The decisive escalation came at the end of July. Japan’s Ministry of Finance conducted a coordinated yen-buying intervention with the U.S. Treasury, the first U.S. participation in yen intervention in years. The ministry said the operation was carried out under a September 2025 joint statement by the two countries’ finance ministers to address excessive volatility and disorderly yen movements. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed the action and said the U.S. would not hesitate to participate in further joint intervention. Japan also said it would use the Federal Reserve’s foreign repo facility in the future.
U.S. participation changed the calculation. It signaled that Washington views yen weakness as a broader financial stability issue, not a purely Japanese problem. President Donald Trump has also expressed concern about yen undervaluation. Katayama said in interviews earlier this month that USD/JPY levels above 160 ahead of the July intervention represented an extremely weak yen, which markets read as a signal that authorities would not tolerate a sustained move above that level.
Katayama renewed her warnings on October 15, after the yen touched its weakest level of the month following hotter U.S. inflation data. She said she was prepared to act in the currency market again if needed and that there had been no change in the stance of Washington and Tokyo since the July joint intervention.
The result is a ceiling the market treats as near-certain. Intervention odds rise as 160 approaches and climb substantially higher if 162 trades. At 158.18, the pair sits 1.15% below 160. Traders who buy dollars near 159 face the risk of a sudden 3 to 5 yen drop on intervention, which limits how many are willing to push the pair higher.
Bank of Japan: 1.25% After Hikes in June and September
The Bank of Japan has accelerated its tightening cycle in 2026. It raised its policy rate by 25 basis points in June and again on September 18, taking the overnight call rate target to 1.25%. That pace, two hikes in four months, marks a sharp change from a campaign that started with just one rate rise a year.
The next meeting runs October 29 to 30, with the decision released at 12:00 p.m. Japan time on October 30, which is 11:00 p.m. ET on October 29. The meeting comes with an updated Quarterly Outlook Report. Sources familiar with the BoJ’s thinking indicated the central bank will leave rates steady in October and raise its inflation forecast. BoJ officials are leaning against a rare back-to-back hike, seeing little need for consecutive increases without signs that upside inflation risks are increasing abruptly. The final decision could still change until the last minute.
December is the expected next move. In a survey of 78 economists conducted October 13 to 19, 54, or nearly 70%, expected the BoJ to raise its policy rate to 1.50% this quarter, almost double the share in the previous survey. Of the 54 who specified a month, 80% chose December, while only 2% chose the October meeting. Overnight swaps imply an 80% chance of a hike by December. A former BoJ executive director said he expects the next hike in December followed by another in March or April, describing the current pace of roughly one hike every three months as appropriate.
The path into 2027 points higher. Thirty-nine of 65 economists, or 60%, expect the policy rate to reach 1.75% by the end of June 2027. Some forecasts see the BoJ raising the rate to 2% during 2027.
Political tension surrounds the BoJ’s path. Prime Minister Takaichi’s administration has pursued large spending and tax-cut plans, and dissent on the BoJ’s Policy Board has been read as a sign that rate hikes could face opposition from the government. That dissent briefly pushed the yen lower. Nearly three-quarters of economists surveyed said further dissenting votes when the board next raises rates could weigh on the yen. Katayama said she sees no conflict between BoJ and government policy and is largely aligned with Governor Kazuo Ueda.
For USD/JPY, the BoJ’s October hold is priced. The quarterly outlook’s inflation forecast and Ueda’s guidance on December will matter more than the decision itself. A clear signal that December is likely would support the yen. Hesitation would weaken it.
The Rate Gap: 275 Basis Points to the Fed’s Upper Bound
The interest rate differential is the force pushing USD/JPY higher. The Federal Reserve’s funds rate stands at 3.75% to 4.00% after a September hike, and the BoJ’s policy rate stands at 1.25%. The gap to the Fed’s upper bound is 275 basis points. That spread rewards investors who borrow in yen at low rates and invest in dollar assets at higher ones, the classic carry trade, and it creates steady demand for dollars against the yen.
Both central banks are expected to move in December. Futures price an 89% to 94% chance of a Fed hike in December and a 16% chance in October. Swaps price an 80% chance of a BoJ hike by December. If both hike by 25 basis points, the gap stays at 275 basis points through year-end. That parallel path explains why USD/JPY has barely moved: neither side is expected to change the relative return on holding dollars versus yen.
The timing creates a small window. The Fed decides on October 28 and the BoJ on October 30, 48 hours apart. Both are expected to hold. In December, the Fed decides on December 8 to 9 and the BoJ on its December meeting date. Whichever bank moves first, and whichever signals more to come, will shift the gap at the margin.
Bond yields reinforce the differential. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield sits at 5.12%. articles.summary: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 7,712, Nasdaq 26,424, Dow 52,495 — SPCX +9%, SMCI +12.7%  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- SpaceX SPCX rises 9.4% premarket after Q3 revenue jumps 161% to $14.58B against a $12.72B estimate.
- Super Micro SMCI gains 12.7% to $36.69 after guiding Q1 sales to $18.5B–$19.5B from $14.5B–$15.5B.
- Netflix NFLX falls 6% to $64.57 as Q4 revenue guidance of $13.442B misses the $13.517B consensus.
U.S. stock futures were higher at 8:13 a.m. ET on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, and the bid had a clear address. S&P 500 futures traded at 7,773.00, up 17.75 points or 0.23%. Dow futures sat at 52,801, up 82 points or 0.16%. Nasdaq 100 futures led at 29,860.25, up 185.00 points or 0.62%. Earlier in the session, at 6:07 a.m. ET, Dow futures had actually been down 66 points while Nasdaq 100 futures were up only 87 points, so the tech skew grew as the morning went on rather than fading.
The setup reverses Tuesday’s leadership. Tuesday was a value, small-cap and health care session in which the Dow added 529.85 points and the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.02%. Wednesday morning hands the baton back to AI hardware, and the trigger came from two after-hours reports: SpaceX (SPCX) posted third-quarter revenue of $14.58 billion against a $12.72 billion consensus and its first profitable quarter as a public company, and Super Micro Computer (SMCI) preannounced September-quarter sales of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion against prior guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion.
Premarket, SpaceX traded up 9.4%, Super Micro rose 12.7% to $36.69, Dell gained 5.5%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise added 4.5%, Vertiv rose 5.1%, Intel climbed 2.3%, AMD added 1.8%, Nvidia gained between 1.5% and 2.1% depending on the print, and CoreWeave rose between 2.2% and 2.5%. Across 26 AI hardware names, premarket gains put back $274 billion of market value, or 17% of the $1.6 trillion those stocks lost during last week’s rout.
The losers list is concentrated in post-earnings disappointments. Netflix (NFLX) fell 6% to $64.57 after guiding fourth-quarter revenue to $13.442 billion against $13.517 billion expected. Intuitive Surgical (ISRG) dropped 7.5% to $405.00 despite a beat on both lines. Danaher slid 4.07% premarket and Thermo Fisher gave up between 0.9% and 2% after beating estimates. The health care sector ETF, which closed at a record on Tuesday, was down 0.47% premarket.
The thesis for the session is narrow and specific. The AI trade has two fresh data points showing spending is still flowing, but the tape is not going to award full credit until Meta Platforms reports after the 4:00 p.m. ET close and tells the market where its $130 billion to $145 billion 2026 capital budget is headed. Tesla reports in the same window. Everything between the 9:30 a.m. open and the 4:00 p.m. bell is positioning against those two prints, with a 10-year Treasury yield at 5.12% and Brent crude back at $109.64 limiting how far multiples can stretch.
Overseas markets gave a mixed backdrop. Korea’s Kospi rose 2.8% to 5,709 after dropping 3.73% on Tuesday on AI concerns, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 gained 1.15% to 64,813 on chip strength. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 0.4% to 23,768, the Shanghai Composite eased 0.3% to 3,724, and India’s Nifty 50 closed down 0.34% at 22,811.35. In Europe, Stoxx 50 futures were up 0.42% ahead of the cash open, with Germany’s DAX indicated 0.45% higher.
Tuesday’s Close: Dow Ripped 529.85 Points While the Nasdaq Stalled
The prior session ended with three indexes telling three different stories. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 529.85 points, or 1.02%, to close at 52,495.88. It opened at 51,959.21, traded a range of 51,910.92 to 52,689.81, and at its intraday low was down 55 points from the 51,966.00 prior close. The blue-chip index sits 4.1% below its 52-week high of 54,744.33, and 22 of its 30 components finished green.
The S&P 500 rose 21.84 points, or 0.28%, to 7,712.57. It opened at 7,679.01, below the 7,690.73 prior close, dipped as much as 0.3% to 7,668.03, then rallied to 7,748.42 before giving back part of the move into the bell. The benchmark is 1.7% below its 52-week high of 7,844.52, which was set earlier this month. Its 52-week low is 6,316.91.
The Nasdaq Composite finished at 26,424.82, down 0.02%. That flat close hides a wide session. The index was down more than 250 points at its low and up 171 points at its high, which means a 420-point round trip ended where it started. Apple fell 1.00% after a downgrade to hold, Meta Platforms lost 1.59% for a fifth straight decline, and Alphabet also closed lower. Nvidia slipped 0.29% to $216.47. Microsoft and Broadcom hovered near unchanged most of the day. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 0.29% to 11,283.81, giving back part of Monday’s rebound.
Volatility compressed. The CBOE Volatility Index dropped 6.1% to 17.31, its lowest reading in several sessions. Volume was light relative to the move in the Dow, with 15.91 billion shares changing hands across U.S. venues against a 20-session average of 17.15 billion. That 7% shortfall in volume is a detail worth holding onto when judging how much conviction sat behind the rotation.
Year to date, the Nasdaq Composite is up 3,182.83 points, or 13.7%, while the Russell 2000 is up 291.51 points, or 11.7%. The gap between the two has been narrowing during October, and Tuesday was the sharpest single-day example of that convergence this month.
Oil fell on Tuesday after spiking intraday. Brent touched $111.99, a five-month high, on tanker attacks, a mine strike near the Strait of Hormuz and claims of strikes on Saudi sites, then settled at $108.79 after Iran and Pakistan held mediation talks. West Texas Intermediate briefly topped $100 before falling to $95.65 on the expiring front month. The 10-year Treasury yield dropped 6 basis points to 5.08% at one point, and the dollar index touched 101.50, its lowest level since October 1. Lower yields and cheaper crude did the heavy lifting for every rate-sensitive group on the board.
The market’s three-way split matters for Wednesday because futures are now pricing the opposite leadership. If Nasdaq 100 futures hold a 0.62% gain into the open while Dow futures stay up only 0.16%, the session starts as a mirror image of Tuesday, and the question becomes whether the rotation money stays put or chases the AI rebound.
Breadth Was the Real Signal: Russell 2000 +1.65%, Equal Weight Beat the S&P by 87 Basis Points
The cleanest read on Tuesday comes from breadth, not from the S&P 500’s 0.28% headline. The Russell 2000 jumped 1.65% to 2,773.42, the best performance among the major indexes. The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP) gained 1.15%, outpacing the cap-weighted benchmark by 87 basis points. On the New York Stock Exchange, advancers beat decliners 1,614 to 559, a ratio of 2.9 to 1, and a sharp reversal from Monday’s tech-only rebound.
When the average stock beats the index by that margin, the megacaps are dragging. That is exactly what happened. Meta, Apple and Alphabet together erased tens of billions in market value, offsetting gains in Eli Lilly and Tesla among the ten largest U.S. companies. Remove that drag and the S&P 500 would have posted a gain closer to the equal-weight figure.
The rotation has been building for more than a week. The 25 best-performing Russell 1000 stocks of the first half of 2026 fell 19% on average last week, while last year’s laggards caught bids. That reversal in momentum lined up with a squeeze in the bond market and growing doubts about whether AI spending will earn a return. Tuesday extended the pattern, with the Dow and small caps carrying the tape.
Fund flows show how conflicted positioning is. The iShares Russell 2000 ETF (IWM) saw $1.1 billion of outflows on the day, then rallied 1.66%. The Invesco QQQ Trust took in $4.8 billion of inflows and slipped 0.10%. The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) lost $3.1 billion in outflows while rising 0.84%. Money moved into the Nasdaq vehicle and out of the small-cap and long-bond vehicles, and price did the reverse in all three cases. That kind of divergence usually reflects hedging and repositioning rather than fresh directional conviction.
There is a case that this breadth surge is more durable than a one-day squeeze. Earnings beats are spreading across sectors that are not tied to AI, including credit bureaus, toys, defense, industrials and pharmaceuticals. Lower oil and lower yields help those groups directly through input costs and discount rates. And with the Federal Reserve priced for a skip in October and a hike in December, the cost of capital is not falling fast enough to rescue long-duration tech multiples on its own.
The counterargument arrives in the premarket. If SpaceX and Super Micro have convinced the market that the AI spending cycle is intact, money that rotated into the Russell 2000 and equal-weight names can rotate right back. The tell at the open will be whether the Russell 2000 holds above 2,773 while the Nasdaq 100 rallies. A session where both lift is a broadening market. A session where small caps give back Tuesday’s 1.65% while chips rip is a return to narrow leadership, and narrow leadership into a Meta capex print is a fragile setup.
Health Care Hit a Record as Yields and Oil Backed Off
Health care led all 11 S&P 500 sectors on Tuesday with a 2.37% gain and closed at an all-time high. The Health Care Select Sector SPDR (XLV) finished at a record $179.86, up 2.26%, which pushed it into overbought territory on short-term momentum gauges. Eli Lilly reached a record high and moved past Berkshire Hathaway by market value. UnitedHealth, Merck, Johnson & Johnson and Amgen, all Dow components, rallied together, and Amgen, Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson and AbbVie each gained more than 2%. Moderna hit its highest level since 2022.

Details of News Corporation's October 20, 2026 ASX Buyback Disclosure
News Corporation, trading its Class A common stock on NASDAQ under the symbol NWSA and Class B common stock as NWS on the Nasdaq Global Select Market, filed an 8-K current report dated October 21, 2026, covering activities from October 20, 2026. The filing confirms the Company's obligation under ASX rules to provide daily disclosures of repurchase transactions to the Australian Securities Exchange. Attached to the filing are two exhibits, Exhibit 99.1 and Exhibit 99.2, containing the information submitted to the ASX on the respective dates noted.
The report reiterates that the Company’s Repurchase Program authorizes the buyback of up to $1 billion aggregate of its outstanding Class A and Class B common stock shares. Additionally, the Company regularly reports on the Repurchase Program in its quarterly and annual filings. The report is signed by Michael L. Bunder, Senior Vice President, Deputy General Counsel, and Corporate Secretary.
The filing also highlights that the ASX disclosures include "forward-looking statements" as defined by the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, encompassing statements about the Company’s intent to repurchase shares. It cautions that actual outcomes may differ materially due to factors such as fluctuations in stock price, market conditions, securities laws, and alternative investment opportunities.
Summary of Disclosed Information
In compliance with ASX requirements, News Corporation disclosed its daily stock repurchase data to the Australian Securities Exchange on October 20, 2026, and filed those disclosures with the SEC as Exhibit 99.1 and Exhibit 99.2 within an 8-K current report.

articles.title: Climate risks threatening economic growth, competitiveness, warns ECB - https://ippmedia.co.tz/
articles.summary: Climate risks threatening economic growth, competitiveness, warns ECB  https://ippmedia.co.tz/
articles.full_text:
Climate change and nature degradation are increasingly threatening economic growth, driving inflation and exposing financial institutions to greater risks, making investment in resilience essential for long-term competitiveness, a senior European Central Bank (ECB) official has warned.
Frank Elderson, a member of the ECB’s Executive Board and Vice-Chair of its Supervisory Board, said climate-related disasters were becoming structural drivers of economic and financial outcomes rather than isolated environmental events.
Speaking at the Green Swan 2026 Conference in Manila on October 19, he said the impacts of extreme weather were already affecting productivity, supply chains, energy production and prices, with consequences extending across national borders.
“The conclusion is clear,” Elderson said, calling for a comprehensive response combining climate adaptation, emissions reduction, sustained investment and international cooperation.
His warning comes amid growing concerns about the economic costs of climate-related disasters, including droughts, floods, wildfires and water shortages. He cited Europe’s summer of 2026, described in his speech as the continent’s warmest on record, as an example of how environmental pressures can disrupt economic activity.
Low water levels in major rivers affected transport, industry and energy production, while extreme temperatures and weather disruptions contributed to pressure on electricity and food prices.
Elderson said these developments had direct implications for central banks because climate shocks could influence economic growth, productivity and inflation, complicating monetary policy decisions.
He also highlighted the financial sector’s exposure to environmental risks, citing ECB research suggesting that severe water scarcity could put up to 24 percent of euro area economic output at risk.
According to him, central banks and financial supervisors must strengthen their economic models, forecasting systems and risk assessments to reflect the growing influence of climate change and nature degradation.
Beyond managing risks, Elderson argued that the green transition should be viewed as a strategy for improving competitiveness, strengthening energy security and supporting long-term prosperity.
He said greater investment in renewable energy and electrification could reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, limiting exposure to geopolitical disruptions and volatile energy prices.
The transition also presents opportunities to improve productivity and protect economic assets, including agricultural land, water resources and ecosystems that underpin food production and industrial activity.
However, he warned that progress remained constrained by policy uncertainty and limited access to finance.
Long-term investments in energy infrastructure, industrial transformation and electrification require substantial upfront capital and predictable policy frameworks. Uncertainty can encourage businesses to delay projects while making banks more cautious about lending.
Elderson said Europe would need hundreds of billions of euros in additional investment annually to meet its climate and nature objectives, underlining the importance of stronger banking finance, deeper capital markets and international investment flows.
He also called for credible policy commitments and common international standards to ensure that businesses investing in the transition were not disadvantaged against competitors that delayed action.
Adaptation, he said, was equally important, requiring investment in early-warning systems, flood prevention, water management, resilient infrastructure and energy systems capable of withstanding extreme weather.
Nevertheless, he cautioned that adaptation alone would not be sufficient because the costs would continue rising without effective measures to limit climate change.
Elderson concluded that climate resilience should be treated as an economic priority rather than solely an environmental concern.
Investing in adaptation and the green transition, he said, could help economies avoid future losses while building more productive, resilient and competitive economic systems.

articles.title: Economists predict Fed Hike's Spillover Manageable, Yuan Assets Show Resilience, CNS report - openPR.com
articles.summary: Economists predict Fed Hike's Spillover Manageable, Yuan Assets Show Resilience, CNS report  openPR.com
articles.full_text:
The two made the remarks in a written interview with China News Service (CNS) conducted here on wednesday, noting that China's macro policies are now being rolled out in quick succession, with their cushioning effect on the economy gradually emerging, while the medium- to long-term allocation value and value-for-money appeal of yuan assets are becoming more prominent as the A-share technology growth sector resonates deeply with the global business cycle.
"The Fed's move may prove to be a precautionary hike in response to inflation risks, and does not signal the start of a new round of sustained tightening," Hu Youwen, General Manager of the Research Institute at Guolian Minsheng Securities, and Tao Chuan, the firm's Chief Economist, told CNS.
The trigger for this hike differs markedly from past tightening cycles. For one thing, the move was not driven by economic overheating or runaway inflation. Energy prices have risen recently and inflation risks have resurfaced; by tightening now, the Fed aims to lock in its anti-inflation gains, with the core objective likely being to safeguard policy credibility and hedge tail inflation risks rather than to suppress the real economy through sustained tightening.
For another, the U.S. economy can hardly withstand sustained, steep rate hikes. Although the job market has recovered, the breadth of job gains remains narrow and household wage growth continues to slow, the economists told CNS.
"If a sustained tightening cycle took hold, U.S. Treasury yields and AI industry financing costs would rise further, creating a double drag on the U.S. fiscal position and core industries," they said.
The market had already largely priced in the September hike, and global core asset prices had moved in advance. With the decision now delivered, the pressure for further global liquidity tightening has eased, and shocks to capital markets, emerging-market currencies and cross-border capital flows should diminish at the margin.
A Fed hike could marginally weaken overseas end-demand and put pressure on parts of China's export supply chains. But this tightening is expected to be less persistent than past cycles, so the overall impact on external demand should be limited. Global AI capital expenditure remains in an upcycle, and with China's manufacturing sector covering a wide range of product categories and backed by a complete industrial ecosystem, related exports are expected to keep benefiting from growth in global industrial investment.
More importantly, shifts in external liquidity will not change the main trajectory of China's economic recovery. Since August, macro policies have entered a phase of intensive implementation, and the downward trend in some economic indicators has moderated, indicating that the cushioning effect of previously introduced policies is beginning to show. The disturbance to China's steady economic performance from changes in the external environment is therefore expected to remain relatively limited, said the economists.
While a Fed hike may affect short-term cross-border capital flows, the medium- and long-term case for foreign investors allocating to yuan assets has not fundamentally changed.
China's equity and bond valuations are within a reasonable range, the economy is recovering steadily and corporate earnings are improving, which makes the value-for-money and safe-haven appeal of yuan assets stand out, the two economists were quoted as saying.
Notably, since the policy-driven rally of late September 2024, known in the domestic market as the "924" rally, the positive correlation between A-shares and U.S. stocks has risen markedly, with particularly close linkage in the technology sector. The Nasdaq epitomizes global technology industry momentum and risk appetite, while the ChiNext Index and the STAR 50 Index are both high-beta growth assets that resonate deeply with the Nasdaq in industrial logic, risk appetite and liquidity expectations.
Although shifts in overseas liquidity may cause short-term disruption to the AI industry, they have not changed its medium- to long-term outlook, the economists predicted, adding that the U.S. AI industry's upcycle remains firmly in place and is expected to feed through further into China's capital markets.
As China's artificial intelligence, high-end manufacturing and semiconductor sectors continue to develop, the A-share technology growth sector is expected to capture more of the benefits of the global technology upcycle, they added.
Overall, this rate hike places relatively limited constraints on China's macro policy, and China can respond on three fronts, the economists pointed out.
On external demand, it should stabilize competitive exporters and their orders, and expand into Belt and Road Initiative partner countries and emerging markets, to mitigate the impact of demand shifts in any single market.
On monetary policy, China should maintain a "domestically oriented" approach while balancing internal and external equilibrium, adjusting policy in line with growth, employment and price conditions and keeping liquidity reasonably ample. It should also make its monitoring of stock, bond and foreign exchange linkages and its expectation management more forward-looking, and explore establishing countercyclical arrangements for long-term capital during external shocks, so as to strengthen the stabilizing allocation role of yuan assets.
On policy coordination, China should strengthen coordination between monetary and fiscal policy, forming a joint force in stabilizing growth, employment and risk prevention, and using the certainty of domestic policy to offset uncertainty in the external environment, the economists suggested.
"By consolidating the domestic base through coordinated policy and meeting long-term allocation demand with asset resilience, China's economy and capital markets are expected to further demonstrate their advantages amid external volatility," they told CNS.
The Fed raised its benchmark federal funds rate target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00% on Sept 16 - its first increase since July 2023 - in a unanimous 12-0 vote. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh described the move as removing some easing rather than increasing restraint, while the median dot plot pointed to the year-end rate rising to 4.1%, from 3.8% projected in June, signaling that further tightening remains on the table.

articles.title: Tokyo FX: Dollar-yen likely to trade in lower 158 range as market eyes US jobs data, Middle East risks - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Tokyo FX: Dollar-yen likely to trade in lower 158 range as market eyes US jobs data, Middle East risks  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
In the Tokyo foreign exchange market on the 22nd, the dollar-yen is expected to lack clear direction, trading centered on the lower 158 level per dollar. In overseas trading the previous day, yen buying led on falling US long-term yields tied to lower crude oil prices and comments from Bank of Japan Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino, but the pair recovered as dollar buying emerged on reports concerning the Middle East situation, reflecting geopolitical risk awareness. Market participants' expected range is 157.50 to 158.60 yen. With the Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan both scheduled to announce monetary policy the following week, moves to take aggressive positions are likely to be limited.
During overseas trading the previous day, the dollar-yen was seen as top-heavy. It was noted that if investor sentiment improves on US tech company earnings, dollar buying as a safe-haven asset could weaken. On the other hand, heightened Middle East tensions and higher crude oil prices underpin safe-haven demand for the dollar. Ahead of next week's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, there is little material likely to significantly alter the outlook for monetary policy, and the market's focus has shifted to the direction of US interest rates.
If US interest rates rise again, that would support the dollar-yen, while continued declines would tend to strengthen dollar selling. With few highly anticipated US economic indicators this week, US weekly initial jobless claims and the US leading economic index will be released on the 22nd.
On the yen side, market attention is on Japanese price trends and expectations for additional Bank of Japan rate hikes. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on the 21st that inflation is shifting from being driven by import prices to inflation accompanied by wage growth, and indicated her view that there is no gap between the government's and the Bank of Japan's policies. If the situation continues in which yen weakness pushes up import prices, expectations for Bank of Japan policy normalization could prompt yen buying.
In phases where the dollar-yen maintains elevated levels, caution over yen-buying intervention by the Japanese government and the Bank of Japan will be a factor capping upside. In the market, the 200-day moving average at 158.56 yen and the 14-day high of 158.95 yen are being watched as upside targets, while the 19th's low of 157.70 yen and the daily Ichimoku chart's baseline at 156.95 yen are seen as downside targets.

|---|---|

| Upside targets | 200-day moving average 158.56 yen, 14-day high 158.95 yen | 
| Downside targets | 19th low 157.70 yen, baseline 156.95 yen | 
| Domestic indicators | Foreign and domestic securities buying/selling contracts, Disco earnings | 
| US indicators | Weekly initial jobless claims, leading economic index | 
| European indicators | Eurozone October consumer confidence index (preliminary) | 
Note: The expected range is based on market participants' forecasts.
In the US, earnings announcements are also scheduled from Blackstone, Honeywell International, Newmont, Procter & Gamble (P&G), and Union Pacific. In Europe, the Eurozone October consumer confidence index (preliminary) will be released.
Among market participants, voices are heard expressing a desire to see whether a rebound in US interest rates will lead to dollar buying back. Two scenarios are envisioned: continued declines in US interest rates favoring yen buying, and a rebound if rate rises or a worsening Middle East situation strengthens dollar demand.
Behind this lies uncertainty over US and Japanese monetary policy. The Federal Reserve has not clearly indicated the direction of rate hikes or cuts, and the Bank of Japan is also at the stage of searching for the timing of additional rate hikes. With monetary policy events scheduled for the following week, this week is likely to be dominated by position-adjustment trading amid a scarcity of fresh material.
Foreign exchange market moves affect Japanese companies and households through export companies' profitability and import prices. If yen weakness progresses, rising import costs would squeeze corporate earnings while providing a tailwind for exporters. If the Japanese government and the Bank of Japan decide to conduct yen-buying intervention, market volatility could temporarily increase.

articles.title: China Securities Regulatory Commission Plans Listed-Company Supervision Rules as IPO, M&A and Refinancing Channels Widen for Hard Tech - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: China Securities Regulatory Commission Plans Listed-Company Supervision Rules as IPO, M&A and Refinancing Channels Widen for Hard Tech  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) Chairman Wu Qing said at the 2026 Financial Street Forum annual meeting that the regulator will focus on supporting "new quality productive forces," implement reform measures for the STAR Market and ChiNext boards in detail, further improve mechanisms for identifying and screening technology companies, adopt more inclusive and adaptive rules for IPOs and M&A, and accelerate the introduction of listed-company supervision regulations. No sooner had he spoken than a cluster of micro-level cases landed: Wenfeng Optoelectronics listed on the Beijing Stock Exchange, Xihe Technology filed its STAR Market IPO registration, and Boying Special Welding plans to acquire 55% of Suzhou Luokelai Marine Equipment Co., Ltd. From market entry to consolidation, the pace at which hard-tech and industrial-upgrade companies are connecting with the capital market is now echoing the policy rollout.
Market participants judge that as institutional supply continues to improve, with IPO, refinancing and M&A tools working in concert, the capital cycle for technology companies will run more smoothly, capital allocation efficiency should rise, and a high-quality listed-company cohort will grow faster.
Entry point: reserving policy dividends for genuine hard tech
Guarding the entry point is above all about identification. The regulator's call to implement STAR Market and ChiNext reform measures in detail and improve the mechanism for identifying and screening technology companies is seen as a finely calibrated, targeted arrangement.
Li Qiusuo, chief domestic strategist at CICC's research department, said innovative technology companies generally have high R&D spending, long paths to profitability and constantly evolving business models, so traditional listing standards centered on profit levels struggle to fully match their financing needs. The reforms help raise the degree of match between the capital market and the financing needs of sci-tech companies, lower the financing and time costs for quality companies, and channel capital toward technological innovation and industrial upgrading.
A Ping An Securities official, meanwhile, flagged room for improvement in the identification mechanism: the criteria for determining "technology attributes" need to be adjusted dynamically as industries evolve and better aligned with the national science and technology strategy and industrial policy, so that companies in new fields are not shut out by lagging indicators; the efficiency of M&A reviews needs to improve, and tools such as installment payments of share consideration should be used more fully; and the "gatekeeper" responsibilities of intermediaries must be enforced, with disclosure and risk warnings strengthened.
The differentiated positioning of the multi-tier market is equally critical. Li Qiusuo argued that listed companies at different stages of development differ widely in financing needs and risk profiles, and that coordinated development of the STAR Market, ChiNext, the Beijing Stock Exchange and the NEEQ would improve the support system covering companies from incubation to financing to listing. Shang Qingjun, a first-level inspector at the CSRC's public companies supervision department, said the regulator will further strengthen the NEEQ's standardized incubation function, improve entry and exit mechanisms, optimize tiered management, enhance the brand effect of the Innovation Tier, and consolidate the Beijing Stock Exchange–NEEQ framework of "progression tier by tier, linkage up and down, top-tier feedback and bottom-tier support."
Mid-stream tools: M&A and refinancing with more inclusiveness
If identification and screening determine "who can get in," M&A and refinancing determine whether companies can keep improving after listing. The regulator is embedding inclusiveness across companies' capital needs throughout their life cycles.
Hu Yuwei, chief policy analyst at China Securities (CSC Financial), said M&A both helps listed companies acquire technology, talent and industrial resources and serves as an important channel for venture capital to exit and reinvest in early-stage innovative companies. Capital market services for technological innovation are shifting from meeting single financing needs to raising the capital-cycle efficiency of the entire innovation system.
Brokerage-sector M&A and consolidation was also singled out for acceleration. Wu Qing said the CSRC will step up its action plan for high-quality development of securities firms, support industry M&A and subsequent integration, and speed up the building of internationally first-class investment banks. Soochow Securities analysts said policy direction has become increasingly clear since 2019, pushing resources toward leading firms through M&A on one hand and guiding small and mid-sized brokers to break out with differentiated strategies on the other, forming a multi-tier industry structure; M&A has accelerated the boutique-ization of smaller brokers, which build stronger balance sheets through organic profit accumulation and external acquisitions, then move from scale expansion to quality and efficiency gains.
Refinancing reform places greater demands on institutional design. The Ping An Securities official suggested more targeted, inclusive measures on refinancing size and interval limits for tech companies that fit the national strategic direction, while genuinely improving disclosure quality so quality companies can participate in refinancing more effectively, forming a virtuous "financing–development–return" loop.
Back-end support: supervision rules complete the institutional puzzle
With identification at the front end and tools in the middle, nurturing a stronger cohort of quality listed companies also requires full-chain regulatory support at the back end. The regulator made clear it will accelerate the introduction of listed-company supervision regulations and improve institutional mechanisms for corporate governance, disclosure and investor protection.
Li Qiusuo said the regulations would help improve listed-company supervision at the level of administrative regulations, enhance the authority and predictability of regulatory rules, and provide a more stable institutional environment for compliant operations and long-term investment; they would also strengthen corporate governance and disclosure requirements, fundamentally improving listed-company quality, guiding companies to place more emphasis on compliant operation and sustainable development, and pushing listed companies to shift from a focus on financing toward a greater focus on investment returns.
Cultivating a quality cohort also requires better corporate governance, guiding listed companies to raise their value through equity incentives, dividends and buybacks, and strictly enforcing and continuously improving the delisting regime. Chen Li, a council member of the China Chief Economist Forum, said the focus of governance should move forward from "entry screening" to "ongoing governance": relying on improved rules to enforce constraints, conducting regular special audits by audit committees, and strengthening clawbacks of executive pay in fraud cases; optimizing performance metrics for equity incentives at tech companies and guiding genuine buybacks, so that incentives are effective, constraints are rigid and exits are smooth.
Impact analysis
Looking at the policy mix, advancing IPO, M&A, refinancing and supervision rules simultaneously means capital market services for tech companies are shifting from "single-point loosening" to "full-chain adaptation." For hard-tech companies planning to list, dynamic adjustment of the identification mechanism and the differentiated positioning of the multi-tier market should reduce listing obstacles caused by lagging indicators; for already-listed companies, more inclusive M&A and refinancing will provide more flexible capital tools for supply-chain integration and sustained R&D spending.
For investors, better institutional supply does not mean lower thresholds. The simultaneous strengthening of supervision rules and intermediary responsibilities means disclosure and corporate governance requirements will be stricter, and while the supply of quality assets increases, the market's screening of listed-company quality will also become more demanding. At the secondary-market level, expectations for brokerage M&A and consolidation and the broadening of venture capital exit channels could become two main themes drawing investor attention, though the pace of policy implementation and specific detailed rules remain to be seen.

articles.title: Energy Dept to loan part of home heating oil reserve to ease prices, drawing bipartisan praise - Fox Business
articles.summary: Energy Dept to loan part of home heating oil reserve to ease prices, drawing bipartisan praise  Fox BusinessEXCLUSIVE: US aims to loan about a third of heating oil reserve in bid to tame prices  ReutersUS to Tap Heating Oil Reserve as Prices Soar Before Election  Bloomberg.comDOE to release 315,000 barrels from Northeast heating oil reserve  WABIFeds tap heating oil reserves as Maine braces for costly winter  newscentermaine.com
articles.full_text:
The Department of Energy (DOE) on Wednesday announced plans to loan up to about one-third of the U.S. emergency heating oil reserve in an effort to ease price pressures facing consumers as global conflicts constrain energy supplies.
The announcement indicated that the DOE will loan up to 315,000 barrels of fuel oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to mitigate supply disruptions. The reserve holds a supply of one million barrels of ultra-low sulfur distillate, which serves as heating oil, at four locations in the Northeast due to the popularity of heating oil as a significant source of home heating in the region.
Under the terms of the DOE's request for proposal, companies that borrow from the reserve in the 2026-27 heating season must return the same volume of oil plus a premium to refill the reserve before the 2027-28 heating season.
"The Trump administration is committed to doing everything in our power to lower energy costs for the American people," said Energy Secretary Chris Wright. "After receiving Senators Collins' and Kings' letter and extensive discussions with Senator Collins, I have directed the Department to exchange barrels from our Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to mitigate heightened home heating oil costs during the upcoming winter."
"Of course, this is a temporary measure to solve a temporary supply disruption. I encourage the governors of New York and New England to work with the Trump administration to build the Constitution Pipeline and replace home heating oil with low-cost natural gas. Doing so would save their residents billions of dollars in home heating and electricity costs," Wright added.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, said in a statement that she is pleased the Trump administration responded to the request to boost the supply of heating oil through reserve releases.
"Approximately half of Maine households rely on fuel oil to heat their homes, and I have repeatedly urged the administration to use every tool to increase supply and lower energy prices. The Department anticipates this release will put downward pressure on home heating oil costs and make a real difference for Maine homeowners as they prepare for winter," Collins said.
Collins noted in a press release that the planned release would represent a 13% increase in home heating oil supplies in New England, and should help lower prices as heating oil costs have risen 70% from a year ago.
Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, added that their state "has been hit especially hard by the run up in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran War and the most obvious example is home heating oil."
King said that Maine is "one of the most dependent states in the country on home heating oil and the cost is absolutely through the roof. This release of stored oil in New England will hopefully be some help."
Releases from the reserve would be completed by Nov. 13 and come from storage sites in Boston, South Portland, Maine; and New Haven, Connecticut.
The volume available per site wouldn't exceed 150,000 barrels, while the minimum offer quantity would be 25,000 barrels. Offerors can submit multiple bid offers, and the process looks to ensure a competitive bidding process in which both fuel retailers and terminal holders can participate.
Bids for the DOE solicitation would be due by next Tuesday, Oct. 27.

articles.title: Redeemer Health hit with steep credit downgrades after missed debt payments - The Business Journals
articles.summary: Redeemer Health hit with steep credit downgrades after missed debt payments  The Business Journals
articles.full_text:
Listen to this article 4 min
Story Highlights
- Fitch and Standard & Poor's downgraded Redeemer Health bonds to D, the lowest rating.
- The Montgomery County health system missed bond payments in September and October.
- Redeemer Health reported a $16.7 million operating loss in fiscal 2025.
Standard & Poor's, Moody's and Fitch have downgraded their credit ratings for Redeemer Health, weeks after the health system failed to make a payment on $71 million in bond debt.
Both Fitch and Standard & Poor's downgraded their ratings on Redeemer Health's bonds to D from B+. The Moody's downgrade was to Caa3 from B1 with the rating under review for further downgrade.
The D rating is the lowest credit rating issued by Fitch and Standard & Poor's and indicates that a borrower has failed to meet one or more of its debt payment obligations. Moody's Caa3 rating is near the bottom of its rating scale and indicates that the debt is subject to very high credit risk.
Moody's, echoing statements made by the other two rating agencies, said its downgrade reflects Redeemer Health's "weak liquidity and operations" which heightens the risk of loss to creditors, along with the uncertainty regarding the organization's ability to address the missed payment and fully cover the debt acceleration.
"The downgrade also considers [Redeemer Health's] history of operating losses, weakened financial flexibility, significant recent management turnover, weak governance and track record, and limited visibility into the organization's current financial position and restructuring plans following the default," Moody's states.
The agency noted the health system reported approximately $128 million of unrestricted cash and investments as of March 31.
Montgomery County-based Redeemer Health, in a statement provided to the Business Journal, said the bond debt rating downgrades were anticipated. The health system reiterated that it is working with its financial advisers and counsel to implement changes to its health system to ensure its continued viability and create a sustainable business model.
"We are working with the agent for the bondholders and other parties, including surrounding health systems, to determine the best path forward for Redeemer Health," the statement concluded.
Redeemer Health operates the 239-bed Holy Redeemer Hospital in the Meadowbrook section of Abington Township. It also operates senior living and short-term rehabilitation facilities, a home-care division and a physician group.
In a public notice filed Oct. 7 by Redeemer Health, the health system stated it missed its Sept. 1 bond payment and had not made its Oct. 1 payment.
The bonds were issued by the Montgomery County Education and Health Authority. The Bank of New York Mellon Corp. is serving as indenture trustee for the bondholders.
As a result of the event of default under the terms of the Redeemer Health bond financing agreement, the notice states that the trustee is accelerating all outstanding obligations, including the principal and interest owed on the bonds. The event of default requires the health system to restructure its debt, which a Redeemer Health spokesperson said is already underway.
The health system is carrying a total of about $90 million in bond debt.
In September, Redeemer Health underwent a leadership change following the departures of CEO Greg Wozniak on Sept. 24 and CFO Kim Cummings on Sept. 30. Jim Logue is serving as interim CEO at Redeemer Health. Logue joined the health system as its chief transformation officer in early 2025. Michael Keen is the health system's new CFO.
In fiscal 2025, the health system posted an operating loss of $16.7 million. It recorded a $53.2 million operating loss in fiscal 2024. Revenue in fiscal 2025 was $479.9 million, up from $442.5 million in fiscal 2024. It has not reported results for fiscal 2026, which ended June 30.
Redeemer Health in January 2025 initiated a $46 million turnaround plan after breaching a debt-service covenant. It is working with Chicago financial advisory firm Kaufman Hall.

articles.title: UK Inflation Rises To 3.5% As Businesses Urge Chancellor To Cut Costs - Minutehack
articles.summary: UK Inflation Rises To 3.5% As Businesses Urge Chancellor To Cut Costs  Minutehack
articles.full_text:
Rising fuel prices push inflation further above the Bank of England's target, adding to pressure on businesses ahead of next week's Budget.
UK inflation rose to 3.5 per cent in September, intensifying pressure on businesses already struggling with high operating costs and raising fresh questions about the Bank of England's next interest rate decision.
The increase in the consumer prices index (CPI), reported by the Office for National Statistics, was driven in part by higher fuel prices and leaves inflation well above the Bank's 2 per cent target.
The figures come a week before the Chancellor's first Budget, with business groups calling for measures to ease energy bills, property taxes and other costs that have weighed on investment and confidence.
The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) warned that persistent inflation was making it harder for companies to plan expenditure and commit to expansion.
Its latest survey of more than 4,000 businesses found that 60 per cent regarded inflation as a concern, making it the most frequently cited economic issue.
Caterina Batog, research and economics analyst at the BCC, said the latest figures were a reminder of the pressures facing employers.
“Inflation is casting a dark shadow over the businesses we represent, who are already struggling with a succession of high costs,” she said.
The BCC also warned that geopolitical tensions in the Middle East could increase energy costs, creating further inflationary pressure for businesses dependent on fuel and electricity.
The figures complicate the outlook for monetary policy. Inflation has remained above the Bank of England's target for two years, while policymakers must balance the risk of persistent price increases against weak economic growth.
Batog said the latest reading would add pressure on the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee to consider raising interest rates at its next meeting.
Higher borrowing costs would present another challenge for businesses seeking finance to invest in equipment, premises and additional staff.
The BCC urged the Chancellor to use the Budget to introduce targeted reductions in business taxation, particularly measures addressing energy costs and business rates.
“This high inflation landscape makes it even more crucial that the Chancellor uses his Budget to cut the cost of doing business,” Batog said.
The latest figures underline the difficult economic backdrop facing ministers as they attempt to encourage private investment without adding to inflationary pressures.

articles.title: UK inflation reaches highest rate in almost a year after fuel surge in a blow to John Healey ahead of the Budget - The Independent
articles.summary: UK inflation reaches highest rate in almost a year after fuel surge in a blow to John Healey ahead of the Budget  The Independent
articles.full_text:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Join today
Already a member? Log in
UK inflation has risen to its highest rate in almost a year as surging petrol and diesel prices pushed up the cost of living, new figures show, providing a gloomy backdrop to John Healey’s first Budget as chancellor next week.
But, in worse news, experts have warned that inflation is set to go even higher and hit 4 per cent, forcing the Bank of England to increase interest rates next month and in February.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the rate of Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation was 3.5 per cent in September, up from 3.1 per cent in August.
This was the highest CPI rate since the 3.6 per cent recorded in October last year, and came in above the 3.4 per cent that most economists had expected for the month.
This means the price of goods and services is rising at a faster rate than it was before, and inflation is drifting further away from the Bank of England’s two per cent target.
Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly at the pump.
Overall, motor fuels soared by 30 per cent in the year to September, up from a 23 per cent annual rise in August, ONS data showed.
Between August and September, average petrol prices rose by 8.2p to 169.5p per litre, which was the highest price recorded in around four years.
Diesel also surged by 10.7p to 192.5p, the highest price since July 2022.
According to RAC figures, average diesel prices surpassed 200p a litre for the first time ever at the beginning of this month.
Fuel costs have been soaring because of the Iran war, which has squeezed global oil and gas supplies.
ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said: “Inflation climbed notably in September to its highest annual rate in almost a year.
“Increased fuel prices were again the main driver, with the cost of diesel the highest since July 2022.
“Other upward pressures included airfares and, to a lesser extent, computer games and live events, which are often volatile.
“These were partially offset by the cost of hotel stays, where prices rose by less than this time last year.
“The annual cost of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continued to rise, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively.”
Responding to the new figures, chancellor John Healey said: “We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide.”
But he said the government’s decision on Wednesday to begin drilling in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea was investment “in our clean energy future and supporting British workers”.
“In my Budget next week, I will keep up this momentum,” he said.
“Maintaining our fiscal discipline and drive for growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space.”
Experts said the latest figures could put more pressure on Mr Healey to unveil new cost of living support measures in his autumn Budget statement next week.
James Smith, economist at the bank ING, told a briefing of journalists that inflation is expected to go to 4 per cent.
He said: “It’s pretty well understood that we’ll probably get to about 4 per cent this winter. That’s why the Bank of England is going to hike rates in November and in February as well.”
However, he suggested that it should start to come down after the spring, allowing for a lowering of the base rate of interest.
“There’s no sense of this broadening out,” he added suggesting that the current rise is “energy intensive inflation.”
Suren Thiru, chief economist for the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW), said inflation was “deepening the financial squeeze on households and businesses”.
“Rising inflation is turning the Budget into a perilous high-wire act for the chancellor, increasing pressure for cost of living support while pushing up government borrowing costs, which is shrinking fiscal headroom and narrowing his policy options,” he said.
It also means mortgage holders and borrowers are facing the prospect of higher interest rates next month, economists think.
Martin Sartorius, lead economist for the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), said September’s inflation rise means an interest rate hike was “firmly on the table” at the Bank of England’s next meeting in November.
He said the Bank’s rate-setting will likely want to “guard against the risk of persistently higher headline inflation” feeding through to other parts of the economy, like shop prices and wages.
Most economists expect inflation to rise further in the months ahead, with an increase to Ofgem’s price cap on household energy bills kicking in at the start of October, meaning higher prices for dual-fuel households over the winter.
Meanwhile, the September inflation rate is typically used to decide the level of increase for many benefits, such as universal credit, tax credits and disability benefits.
This rate is also a key part of the pension triple lock, which is used to decide how much pensions will increase by in the following April.
But the increase is based on either this inflation rate, average earnings growth between May and July, or 2.5 per cent.
State pensions are, therefore, widely expected to increase by 3.9 per cent next year based on wage growth figures, which is the highest of the three.
The data also showed that Consumer Price Index including Housing (CPIH), the ONS’s preferred measure of inflation, rose to 3.6 per cent in September from 3.3 per cent last month.
Meanwhile, Retail Prices Index (RPI) inflation rose to 3.9 per cent from 3.4 per cent in August.

articles.title: What Moves LME Base Metal Prices? - UK Investor Magazine
articles.summary: What Moves LME Base Metal Prices?  UK Investor Magazine
articles.full_text:
The London Metal Exchange is the world’s largest market for futures built on base metals like copper, tin, and other important industrial metals. It offers precious metal contracts too, which often outshine base metals in the public consciousness, but most traders have some idea of what moves silver and gold. Here, we’ve gathered some common factors that move base metals instead.
Mining Supply, Disruptions and Smelting Caps
Like all commodities, base metals are exposed to underlying real-world events that can impact their price. In fact, when compared to precious metals, base metals have higher exposure to industrial use cases like construction and technological development. While silver and gold do have a technological edge to them, they’re often valued and hoarded for status and political importance alone.
With that covered, let’s start at the beginning with the mines where copper, tin, aluminium, and zinc get pulled out of the ground. There are so many things that can disrupt mining activity at some of the world’s major mines, ranging from labour negotiations to on-site accidents, plus some political exposure through major suppliers like Chile or Indonesia. They can create supply deficits, driving the price of said metals up with volatility. Likewise, smelting and export caps can introduce non-supply related restrictions, like China’s hard cap for aluminium or Indonesia’s hawkishness over nickel.
One of the main benefits of the internet is the ability to tap into news feeds across most of the globe to identify disruptions as they happen. This can give traders and investors small windows of opportunity, especially when combined with an online trading platform built for commodity spreads, including CFDs for copper price action. Generally, investors should remember that supply disruptions will drive price upward, often in short timeframes, as base metal supply isn’t as extensive as gold, and mines take years to open.
Demand for Technological Development & Interest Rates
While supply is all about the mining and shipping of base metals, demand-side factors on price come from how the metals are used. China is important here too, as it’s the biggest consumer of base metals worldwide. Traders keep an eye on their manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) to see if their manufacturing sector is growing (over 50) or flagging (under 50). Growth means more demand, driving prices up if supply isn’t catching up.
More topical is the growing role of copper, nickel and aluminium in renewable energy hardware, electric car wiring and the AI data centre boom. Copper is far and away the most exposed here, owing to its conductive properties, as hyperscalers rush to build data centres all over the planet.
On the macro level, base metal consumption can also be an indicator of the economy as a whole. A healthy economy drives base metal usage, often through massive construction projects funded partially or in whole by debt. This also means high interest rates will drive the price of base metals down, as industrial demand weakens and physical holders de-stock because warehouse financing gets more expensive. The same rates would also strengthen the US Dollar, which makes metals more expensive for buyers using other currencies.
Naturally, those exposed to base metals should curate a feed that targets both local, mining-level events for their chosen metal, plus macroeconomic drivers that also affect price action. Unlike precious metals, base metals can experience more short-term volatility when supply or demand shifts, but positioning is always key.

articles.title: Cost of living crisis deepens as fuel price surge pushes UK inflation to 10-month high of 3.5% - The News International
articles.summary: Cost of living crisis deepens as fuel price surge pushes UK inflation to 10-month high of 3.5%  The News International
articles.full_text:
Surging motor fuel costs push the Consumer Prices Index to a 10-month high, sparking renewed debate over a potential interest rate hike by the Bank of England
The UK’s annual inflation rate accelerated to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, exceeding analyst expectations of 3.4% and reaching a 10-month high, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
The increase was driven primarily by rising transport and motor fuel costs, with average diesel prices reaching their highest level since July 2022 amid soaring petrol and diesel prices linked to the US-Iran war.
Transport prices rose 6.6% year-on-year, up from 4.6% in August, making the sector the largest contributor to the increase in annual inflation, the ONS said.
Services inflation also accelerated to 3.7%, while housing and household services and communication costs rose 5.3% and 5.8%, respectively. Food inflation remained unchanged at 1.3%.
Core CPI inflation increased to 2.8% from 2.6%. On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose 0.4%, following a 0.5% increase in August.
The higher-than-expected reading comes a week before the Labour government presents its annual budget on 28 October, with cost-of-living pressures expected to remain a key concern.
Danni Hewson, head of financial analysis at AJ Bell, said the energy price cap rose slightly in October, with households facing the prospect of a larger increase early next year.
She added that rising service costs, raw material prices and transportation expenses were adding to businesses’ costs.
“The knowledge that funding our lives is only going to get harder in the coming months will impact consumer confidence,” Hewson said.
The latest figures could complicate the Bank of England’s efforts to control inflation. The central bank is widely expected to consider raising interest rates at its meeting on 5 November, potentially marking its first increase since 2023.
Renewed inflationary pressures have also raised concerns about monetary policy in other major economies, including the United States and the eurozone.

articles.title: UK Faces Christmas Interest Rate-Hike Double Whammy Amid Inflation Surge - Investorideas.com
articles.summary: UK Faces Christmas Interest Rate-Hike Double Whammy Amid Inflation Surge  Investorideas.com
articles.full_text:
Main · Commentary
UK Faces Christmas Interest Rate-Hike Double Whammy Amid Inflation Surge
deVere CEO Nigel Green expects two Bank of England rate rises before Christmas as inflation spreads from the petrol pump into services.
Investorideas.com (www.investorideas.com newswire) a trusted platform for investing ideas including AI and robotics stocks issues market commentary from deVere Group.
Millions of British families and businesses are likely to be hammered by two interest rate rises before Christmas as an inflation surge that began at the petrol pump spreads into everyday bills and costs, warns the CEO of deVere Group, one of the world's largest independent financial advisory organisations.
The comments from Nigel Green come as official figures show UK inflation jumped to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% economists had pencilled in.
It's the third consecutive monthly rise and the highest annual rate in a year.
He comments: "This is the third rise in a row, and once again it's come in higher than expected. The Bank of England has very little room left to sit on its hands.
"Britain buys a lot of its energy from abroad, so when oil prices jump, the country feels it quickly. Drivers and haulage firms have been paying for it at the pumps for months, and now it's showing up right across the economy."
Motor fuel prices soared 29.8% in the year to September, up from around 23% in August and the steepest climb since the summer of 2022. Prices rose 0.4% in September alone, ahead of the 0.3% forecast.
Crucially, the pressure has spread well beyond the forecourt. Services inflation accelerated to 3.7% from 3.4%, while core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, climbed to 2.8% from 2.6%, beating forecasts. Goods inflation reached 3.2%, its highest since September 2023.
"What concerns me most is services," notes the deVere CEO.
"Fuel prices move up and down with the oil market. When businesses start charging more for services, those increases usually stick. If the Bank sees that happening, it'll keep raising rates."
Markets put the odds of a quarter-point hike to 4% next month at 98%, with most traders also expecting another rise in December.
Nigel Green predicts the Bank will deliver both, and believes rates are likely to stay elevated for much of 2027.
"I'd now expect a hike in November and another in December," he says. "Inflation's heading the wrong way, it's spreading into services, and the Bank knows it was too slow last time.
"Having raised rates twice, it's hardly going to turn around and cut them a few months later. Unless the economy weakens badly, cuts next spring look very unlikely to me."
Britain now also stands out among its neighbours, with inflation running above both France at 3.4% and Germany at 3.3%.
"Inflation was under 3% as recently as July, and now Britain's running hotter than France and Germany," explains the deVere CEO. "It's quite a turnaround in a matter of months."
The squeeze is likely to land hardest on stretched households. Real wage growth had ground to a halt even before the energy shock struck, and unemployment has hovered around 5% for much of the year.
"A lot of families are already paying more to fill the car and heat the house, and their wages haven't kept pace," he says.
"Now their mortgage is likely to go up as well. People coming off fixed deals next year are going to notice a big difference in what they pay each month.
"Savers aren't immune either. With inflation at 3.5%, money left sitting in a low-paying account is losing value every month."
Businesses face a similar bind, with higher energy and transport bills now set to be joined by dearer borrowing.
"Firms are getting it from both sides," says Nigel Green. "Their running costs are up, and the cost of a loan or an overdraft is about to rise again.
"A lot of companies that borrowed cheaply a few years ago will be refinancing at far higher rates.
"Smaller businesses have already absorbed as much as they can. Some will raise prices, others will hold back on hiring or investment, and either way it slows the economy down."
He believes the Bank's resolve is being shaped by the memory of its last inflation fight.
"The Bank was too slow in 2021, and it's been paying for it ever since," he concludes.
"It won't make the same mistake twice, even if the economy takes a knock. Higher borrowing costs are going to be part of life for British households and businesses for a good while yet."

articles.summary: UK inflation surges to 3.5% as November interest rate rise looms  London Business News
articles.full_text:
UK inflation has accelerated to its highest level in almost a year, strengthening expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month as surging fuel costs and higher winter energy bills threaten to prolong the squeeze on households.
Consumer Prices Index inflation rose to 3.5 per cent in September, up from 3.1 per cent in August, according to figures published by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday. The reading exceeded economists’ expectations and moved inflation further away from the Bank’s 2 per cent target.
Motor fuel was a major driver, with petrol and diesel prices rising by 30 per cent in the year to September as the US-Israeli war with Iran disrupted global oil and gas supplies and pushed up wholesale prices.
The renewed inflationary pressure presents a challenge for policymakers, who must weigh the risk of higher prices becoming entrenched against the strain that increased borrowing costs would place on mortgage holders and businesses.
Martin Sartorius, lead economist at the Confederation of British Industry, said the latest figures meant an interest rate increase was “firmly on the table” at the Bank’s November meeting.
Policymakers would want to “guard against the risk of persistently higher headline inflation becoming embedded in future wage and price-setting behaviour”, he added.
Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said further energy price increases were “inevitable”, with continuing tensions in the Middle East delaying the prospect of inflation easing. He expects rates to rise in November and again in subsequent months.
There was some relief for consumers: food and drink inflation remained unchanged at 1.3 per cent, while prices fell 0.2 per cent between August and September. But analysts warned that supermarket competition might not be enough to contain food costs indefinitely.
Danni Hewson, head of financial analysis at AJ Bell, said the “knowledge that funding our lives is only going to get harder in the coming months will impact consumer confidence”.
Consumers could bolster savings and postpone major purchases, she added, increasing the pressure on the government to provide support.
Chancellor John Healey, who is due to deliver his autumn Budget next week, said he would “look to do more” to provide “breathing space” on living costs.
The September inflation figure will also influence benefit increases and the state pension triple lock. However, pensions are widely expected to rise by 3.9 per cent next April, reflecting stronger wage growth rather than inflation.
The latest figures underline the difficult choices facing policymakers: containing inflation may require higher interest rates just as households confront another winter of elevated living costs.
