articles.title: USD/JPY Trading: What Moves the Dollar-Yen Exchange Rate? - MarylandReporter.com
articles.summary: USD/JPY Trading: What Moves the Dollar-Yen Exchange Rate?  MarylandReporter.com
articles.full_text:
One U.S. dollar now buys roughly 158 Japanese yen, a rate few currency watchers would have predicted a few years ago. The yen has been trading near its weakest level against the dollar in four decades. The slide grew steep enough that Tokyo and Washington recently stepped into the market together.
For Maryland, the exchange rate matters beyond the trading screens. The Port of Baltimore ranks second in the nation for autos and light trucks, handling more than 700,000 of them last year, according to the governor’s office. Japanese brands also loom large in the U.S. car market. The Toyota RAV4 is the top-selling Japanese-brand vehicle and the best-selling SUV in the United States. Shifts in the yen change the cost of imported vehicles, machinery and parts, and that changes the calculations of the businesses that buy them.
Why the Dollar-Yen Pair Draws So Much Attention
The quote shows how many yen one dollar buys. A rising number means a stronger dollar, and a falling one means the yen is gaining ground. USD/JPY is among the most actively traded pairs in a global currency market that turns over roughly $9.6 trillion a day, according to the latest survey by the Bank for International Settlements.
That depth helps explain why the pair is a fixture of retail forex trading, where individuals speculate on exchange rate moves through brokers rather than swapping physical cash. In the U.S., firms offering that service to the public must register with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and belong to the National Futures Association. Heavy volume does not guarantee calm, however. The yen can swing several percent in a matter of days when the forces below collide.
The Interest Rate Gap Still Sets the Tone
No factor shapes the pair more than the difference between American and Japanese borrowing costs. Investors can borrow yen cheaply and put the money into higher-yielding dollar assets, a strategy known as the carry trade. The wider the gap, the stronger the pull away from the yen.
That gap remains wide even though both central banks are now raising rates. The Federal Reserve, chaired by Kevin Warsh, has lifted its benchmark rate to a range of 3.75% to 4% as energy costs keep inflation elevated. The Bank of Japan spent years holding rates at or below zero and has now raised its policy rate to 1.25%.
A Japanese hike would normally support the yen. Yet when the Bank of Japan made its latest move, the currency slipped. A spread of more than two and a half percentage points still favored the dollar, and Fed officials had just signaled another increase was likely. Currency markets tend to trade the expected path of policy rather than any single decision.
Lessons From the 2024 Carry Trade Unwind
The carry trade can reverse violently, and 2024 offered a vivid example. With the dollar fetching more than 160 yen, the Bank of Japan raised rates, and a weak U.S. jobs report followed soon after. Leveraged positions funded in yen were unwound at speed.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell more than 12% in a single session, its largest one-day point drop on record. Within weeks, USD/JPY slid to around 142. The episode showed how quickly a crowded position can turn when both sides of the rate gap shift at once.
Washington and Tokyo Step In
Governments can also move the rate directly. With the yen sliding toward 164 per dollar, Japan’s Ministry of Finance bought yen in coordination with the U.S. Treasury. Officials in both capitals confirmed the operation shortly afterward and said they stood ready to act again, as The Japan Times reported. Joint action of this kind is rare, and the two countries had not bought yen together in decades.
The yen jumped right after the intervention, then gave back part of the gain as the pair drifted toward 158. That supports a view analysts voiced at the time: intervention can interrupt a slide, but rate differentials and economic fundamentals usually set the longer trend.
Oil, Trade and a Less Dependable Safe Haven
Japan imports almost all of the crude it uses, most of it from the Middle East, so oil prices flow straight into its trade accounts. When oil climbs, importers need more dollars to pay for it, and that steady selling of yen weighs on the currency. The conflict involving Iran pushed energy prices higher and, at several points, the yen lower.
That pattern complicates the yen’s reputation as a refuge in times of turmoil. The currency still tends to rally when investors rush to close risky bets, as the 2024 unwind showed, but an energy shock now hits Japan’s economy directly. Trade data can also work in the yen’s favor. When Japan’s latest current account figures beat forecasts by a wide margin, the yen held steady near 158.
Final Thoughts on What Traders Are Watching Next
The Fed and the Bank of Japan meet again within days of each other. After softer U.S. data, futures pricing has moved away from a second straight Fed hike. In Tokyo, the question is whether policymakers keep up the quicker pace of increases they adopted this year.
Add verbal warnings from Japan’s Finance Ministry, the direction of Treasury yields and the price of crude, and the dollar-yen rate becomes a running scorecard of two economies under very different pressures. For Maryland importers, travelers bound for Japan and anyone following the pair, those signals say more than any single forecast.

articles.title: Boeing's largest 737 MAX jet wins FAA certification, clearing way for deliveries of 1,555 ordered planes - Fox Business
articles.summary: Boeing's largest 737 MAX jet wins FAA certification, clearing way for deliveries of 1,555 ordered planes  Fox BusinessFAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service  NPRBoeing’s Large 737 Max Jet Secures U.S. Approval  The New York TimesBoeing Finally Gets FAA Approval for Its 737 Max 10 Jet. This Is Big.  Barron'sUS set to announce certification of Boeing 737 MAX 10 on Tuesday, sources say  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Boeing's largest 737 MAX aircraft has received Federal Aviation Administration certification, clearing the way for deliveries of a jet with 1,555 orders that represent a third of the company's outstanding 737 MAX order book.
The FAA announced Tuesday that it had certified the 737 MAX 10 after years of regulatory and safety reviews, removing a major hurdle for Boeing as it prepares to begin deliveries to airlines in the coming months.
Boeing said the aircraft has received orders from more than 30 customers worldwide, making the MAX 10 a key part of the company's commercial airplane backlog.
The approval also marks a significant milestone for Boeing's 737 MAX program, which has received 7,350 orders across the aircraft family, with nearly 2,500 planes delivered through the end of September 2026.
"Completing the certification program clears the path for us to deliver a Boeing airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation," Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said in a statement.
"The 737-10 offers greater capacity, longer range and the best seat economics in its class, a platform that will create more value and opportunities for airlines around the world," Pope added.
The 737 MAX 10, the largest aircraft in Boeing's single-aisle MAX family, can seat up to 230 passengers, although airlines will typically configure the jet for 185 to 210 passengers in a two-class layout, according to Boeing. The aircraft has a range of up to 3,100 nautical miles.
Certification followed an extensive FAA safety review and testing program. Boeing said the process involved nearly 1,000 test flights, more than 2,000 flight hours and 1,000 hours of ground testing.
The aircraft includes safety enhancements, among them an updated flight-control system and an enhanced angle-of-attack sensor. Boeing said those improvements will eventually become standard across the 737 MAX family.
"The FAA's decision follows a thorough review of the aircraft's design and safety requirements," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said. "We will continue to hold Boeing to the highest safety standards as the company begins production of the 737 MAX-10."
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy also welcomed the approval, highlighting its significance for the US aerospace manufacturing industry.
"This is a major win for American manufacturing and our nation's status as a global aviation powerhouse," Duffy said in the FAA's announcement.
The certification means all four variants of Boeing's 737 MAX family have now received FAA approval, following the certification of the smaller 737 MAX 7 earlier this year.

articles.title: Merifund Capital Management says Treasury auction eased selloff - Invezz
articles.summary: Merifund Capital Management says Treasury auction eased selloff  Invezz
articles.full_text:
- US Treasury yields hit multi-decade highs before a $39 billion auction drew firm demand and eased pressure.
- Fiscal deficits, elevated oil prices and AI borrowing fuel a global bond sell-off across Europe and Japan.
- Higher yields pressure equities but improve bond income prospects, offering patient investors a stronger cushion against future losses.
Government bond markets face their sternest test in a generation this week, with US Treasury yields at levels not recorded in more than 24 years.
The 10-year yield rises above 5.36%, and the 30-year touches 5.735% before a $39 billion midweek auction of 10-year notes offers meaningful relief, as firm demand absorbs the new supply.
Analysis from Merifund Capital Management sets out why the timing of that sale matters for long-term investors.
The auction illustrates how a well-received sale of government debt can steady a market close to losing its nerve.
Ten-year notes cleared with a tail of 0.2 basis points, the gap between expected and actual yields, and a bid-to-cover ratio of 2.43 times, the dollars bid for each dollar on offer, against averages of 0.3 basis points and 2.49 over the previous six auctions.
Domestic direct bidders take 23.9% of the issue, foreign and institutional indirect bidders 65.3% and primary dealers 10.8%, against recent averages of 19.2%, 71% and 9.8%, respectively.
Domestic buyers step in as indirect demand softens, a calculated judgement on value rather than a sign of distress.
The 10-year yield climbs to its intraday peak in the hours before the result, then eases back towards 5.276% as the strength of demand becomes clear.
Yields often rise ahead of a large auction and fall back once supply is placed, a pattern that intensifies when dealers have less room to carry risk.
The reversal matters because the sale lands as yields test their highest levels in more than two decades.
The longer end of the curve tells the most striking story, defying the textbook link between central bank policy and borrowing costs.
The 30-year yield has risen by about 120 basis points since the Federal Reserve began cutting rates just over two years ago, the largest increase during an easing cycle in roughly four decades.
The Fed sets the price of overnight money, not the return investors demand to lend for 30 years.
Speaking in his capacity as Director of Private Equity at Merifund Capital Management Pte. Ltd., Anthony Saunders cautions that one well-covered sale does not end the volatility, and that the more telling signal lies in whether yields fall across consecutive sessions rather than retreat from an intraday high.
A reversal confined to a single trading day can unwind as quickly as it appears.
He reads the auction result itself as “a reminder that, at the right price, the world’s deepest bond market still finds willing buyers”.
Sovereign debt markets across Europe and Japan sell off alongside Treasuries, with Japanese 10-year yields touching levels unseen in about 30 years.
French 10-year yields reach 4.92%, their highest in more than two decades, while Italian equivalents trade near 4.6% and German Bunds at 3.5% over the same sessions.
The 30-year gilt yield crosses 6% during the same sell-off, a threshold last breached more than a quarter of a century ago.
Behind the move sit persistent fiscal deficits, Brent crude near $121.5 a barrel in recent sessions and roughly $193.5 billion of bonds issued by the five largest technology companies for artificial intelligence infrastructure by mid-year alone.
The Federal Reserve holds the federal funds target range at 3.5% to 3.75% after its most recent meeting, citing inflation above its 2% objective.
Markets now price in at least three further rate increases before the middle of next year, a repricing Saunders characterises as “a market that has stopped waiting for the Fed to rescue it and started demanding to be paid for the risk instead”.
Options markets also assign a greater probability to rates settling above the path policymakers project.
Equity markets feel the strain as higher Treasury yields raise the discount rate applied to future corporate profits.
The Nasdaq Composite falls 1.13% to 26,936.04 on the day, after two record-setting sessions, while the S&P 500 sheds 0.75%.
European banks fare worse, with the STOXX Europe Banks index down 3.5% in a single session and Société Générale, Deutsche Bank, UniCredit and Intesa Sanpaolo each more than 4% lower.
The arithmetic of higher yields cuts both ways for long-term investors, setting near-term capital losses against income unmatched during the preceding low-rate era.
Aggregate bond indices now yield more than at any point in decades, a thicker cushion against further yield increases.
Merifund Capital Management’s reading of the week suggests that demand for government debt remains intact and that higher yields now strengthen the income case for patient bondholders.
About Merifund Capital Management
Founded in 2010, Singapore-based Merifund Capital Management Pte. Ltd. (UEN: 201024554E) is an established hedge-fund manager running global macro, long/short equity, event-driven and systematic trading strategies alongside traditional long-only asset and portfolio management.
Derivatives are deployed selectively to capture opportunities, with capital preservation, liquidity, and careful risk control central to its approach, and its ESG integration reflects a commitment to exacting global sustainability standards.
Its client base spans family offices, foundations, endowments and accredited investors, and the firm is extending its reach to retail investors. Further insights are available at https://merifund.com/insights. Media and general enquiries can be directed to Tao Yang at media@merifund.com, with further information at https://merifund.com.

articles.title: UK inflation rise to highest in almost a year as Iran war drives fuel prices higher - myMotherLode.com
articles.summary: UK inflation rise to highest in almost a year as Iran war drives fuel prices higher  myMotherLode.com
articles.full_text:
Published Oct 21, 2026 4:21 am : Updated Oct 21, 2026 12:05 pm
LONDON (AP) — Inflation in the U.K. rose to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to ratchet up fuel prices, official figures showed Wednesday, cementing market expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month.
The Office for National Statistics said consumer prices rose by 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August. That’s the highest reading since October last year, and above the 3.4% that most economists had been expecting for the month.
The increase takes inflation further above the Bank of England’s target rate of 2%.
Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly at the pump. Overall, motor fuels soared by 30% in the year to September, up from a 23% annual rise in August.
Fuel costs have been soaring because of the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz, which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies.
Treasury chief John Healey said his budget statement next week will aim to give businesses and families “some breathing space” from the upward march in the cost of living.
Whatever measures he comes up with to keep a lid on rising prices, economists expect the Bank of England to increase interest rates at its next meeting on Nov. 5. Last month, rate-setters held the bank’s main rate at 3.75% but gave a big hint that they were ready to hike soon.
“With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise,” said Suren Thiru, chief economist at ICAEW.
Most economists expect an increase in the bank’s main rate to 4%. Other central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, have raised rates recently.
Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
By PAN PYLAS
Associated Press

The blue-chip FTSE 100 index rose 0.1% to 10,752.88 points, after two sessions of declines in a row. The midcap FTSE 250 was up 0.3%.
• UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, above economists' expectations of 3.4%, as the US-Israeli war on Iran pushed up energy prices
• Money markets are near certain of a 25-basis-point BoE rate hike in November, according to LSEG data
• Finance Minister John Healey came under pressure ahead of next week's budget after official data showed government borrowing exceeded forecasts for a second straight month, pushing public debt above £3 trillion ($4.01 trillion)

• Energy giants gained, with BP and Shell among the biggest boosts to the FTSE 100
• Britain approved the Jackdaw North Sea gas field, ending years of legal and political wrangling as the Labour government seeks to balance its climate goals with energy security concerns
• Asset manager Aberdeen Group, among the top losers on the FTSE 100, fell 4% after flagging a slower-than-expected return to adviser-segment inflows
• Midcaps: bicycles-to-car parts retailer Halfords dropped about 8.6%, the steepest on the FTSE 250, after first-half results

articles.summary: SpaceX IPO scorecard: How SPCX stacks up after 90 days  Opening Bell Daily
articles.full_text:
Ninety trading days after going public, SpaceX is doing something Facebook couldn’t at the same point. Its stock is above its IPO price.
That matters because Facebook is the classic example of mega-tech IPOs, and SpaceX’s roughly $75 billion IPO is the latest test of it.
Facebook didn’t close back above its IPO price until August 2013, more than 14 months after its debut.
Now put SpaceX next to three of the most-watched tech IPOs of the past 15 years. The chart below shows each one at its 90th trading-day close against its IPO price.
SpaceX has handily outperformed Facebook, though it’s still well behind Arm and Alibaba, both of which were up more than 40% at the same point.
SpaceX priced at $135 a share on June 12 and closed October 20 at $147.79.
In between, the stock went as high as $201.80 in June before falling as low as $108 in August.
The latest numbers give Elon bulls more to work with.
SpaceX crushed earnings estimates after the bell Tuesday, with revenue hitting $14.58 billion, up 161% from a year ago and well above the roughly $12.7 billion Wall Street expected.
Notably, its Super Intelligence segment, which includes its AI business and X’s advertising, now brings in about 52% of sales.
That includes $608 million from Cursor, which it bought in August.
Meanwhile, revenue from Connectivity, the segment that includes Starlink, grew 69%.
The company also posted $2.8 billion in operating income after losing money a year earlier.
And in a full-circle moment for IPO history, at about $2 trillion, SpaceX is now worth more than Facebook’s parent company, Meta.
Thursday brings one more test for the rocket company. That’s when up to 1.3 billion more shares held by pre-IPO shareholders become eligible for sale, worth about $192 billion.
While no one would say 90 days makes a track record, a stock that can lose nearly half its value and still sit above its offer price has earned a second look.

🛢 Oil fell as traders hoped for progress on US-Iran diplomacy. Brent crude settled down 0.7% at $108.79 a barrel after touching $111.99 earlier in the session. (CNBC)

articles.title: Are Bonds Pricing In A Fed Policy Mistake? - Real Investment Advice
articles.summary: Are Bonds Pricing In A Fed Policy Mistake?  Real Investment Advice
articles.full_text:
Imagine someone looking into their crystal ball and telling you at the beginning of October that the coming September CPI data would be higher than expected, and producer prices (PPI) would rise 1.3% for the month, well above the 0.5% forecast. On top of the bad inflation news, they also said more inflation pressure was brewing, with crude oil prices rising $10 through the first two weeks of the month. Based on that foresight, where would you guess the 10-year Treasury yield would be? To help you answer, the ten-year US Treasury yield was flirting with 5.25% on October 1. We bet most professional bond traders would have bet on 5.50% or even higher.
On October 14th, the 10-year Treasury yield surged after the CPI report, hitting 5.33% minutes after the release. A few days later, it was markedly lower at 5.03%. The 30-year yield fell by a similar amount. Bonds rallied into the teeth of the bad inflation data.
Mohamed El-Erian, ex CEO of PIMCO and renowned bond expert, asked the obvious question on X:
Why are US government bond yields falling despite hotter-than-expected CPI and PPI inflation prints?
He offered two valid rationalizations. In this article, we walk through his two AI-related explanations and add two of our own. Importantly, we emphasize one we think matters most: the bond market may be starting to price in the risk that the Fed is being pushed into a policy mistake.
Explanation One: A Flight To Quality Out Of Tech
El-Erian’s first driver is a flight to quality “out of formerly high-flying tech stocks that are now coming under pressure.“
- Many semiconductor stocks have been under pressure. The SOX semiconductor index fell almost 20% between October 1 and the PPI release on the 15th.
- The Nasdaq, with a large semiconductor weighting, fell in sympathy. Foreign markets, including the tech-heavy Korea’s KOSPI and Japan’s Nikkei, were also down sharply.
- As we show below, healthcare (XLV), consumer staples (XLP) and other beaten-up value sectors have rallied since October 1, while technology (XLK) moved in the opposite direction. This rotation was primarily a flight to quality within the equity market, but El-Erian thinks it may have also sparked some bond buying.
Additionally, El-Erian notes there are “emerging pockets of credit stress in the most vulnerable segments.” To his point, CoreWeave, a large data center provider, saw yields on its debt rise from 9% to 15%. Because investors are demanding such high yields for CoreWeave’s debt and some of its competitors, there is a growing concern that CoreWeave might be the AI trade’s canary in the coal mine.
Credit-related issues, such as those noted, often lead to a flight to quality from corporate bonds to US Treasuries.
Explanation Two: Is Tech Still A Growth Engine?
El-Erian’s second driver carries broader macroeconomic implications. AI-related capital spending has been a primary engine of economic growth. If investors are less willing to fund the AI build-out, and if firms can’t afford to fund it, does the economic growth outlook dim?
Saxo’s Charu Chanana noted:
Investors are becoming less willing to finance AI infrastructure growth at any cost.
With 10-year yields above 5% and some AI-related credit spreads at junk bond levels, the cost of financing data centers has risen sharply. Less AI capex means less GDP growth, and lower expected growth argues for lower inflation, which results in lower long-term yields.
Explanation Three: Short Covering And Signs Of Significant Demand
Our first addition to El-Erian’s list is short covering. The bond market entered October leaning heavily toward higher yields.
To wit, CFTC data showed asset managers added more than 100,000 contracts to their short 10-year Treasury futures exposure in the week ending September 22, one of the largest weekly additions since 2023, according to Bloomberg. Furthermore, open interest in 10-year futures rose in 13 of 14 sessions through late September, and in 5-year futures in 11 of 12 sessions. Those are consistent with new short positions being added as yields rose.
The 10- and 30-year Treasury auctions on October 7th and 8th appear to have foreshadowed the reversal. Many investors expected weak demand for the new supply of debt. They got the opposite. Per our Commentary Bond Auctions: You Never Hear About The Good Ones:
The 10-year note auction on Wednesday sold $39 billion at a 5.300% high yield. It stopped 1.7 basis points through the when-issued level, meaning it cleared much better than the market expected. Thursday’s 30-year $22.5 billion bond auction was similar. The box plots below, courtesy of Exante Data, show how far outside normal both readings sit. The bid-to-cover measures the amount of dollars bid for every dollar sold. The 10-year came in at 2.77 compared to a twelve-month average of 2.51, higher than any of the last 50 auctions. The 30-year was 2.54 against a 2.40 median, at the upper edge of the last 50 auctions.
Primary dealer participation may be the most important auction statistic. The Treasury’s primary dealers must bid and absorb whatever nobody else wants. When an auction has a high percentage dealer take, it means the auction struggled, and Wall Street got stuck with inventory. Dealers took a mere 2.5% of the 10-year, their lowest share on record for the tenor, and 6.8% of the 30-year. Indirect bidders, largely foreign central banks and domestic institutions, took 80.3% and 72.3%, both far above their averages.
When dealers are left buying little at Treasury auctions, as we saw, it means real money buyers are absorbing supply at these yields. While the bond market didn’t rally on the strong auctions, it certainly put short sellers on notice that demand was robust at yields above 5%. The rising demand may have prompted Treasury-bond buying to cover short positions. Given how offside the market was, the buying created a circular effect, forcing more short sellers to cover.
Explanation Four: The Bond Market Smells A Policy Mistake
The bond market may be beginning to believe that this month’s hot inflation data will force the Fed’s hand toward more, not fewer, rate hikes, ultimately resulting in a policy error.
The yield curve’s changing shape over the past two weeks supports our view. The 2yr-10yr yield curve was 57 basis points on October 7th. Following the CPI and PPI reports, it flattened to 32 basis points. That’s a relatively large 25-basis-point decline in two weeks, with most of it occurring on the days of the inflation data.
When all yields decline, but long-end yields fall more than short-term yields, that is called a bull flattener. A market that expects the Fed to tighten into a weakening economy buys long bonds and flattens the curve. A market fearing runaway inflation should result in a bear steepener reaction.
The front end of the yield curve prices the odds of Fed rate hikes. The long end is pricing the consequences.
Reasons To Fret A Policy Mistake
There are a few reasons we think the bond market should worry about the Fed.
First, the recent increase in inflation is largely a supply shock. Gasoline and diesel prices are rising because of the conflict with Iran, not because consumers are overheating. The Fed can’t produce oil, but it can reduce demand for everything else.
Second, the labor market is weak. September payrolls rose just 29,000 and prior months were revised down by 60,000. Furthermore, the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% and real earnings are flat to slightly negative, leaving little evidence of an inflationary wage-price spiral.
Third, consumers are being squeezed. The most recent retail sales beat estimates at 0.8%, but gasoline sales drove most of the gain. To wit, the Control Group, which the BEA uses in its GDP calculation, rose only 0.1. Essentially, higher gas prices are crowding out other spending.
Fourth, Fed policy is already restrictive by the Fed’s own math. The September rate hike raised Fed Funds to 3.75% to 4.00%, above the Fed’s own estimate of the longer-run neutral rate at 3.20%. The median dot plots in the latest Fed Economic Projections (SEP), along with commentary from some Fed members, suggest another rate hike or two is quite possible.
Lastly, financial conditions are tightening. The 10-year yield above 5%, 30-year mortgage rates near 7.50%, an 18-month high in the dollar, and widening credit spreads are all doing the Fed’s work. Fed Funds rate hikes make financial conditions even more restrictive.
The Hawks Case
To be fair, Fed hawks have a rational case for raising rates further. The recent CPI report showed broader price increases across many goods and services, core PCE running near 3%, and, probably more importantly, inflation has been above the Fed’s target for more than five years. The Fed is rightly concerned about inflation expectations becoming unanchored.
But the bond market is not voting on whether inflation is too high or what it has been. It is voting on where inflation will be and whether the Fed’s inflation cure will not only heal the patient of its inflation problem but bring on recessionary side effects.
Summary
Falling bond yields amid hot inflation data are not a paradox. They reflect a flight to quality out of tech, doubts about AI as a growth engine, the unwinding of crowded short positions, and strong demand.
Most importantly, in our view, they signal concern that the Fed is responding to an energy-driven inflation shock and that inflation has been too high for too long, tightening into a slowing economy. The shape of the yield curve and the direction of long-end yields offer a good roadmap for what may happen next.

articles.title: Seturion Wins DLT TSS License: What Boerse Stuttgart Got - FinanceFeeds
articles.summary: Seturion Wins DLT TSS License: What Boerse Stuttgart Got  FinanceFeeds
articles.full_text:
Boerse Stuttgart Group has obtained a DLT Trading and Settlement System license under the European Union’s DLT Pilot Regime, giving its Seturion platform a regulatory basis to operate as a digital settlement system for tokenised assets. The group describes itself as the first European exchange group to obtain a DLT TSS license. That qualifier matters: ESMA’s register already lists other authorised European DLT trading-and-settlement systems, including 21X, Axiology, LISE and Securitize Europe. The new distinction is the exchange-group operator, not the first permission of this type in Europe.
What the Authorization Covers
The DLT Pilot Regime was created to let market infrastructures test distributed-ledger trading and settlement under tailored permissions and exemptions while preserving core investor-protection and market-integrity safeguards. A DLT TSS combines functions normally performed by a trading venue and a securities settlement system. Boerse Stuttgart says BaFin granted the permission after a process involving ESMA and the European Central Bank. ESMA’s current list records Seturion as a German DLT TSS, with the Baden-Württembergische Wertpapierbörse as operator and BaFin as the national competent authority.
The register is useful because it shows what the headline does and does not mean. The Seturion entry lists specific exemptions from parts of the Central Securities Depositories Regulation, including provisions on book-entry form, settlement fails, settlement finality, cash settlement and links to other market infrastructures. It lists no MiFID II exemption. This is not a general waiver from European market rules: the operator has a specific permission, within a pilot framework, and remains subject to the requirements and conditions that apply to its activities.
That distinction also clarifies why the license is commercially meaningful. A single operator can combine trading and post-trade functions in the DLT system, potentially reducing the hand-offs between a venue, a central securities depository and other providers. But a license does not itself create a deep market, make every token eligible or ensure interoperability with legacy settlement systems. ESMA’s review of the regime found that early uptake was limited and identified legal and operational friction, including interoperability and access to central bank money, as issues for the broader pilot.
Seturion’s Open Network Has to Win Participants
Seturion is intended to connect banks, brokers and trading venues to a shared settlement platform. Boerse Stuttgart says it supports public and private blockchains and can settle against on-chain money or central bank money. The group says banks and brokers could reduce settlement costs by as much as 90% and achieve shorter cycles through direct peer-to-peer settlement. That figure is the company’s estimate, not an independently reported result. Savings will depend on the asset, transaction volume, existing post-trade costs, connectivity and how much of a participant’s workflow can move to the platform.
The group has been building a network ahead of the license. Société Générale, SG-FORGE and flatexDEGIRO joined Seturion as strategic partners, while Nasdaq plans to connect its European venues. SG-FORGE can provide euro and dollar stablecoins for settlement under that partnership. Seturion has also been described as open to further participants rather than a closed, single-group network.
Connecting trading venues that do not hold their own DLT TSS license could widen distribution, but the allocation of responsibilities still needs to be clear. A venue may handle order matching and participant access while Seturion performs settlement. Participants will need to know which entity handles recordkeeping, failed transfers, asset servicing, corporate actions, disputes and recovery if a smart contract or network becomes unavailable. The business case depends on simplifying those steps without creating a new set of isolated links around a common ledger.
The Cash Leg Is a Decisive Design Choice
Tokenised securities can settle only as efficiently as the cash used to pay for them. On-chain money can keep both legs of a transaction within a digital workflow, while central bank money offers a public-sector settlement asset but requires the relevant technical and operational access. These options are not interchangeable. Stablecoins introduce issuer, redemption and liquidity considerations; central bank money requires infrastructure and participation arrangements. The license’s specific cash-settlement permissions therefore matter as much as its headline authorization.
The debate is already broader than one platform. The Eurosystem’s Pontes project is intended to connect DLT platforms with central-bank settlement, while FinanceFeeds has examined how tokenised trading can remain fragmented after execution. Seturion’s support for both on-chain money and central bank money could make it a bridge across these models, if the integrations become operational and market participants agree on common standards.
A License Resolves One Risk, Not the Adoption Problem
Seturion CEO Lidia Kurt said the authorization enables the platform to build a regulated post-trade system open to European banks, brokers and venues. Boerse Stuttgart Group CEO Matthias Voelkel framed it as a step toward a more unified capital market. The authorization removes a regulatory barrier for the group’s model, but execution now turns to onboarding, technology integration and the economics of moving real flow.
European market infrastructure has spent years building national systems, legal conventions and operating relationships. Replacing or connecting them requires more than a blockchain settlement engine. Seturion will need issuers to bring assets, venues to route transactions, intermediaries to integrate and institutions to trust the finality and servicing model. The distinction between “first exchange group” and “first European DLT TSS” is not just semantic: it points to a competitive field that already includes specialist operators. Boerse Stuttgart’s advantage will depend on its existing venue relationships and ability to make the open network useful at scale.

articles.title: FTSE 100 Declines as UK Inflation Rises to 3.5% in September - Yahoo Finance UK
articles.summary: FTSE 100 Declines as UK Inflation Rises to 3.5% in September  Yahoo Finance UK
articles.full_text:
The FTSE 100 traded lower on Wednesday after UK inflation accelerated more than expected in September, adding to uncertainty over the Bank of England's interest rate outlook. Oil prices also advanced amid continuing tensions in the Middle East and concerns about energy supplies.
The FTSE 100 declined 0.24% as of 07:18 GMT, while European equity markets showed mixed movements. Germany's DAX fell 0.16%, while France's CAC 40 gained 0.10%.
Sterling weakened 0.02% against the US dollar to $1.3379.
Figures released by the Office for National Statistics showed that UK consumer price inflation increased to 3.5% in September, compared with 3.1% in August.
The annual reading exceeded economists' expectations of 3.4% and represented the highest inflation rate since October 2025.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices rose 0.4%, compared with forecasts for a 0.3% increase.
Core inflation, which excludes certain volatile components, was in line with expectations at 2.8%.
Fuel prices contributed to the inflation backdrop, with petrol averaging 169.5 pence per litre, its highest level since August 2022.
The figures were released ahead of the UK Government's Budget, scheduled for 28 October, and added to market discussions about the potential direction of monetary policy.
Higher inflation has raised questions about whether the Bank of England may need to increase interest rates to contain price pressures.
Geopolitical developments also remained a focus for financial markets, particularly diplomatic efforts involving the United States and Iran and the implications for international shipping routes.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said several countries were participating in diplomatic discussions concerning Iran, with mediation efforts continuing.
Rubio indicated that any agreement would ultimately require a decision by President Donald Trump. He also described reaching an agreement as extremely difficult and said economic pressure would continue until Iran stopped targeting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the strait would remain closed until Washington accepted Tehran's conditions. Indirect negotiations were continuing through Pakistan and Qatar.
Trump separately indicated that he expected the conflict to conclude quickly and suggested that oil prices would decline substantially following its resolution.
In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told parliament that a suspected plot involving RAF Fairford was almost certainly directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard. Police had re-arrested two men in connection with the matter.

articles.title: Stock Market Crash: Key factors behind the steep Sensex-Nifty sell-off on Oct 21 - TradingView
articles.summary: Stock Market Crash: Key factors behind the steep Sensex-Nifty sell-off on Oct 21  TradingViewSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
Indian equity markets wiped out over ₹8 lakh crore in investor wealth on Wednesday, October 21, as a sharp intraday reversal dragged the benchmark indices lower. The sell-off came after the markets had opened higher, with the Sensex falling more than 1,300 points from its intraday high and the Nifty slipping nearly 2% from its peak before recovering some losses.
At the close, the Sensex fell 143 points to 73,710, while the Nifty 50 declined 78 points to 22,811. The broader market remained under pressure, with the Nifty Midcap index falling nearly 2% and the Smallcap index declining around 2.4%.
Here are the key factors that may have contributed to Wednesday's market decline:
Higher crude oil prices
Brent crude prices climbed above $110 a barrel on Wednesday, renewing concerns over India's oil import bill and the potential impact of elevated energy costs on inflation and corporate profitability. India is a major crude oil importer, making domestic markets sensitive to sustained increases in oil prices.
Rising bond yields
Higher bond yields remained another concern for investors. Rising yields can make bonds more attractive relative to equities and increase borrowing costs. However, the specific claim that India's 10-year government bond yield touched 7.43%, its highest level since 2023, should be retained only after verifying the relevant market data for Wednesday.
Sharp reversal after an early rally
The benchmark indices opened higher and climbed nearly 1% before reversing sharply during the session. The Sensex fell more than 1,300 points from its intraday high, while the Nifty dropped nearly 2% from its peak. The reversal suggests that selling intensified after the early gains, although the move alone does not establish a single cause.
Stock-specific earnings pressure
Company-specific developments added to the weakness in several stocks. Bajaj Finance fell over 3% amid concerns about its margin outlook. ABB India declined 6% following ABB PLC's results, while SRF dropped 5% after a weak set of results, with most segments missing estimates. Vishal Mega Mart fell nearly 5% after reporting lower same-store sales growth.
Auto stocks also declined around 2–3% as investors reacted to October vehicle registration data. These moves added to the pressure across sectors and the broader market.
What next for the market?
Sudeep Shah of SBI Securities identified the 22,670–22,690 zone as a crucial support for the Nifty, with resistance at 22,980–23,000. A break below the support zone could expose the index to the next support at 22,500–22,520.

articles.title: UK inflation: What is the rate and why are prices still rising? - BBC
articles.summary: UK inflation: What is the rate and why are prices still rising?  BBC
articles.full_text:
What is happening to UK prices?
Inflation in the UK rose to 3.5% in the year to September, the highest rate in nearly a year and above the Bank of England's 2% target.
The rise was slightly higher than economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices.
Inflation is widely expected to rise again in the coming months.
What is inflation?
Inflation is the increase in the price of something over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs £1 but is £1.05 a year later, then annual milk inflation is 5%.
How is the UK's inflation rate measured and what does it mean for UK interest rates?
The prices of hundreds of everyday items, including food and fuel, are tracked by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
This virtual "basket of goods" is regularly updated to reflect shopping trends, with alcohol-free beer, dashboard cameras, and pet grooming equipment among items added in 2026, while premium bottled lager and sheets of wrapping paper were removed.
The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation.
The main inflation measure is called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), and the latest figure is published every month.
The Bank of England looks closely at the inflation figures when deciding whether to increase, lower or hold its base interest rate, which is currently 3.75%.
Putting rates up makes borrowing more expensive, giving people and businesses less money to spend, reducing demand for goods and slowing price rises.
But it is a careful balancing act – increasing borrowing costs also risks harming the economy.
For example, homeowners face higher mortgage repayments, which can outweigh better savings deals.
Businesses also borrow less, making them less likely to create jobs. Some may cut staff and reduce investment.
What is happening to UK inflation?
Although CPI inflation of 3.5% remains above the Bank of England's 2% target, it is well below the 11.1% figure reached in October 2022 as gas and oil prices soared in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
That was the highest rate for 40 years.
While inflation has fallen significantly since then, prices have not. They have just risen less quickly.
The higher figure for September was mostly caused by higher prices for motor fuel, which rose by 29.8% compared to September last year.
Food price inflation remained at 1.3%.
But it can take a year for changes in the cost of food to filter through to the shop floor because of the way supply chains work, so prices could still rise as a result of the widespread disruption caused by the war in Iran.
How do energy prices affect UK inflation?
Inflation soared in 2022 because oil and gas were in greater demand after the Covid pandemic, and energy prices surged again when Russia invaded Ukraine.
Before the war in the Middle East broke out, UK inflation had been expected to be at or around the target level of 2% over the next five years, according to the official forecasts published in March 2026.
But in April, the Bank of England warned that disruption to global energy markets could push UK inflation as high as 6% in the worst-case scenario.
When the latest ceasefire took effect, analysts said it could limit further inflation hikes. Oil prices initially fell sharply after the deal was announced, but have risen again since the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July.
As a result, UK petrol prices are likely to climb back up. This - coupled with the 4% increase in household energy bills from 1 October when the latest Ofgem price cap took effect - is expected to push UK inflation higher.
As part of his pledge to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living, Prime Minister Andy Burnham scrapped VAT on household electricity bills in October. It is predicted to have a small downward impact on inflation.
Precisely because food and energy prices can be very volatile, the Bank of England also considers other economic measures such as "core inflation", which excludes these costs.
Core CPI was 2.8% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 2.6% in the 12 months to August.
What is happening to UK interest rates and will they fall again?
The Bank cut interest rates six times between August 2024 and June 2026, which brought rates down to 3.75%, the lowest level since early 2023.
In April, the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee indicated it would act "forcefully" if oil prices did not start to fall, with up to six rate hikes in a worst-case scenario.
At its September meeting, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.
Are wages keeping up with inflation?
The Bank also looks closely at what is happening to wages and unemployment.
The latest official figures show that regular pay in the UK grew ahead of inflation in the three months to August.
Average annual growth in pay, excluding bonuses, during the three-month period was 3.7%.
After taking inflation into account, it means regular pay grew by 0.8% between June and August.
What is happening to inflation and interest rates in Europe and the US?
The US and eurozone countries have also been trying to limit price increases, but also face challenges with inflation.
The inflation rate for countries using the euro was 3.8% in September, according to EU data - up from 3.2% in August.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice in recent months to 2.5%.
US inflation was in 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August, with prices there also affected by higher fuel costs.
The Federal Reserve cited "too high" inflation when it raised interest rates for the first time in three years in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%.
The move came despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.

articles.title: UK inflation rises to 3.5% in September: ONS - Mortgage Strategy
articles.summary: UK inflation rises to 3.5% in September: ONS  Mortgage Strategy
articles.full_text:
UK inflation has risen to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) reveals.
The latest figure is an increase on August when inflation stood at 3.1%.
Last month, the Bank of England decided to hold base rate at 3.75%, with the hope of keeping inflation under control.
The Monetary Policy Committee’s next meeting is on 5 November, the week following the Autumn Budget.
The latest data marks two years since inflation was below the BoE’s 2% target.
Commenting on today’s inflation data, Sprive chief executive Jinesh Vohra says the increase “puts further pressure on the Bank of England to keep interest rates higher for longer, with a rate rise now very likely”.
“Mortgages are already at a three year high, and a rate rise could mean mortgage rates remain higher for longer, putting even more pressure on household budgets.”
SPF Private Clients chief executive Mark Harris suggests the chance of an interest rate rise before the end of the year looks “increasingly likely” given the rise in inflation.
Harris adds: “Swap rates, which underpin the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages, have been volatile in recent weeks, resulting in mixed pricing movements by lenders with some trimming rates while others increase pricing. The average shelf-life of products has also contracted as lenders try to deal with changing funding costs.”
Mortgage Advice Bureau strategic relationship director Rachel Geddes says: “After two rises in a row, a third was always a real possibility, so today’s figure of 3.5% doesn’t tell us anything we didn’t expect.”
“There is some good news, though. In the three months to July, regular wages were 3.5% higher than a year earlier, according to the Office for National Statistics. Once rising prices are taken into account, that’s an increase of 0.6%, so pay is only just ahead of prices.”

articles.title: Philippines Leads ASEAN Cement Federation to Drive Decarbonization and Sustainability - Daily Tribune
articles.summary: Philippines Leads ASEAN Cement Federation to Drive Decarbonization and Sustainability  Daily Tribune
articles.full_text:
The Philippines has assumed leadership of the ASEAN Federation of Cement Manufacturers (AFCM) for the 2026–2028 term, positioning local industry leaders to help steer regional efforts on decarbonization, energy costs and excess production capacity.
The leadership transition was formalized during the 47th AFCM Council Meeting and 23rd AFCM Conference, held from 14 to 16 October 2026 in Bali, Indonesia. Industry representatives discussed the sector’s challenges and opportunities, including decarbonization and the long-term competitiveness of ASEAN cement producers.
The AFCM represents cement industry associations from eight countries: Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
During the council meeting, members elected John Reinier Dizon, president of the Cement Manufacturers Association of the Philippines (CeMAP) and Republic Cement, as AFCM president. Roberto Martin Gerardo Javier, commercial vice president of Concreat Holdings Philippines, was elected secretary general, while CeMAP executive director Renato Baja was named deputy secretary general.
Dizon emphasized the importance of responsible leadership in ensuring the industry remains sustainable for future generations.
“We are caretakers of this industry. Our responsibility is to leave it better for future generations,” he said.
Under Philippine leadership, AFCM will continue advancing its regional decarbonization agenda through the wider adoption of low-carbon cement, alternative fuels, supplementary cementitious materials and energy-efficient technologies. The federation will also pursue business development initiatives to help strengthen the industry’s long-term competitiveness.
These efforts aim to reduce cement production’s environmental footprint while preserving the sector’s ability to supply materials for the region’s growing infrastructure requirements.
ASEAN cement markets face common pressures from excess regional production capacity, volatile energy prices and increasingly demanding sustainability requirements. The Philippines will work with member countries to strengthen knowledge-sharing, encourage technological innovation and deepen regional cooperation.
The federation’s agenda will seek to balance environmental commitments with the need to maintain competitive cement industries capable of supporting infrastructure development and economic growth across Southeast Asia.
Through its leadership role, the Philippines aims to contribute to a more competitive, resilient and sustainable ASEAN cement industry while helping advance the region’s transition toward a lower-carbon future.

articles.title: UK inflation jumps to higher-than-expected 3.5%: What this means for borrowers and savers - The Scotsman
articles.summary: UK inflation jumps to higher-than-expected 3.5%: What this means for borrowers and savers  The Scotsman
articles.full_text:
“It’s not just that everyday essentials cost more, it’s that the prospect of cheaper borrowing is moving further away”
The latest grim news on the inflation run was even worse than most economists had been anticipating, but perhaps it shouldn’t have come as a surprise.
As energy bills creep ever higher and prices at the pumps hover around record levels the general rate of inflation has risen to its highest rate in almost a year.
The latest official figures show the annual measure of consumer prices index (CPI) inflation hitting 3.5 per cent in September, up from 3.1 per cent in August, and above the 3.4 per cent reading that most experts had been expecting. September’s figure is the highest CPI rate since the 3.6 per cent recorded in October last year, though it remains well below the 11.1 per cent peak recorded in October 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the subsequent spike in oil prices.
Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly motor fuels. Average petrol and diesel prices reached their highest level in four years in September, according to the latest Office for National Statistics’ (ONS) data.
The higher-than-expected headline inflation rise to 3.5 per cent continues an unwelcome upward trend, and will put pressure on the Bank of England (BoE) to hike interest rates as it attempts to get the rate back towards its 2 per cent long-term target while avoiding strangling economic growth. The central bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) is due to meet on two more occasions before the turn of the year - November 5 and December 17.
A hike next month is now looking increasingly likely, indeed many analysts see a quarter-point increase in the bank base rate to 4 per cent a dead certainty, and there will be further pain ahead for millions of borrowers.
Felix Feather, economist at Aberdeen Investments, said: “The UK’s headline inflation rate jumped from 3.1 per cent to 3.5 per cent in September, locking in a Bank of England hike in November.
“Fuel prices were the most important factor driving the increase. But, importantly, core inflation also picked up from 2.6 per cent to 2.8 per cent. The rise in services inflation from 3.4 per cent to 3.7 per cent is particularly concerning, as it mostly reflects domestic factors rather than the cost of imports. And the rise of inflation isn’t done yet.
“We expect the headline rate to peak over 4 per cent in the first quarter of 2027 after the cap on household energy bills is lifted by around 25 per cent. That should prompt a further BoE hike in February next year,” he added.
If, or more likely when, interest rates head north, existing fixed-rate mortgage holders will not see their payments change immediately, but people approaching the end of a deal are likely to face significantly higher refinancing costs. Those average fixed rates are already sitting close to 6 per cent.
Savers may benefit if interest rates remain higher for longer, but experts have warned that the figure advertised on an account does not tell the full story. Any savings rate below 3.5 per cent at present would fail to keep pace with inflation, meaning the money would continue to lose purchasing power.
Philly Ponniah, chartered wealth manager and financial coach at Philly Financial, said: “Inflation rising to 3.5 per cent is another blow for households already feeling squeezed. It’s not just that everyday essentials cost more, it’s that the prospect of cheaper borrowing is moving further away.
“For mortgage holders, higher inflation increases the pressure on the Bank of England to keep interest rates higher or raise them further. Those on fixed deals have some protection for now, but anyone re-mortgaging needs to prepare for potentially higher repayments.
“For savers, higher interest rates might sound like good news, but it’s the return after inflation that really matters. If your savings earn 3 per cent while inflation is 3.5 per cent, you’re still losing purchasing power.”
Kevin Brown, savings expert at Glasgow-based financial mutual Scottish Friendly, added: “For consumers, making sure savings are earning a competitive return after inflation, building a financial buffer where possible, and considering longer-term investing when it makes sense to do so remain sensible ways to protect their finances.”
Overall, motor fuels soared by 30 per cent in the year to September, up from a 23 per cent annual rise in August, the ONS data showed. Between August and September, average petrol prices rose by 8.2p to 169.5p per litre, which was the highest price recorded in around four years. Diesel surged by 10.7p to 192.5p, the highest price since July 2022.
According to RAC figures, average diesel prices surpassed 200p a litre for the first time ever at the beginning of this month.
Fuel costs have been soaring because of the conflict in the Middle East which has squeezed global oil and gas supplies.
ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said: “Inflation climbed notably in September to its highest annual rate in almost a year. Increased fuel prices were again the main driver, with the cost of diesel the highest since July 2022.
“Other upward pressures included airfares and, to a lesser extent, computer games and live events, which are often volatile. These were partially offset by the cost of hotel stays, where prices rose by less than this time last year.
“The annual cost of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continued to rise, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively.”

articles.title: Why Treasury yields move together but become more volatile further out the curve - investingLive
articles.summary: Why Treasury yields move together but become more volatile further out the curve  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- Treasury yields across the curve are primarily driven by expectations for the future path of Federal Reserve monetary policy. The front end is more directly tied to near-term rate expectations, while the long end is more sensitive to changes in growth and inflation expectations while also having a term premium. This explains why yields across different maturities tend to move together, but changes in yields can become larger and more volatile further out the curve.
Treasury yields are primarily driven by expectations for the future path of Federal Reserve monetary policy. This relationship is especially strong at the front end of the yield curve, where yields are closely linked to expectations about how the Fed will adjust interest rates over the near-term. However, monetary policy expectations remain important even at the long end of the curve. The difference is that longer-term yields are also more sensitive to changes in the economic outlook, inflation expectations and the compensation investors demand for holding long-duration bonds, called term premium.
The front-end is driven by monetary policy expectations
The 2-year Treasury yield is one of the most useful indicators of market expectations for Federal Reserve policy. If markets begin to expect the Fed to raise interest rates in the coming months, the two-year yield will generally rise. Conversely, if economic data weakens or inflation moderates, markets will start to price in rate cuts and the 2-year yield will generally fall.
The key point is that markets are forward-looking. Treasury yields reflect expectations for future short-term interest rates over the life of the bond. Consequently, yields will move well before the Fed actually changes its policy rate. That doesn't mean the market will always be right. Sometimes the market gets things wrong, but the change in expectations still drives yields higher or lower depending on the economic context and incoming information.
The long-end is still driven by monetary policy expectations
The 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields are often framed as though they move independently of the Fed. But that's misleading. Expectations for monetary policy remain a fundamental driver of longer-term yields, but their influence is more complex because investors must consider a much longer economic horizon.
A longer-term Treasury yield can be decomposed into two components: expected future short-term interest rates and a term premium. The first component links long-term yields directly to monetary policy expectations. If investors expect the Fed to maintain restrictive policy for longer, or believe that short-term rates will settle at a higher level over the coming decade, longer-term yields will generally face upward pressure.
The second component helps explain why long-term yields can move significantly even when expectations for the federal funds rate change very little. The term premium can rise when uncertainty about inflation increases for example, as investors will demand greater compensation for bearing duration risk. Changes in the supply and demand for Treasuries can also influence this premium, although it's a very minor part. The term premium is not seomthing that is observable or can be accurately calculated. It changes based on the economic context.
Chart: Federal Funds Rate (black), 2y yield (red), 5y yield (green), 10y yield (violet), 30y yield (blue)
Long-term yields are more sensitive to growth and inflation
Although monetary policy expectations matter across the entire yield curve, the further we move out in maturity, the more economic developments can influence the outlook for interest rates over the longer run.
Suppose we get a very strong US PMI report that changes expectations about growth. The data might lead markets to expect more Fed rate hikes, pushing the 2-year yield higher, but the implications for the 10-year yield can extend beyond the next few Fed meetings. Stronger growth could imply a higher equilibrium real interest rate, stronger underlying demand and potentially greater inflationary pressure. If investors think that the economy can sustain higher interest rates over the long run, long-term yields may rise by more than the 2-year yield.
This is what generally leads to a bear steepening of the curve as long-term bonds fall faster than short-term bonds. That's exactly what happened after the September's US Flash PMI, as you can see in the chart below.
The same logic applies to inflation. A temporary increase in inflation might change expectations for the next few Fed meetings, but a persistent inflation shock can alter expectations for inflation over many years. Investors may also demand a higher term premium because of increased uncertainty.
The reverse is also true. A deterioration in the growth outlook can push yields lower as markets anticipate monetary easing. This is why before an economic slowdown or even a recession, the 10-year yield falls faster than the 2-year yield. This can happen even during a Federal Reserve tightening cycle if the markets think that the central bank overtightened and will have to cut interest rates sooner than expected.
This is why longer-term yields can experience larger swings than shorter-term yields. They reflect not only the expected response of monetary policy in the near-term but also changing views about the economy over a longer horizon.

articles.title: UK inflation jumps to highest rate in almost a year after fuel prices climb - EDP24
articles.summary: UK inflation jumps to highest rate in almost a year after fuel prices climb  EDP24
articles.full_text:
UK inflation has risen to its highest rate in almost a year as surging petrol and diesel prices pushed up the cost of living, new figures show.
The rate of Consumer Prices Index (CPI) inflation was 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.
This was the highest CPI rate since the 3.6% recorded in October last year, and came in above the 3.4% that most economists had been expecting for the month.
It means the price of goods and services across the economy are rising at a faster rate than they were before, and inflation is drifting further away from the Bank of England’s 2% target rate.
Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly at the pump.
Overall, motor fuels soared by 30% in the year to September, up from a 23% annual rise in August, ONS data showed.
Between August and September, average petrol prices rose by 8.2p to 169.5p per litre, which was the highest price recorded in around four years.
Diesel also surged by 10.7p to 192.5p, the highest price since July 2022.
According to RAC figures, average diesel prices surpassed 200p a litre for the first time ever at the beginning of this month.
Fuel costs have been soaring because of the Iran war which has squeezed global oil and gas supplies.
ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said: “Inflation climbed notably in September to its highest annual rate in almost a year.
“Increased fuel prices were again the main driver, with the cost of diesel the highest since July 2022.
“Other upward pressures included airfares and, to a lesser extent, computer games and live events, which are often volatile.
“These were partially offset by the cost of hotel stays, where prices rose by less than this time last year.
“The annual cost of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continued to rise, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively.”
Responding to the new figures, Chancellor John Healey said: “We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide.”
But he said the Government’s decision on Wednesday to begin drilling in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea was investment “in our clean energy future and supporting British workers”.
“In my Budget next week, I will keep up this momentum,” he said.
“Maintaining our fiscal discipline and drive for growth in every postcode, while giving businesses and families some breathing space.”
Experts said the latest figures could put more pressure on Mr Healey to unveil new cost-of-living support measures in his autumn Budget statement next week.
Suren Thiru, chief economist for the Institute of Chartered Accountants England and Wales (ICAEW), said inflation was “deepening the financial squeeze on households and businesses”.
“Rising inflation is turning the Budget into a perilous high-wire act for the Chancellor, increasing pressure for cost-of-living support while pushing up Government borrowing costs, which is shrinking fiscal headroom and narrowing his policy options,” he said.
It also means mortgage holders and borrowers are facing the prospect of higher interest rates next month, economists think.
Martin Sartorius, lead economist for the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said September’s inflation rise means an interest rate hike was “firmly on the table” at the Bank of England’s next meeting in November.
He said the Bank’s rate-setting will likely want to “guard against the risk of persistently higher headline inflation” feeding through to other parts of the economy, like shop prices and wages.
Most economists expect inflation to rise further in the months ahead, with an increase to Ofgem’s price cap on household energy bills kicking in at the start of October, meaning higher prices for dual-fuel households over the winter.
Meanwhile, the September inflation rate is typically used to decide the level of increase for many benefits, such as universal credit, tax credits and disability benefits.
This rate is also a key part of the pension triple lock, which is used to decide how much pensions will increase by in the following April.
But the increase is based on either this inflation rate, average earnings growth between May and July, or 2.5%.
State pensions are, therefore, widely expected to increase by 3.9% next year based on wage growth figures which is the highest of the three.
The data also showed that Consumer Price Index including Housing (CPIH), the ONS’s preferred measure of inflation, rose to 3.6% in September from 3.3% last month.
Meanwhile, Retail Prices Index (RPI) inflation rose to 3.9% from 3.4% in August.

articles.title: Asia must guard against another financial crisis, Philippines central bank chief says - The Star
articles.summary: Asia must guard against another financial crisis, Philippines central bank chief says  The Star
articles.full_text:
BANGKOK: Asian countries must remind themselves about what happened during the region's financial crisis in the late 1990s and guard against a recurrence of such shocks, the head of the Philippine central bank said on Wednesday.
Before the Asian financial crisis started in 1997, regional economies saw huge capital inflows that prompted the World Bank to describe it as the "East Asian miracle," Eli Remolona, governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Philippines, said in an IMF panel on the outlook for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
"Investment poured into Asia, and then you had the crisis because it wasn't really a miracle. I think we have to remind ourselves about that. We have to guard against that kind of crisis," he said. "We have not really been making a lot of effort looking at that kind of crisis."
The remarks came at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank being held in Bangkok, Thailand, which was an epicentre of the Asian financial crisis.
Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, pushed back against the view, arguing in the panel discussion that the IMF has made progress assessing financial vulnerabilities and potential spillovers among each economy.
"We have taken (the crisis) to heart, and we've dealt with a framework to talk about how should countries deal with volatile capital flows in terms ... such as when should they intervene in foreign exchange markets and so on," Srinivasan said.
Srinivasan also said while ASEAN economies have weathered the trade tensions caused by US tariffs fairly well, their energy intensity could be among risks to the outlook as some countries rely heavily on oil and gas imports.
Atsushi Mimura, Japan's vice finance minister for international affairs, also cited the energy shock from the Middle East conflict, as well as rising inflation, as among short-term risks to the region's outlook.
"Of course, we all know that (fiscal support) should be 'triple T' - targeted, tailored and temporary," Mimura said on how economies should exercise discipline in delivering spending to cushion the blow to households and firms from the energy shock.
As many countries face competitive pressure from China, ASEAN countries should focus on further strengthening investment to diversify supply chains in critical minerals and energy, Mimura said, a drive Japan was willing to support.
"All ASEAN countries should definitely further invest so that they can always catch up with AI and innovation," Mimura told the panel. "At the same time, I think ASEAN countries are really well positioned in the supply chain for digitalisation because they're producing critical minerals."
The 11-member ASEAN bloc comprises Brunei, Cambodia, East Timor, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. - Reuters

articles.title: Ambani’s Jio seeks India’s biggest-ever US$108 billion IPO: Will investors bite? - The Business Times
articles.summary: Ambani’s Jio seeks India’s biggest-ever US$108 billion IPO: Will investors bite?  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
The listing comes as foreign portfolio investors steadily withdraw money from local equities
[BENGALURU] Jio Platforms, which has transformed how millions of Indians connect to the Internet, is preparing for an initial public offering of 302 billion rupees (US$3.2 billion), in what is set to be India’s largest.
The listing will test whether its earnings and growth prospects can justify a US$108 billion valuation, while offering a gauge of foreign investor appetite for India amid sustained equity outflows.
Public bidding opened on Wednesday (Oct 21).
So far, institutional investors’ response has been strong. Jio’s anchor-investor book attracted bids worth 2.5 trillion rupees, about 30 times the amount reserved for the category, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The investor pool included global asset managers such as BlackRock and Fidelity Investments, alongside sovereign wealth funds including Singapore’s GIC, going by the company’s filing.
Jio’s listing could strengthen its capacity to pursue investments in areas such as satellite connectivity and data centres, while potentially positioning it for future network technologies, including 6G, said Mahesh Uppal, a telecommunications policy and regulatory expert and director at Com First (India).
Jio, the telecoms and digital services business controlled by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, has set an IPO price band of 1,065 to 1,119 rupees a share, valuing the company at up to 10.3 trillion rupees.
That would make it India’s fourth-largest listed company by market capitalisation, after Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank.
Growth built on scale
India’s mobile broadband market is dominated by three private operators, which together accounted for more than 97 per cent of subscribers as at Jun 30.
Jio led with a 49.78 per cent market share, followed by Bharti Airtel at 35.47 per cent, and Vodafone Idea, 12.51 per cent. State-owned Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) held the remaining 2.2 per cent.
Emkay Research in a note said that Jio had scaled to 1.5 trillion rupees in revenue in the 2026 financial year, within a decade of its launch. Revenue from operations grew at a compound annual growth rate of 15.8 per cent between FY2024 and FY2026.
When the company launched in 2016, it offered free voice calls and aggressively priced data, forcing established operators to slash tariffs and accelerating the adoption of mobile Internet.
What had been an expensive service for many consumers became accessible to a much wider population, helping fuel the growth of digital payments, online entertainment and other Internet-based services.
The launch was also a defining moment in Ambani’s strategy to diversify Reliance Industries, a sprawling conglomerate with longstanding interests in energy and petrochemicals, into telecoms and digital services.
The result is a scale few telecoms operators can match. As at June 2026, it had 533.3 million customers, accounted for about half of the country’s wireless broadband subscribers and carried roughly 60 per cent of its wireless data traffic.
Jio’s average revenue per user, a key measure of how much the company earns from each customer, rose from 182 rupees in FY2024 to 214 rupees in FY2026, and reached 216 rupees in the first quarter of FY2027.
Tariff increases and greater adoption of premium plans could improve monetisation, while bundled services and enterprise offerings could deepen customer relationships.
The bigger opportunity, however, lies in generating incremental revenue beyond connectivity, said Prabhu Ram, vice-president of the industry research group at CyberMedia Research.
“Jio’s scale provides a powerful platform, but investors will increasingly judge it on returns on capital and earnings growth, rather than subscriber numbers alone,” he said.
Can the premium be justified?
Jio’s valuation appears to carry a premium, although Reliance businesses have historically commanded higher valuations, said Faisal Kawoosa, chief analyst of Techarc.
Jio’s strategy also sets it apart from a conventional telecom operator, he added. By building digital services alongside its connectivity business, it has positioned itself to benefit from the expansion of India’s digital economy.
At the upper end of its IPO price band, Jio is valued at about 33.3 times its FY2026 earnings and 15.6 times its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, based on Emkay Research’s calculations, a premium that puts the spotlight on how much growth investors are already pricing in.
The offering is set to break India’s IPO record, surpassing Hyundai Motor India’s 2024 listing, which raised 278.56 billion rupees.
Jio’s issue comprises entirely newly issued shares and is expected to raise up to 302.13 billion rupees, about 8.4 per cent more than Hyundai’s offering.
A test of foreign investor appetite
Jio’s IPO comes at a time when foreign portfolio investors have been steadily withdrawing money from Indian equities, with outflows exceeding 520 billion rupees in October to the week ended Oct 16.
The sustained selling has weighed on the market, making the response to one of India’s largest public offerings an important test of investor appetite for Indian assets.
The anchor allocation drew participation from more than 200 investor entities, spanning global asset managers, sovereign wealth funds, pension funds, technology-focused investors and prominent Indian family offices.
The response highlights the breadth of institutional interest in the offering, although demand from anchor investors does not necessarily indicate how the broader market will respond once the IPO opens to public investors.
Kawoosa sees the interest as primarily company-specific and sector-specific, rather than evidence that overseas investors have changed their view of India.
Ram of CyberMedia said a successful listing could help establish a valuation benchmark for India’s digital economy, and strengthen sentiment towards the country’s capital markets. But the offering alone is unlikely to reverse the broader trend of foreign investor outflows.
“One IPO cannot by itself overcome the broader headwinds facing India or reverse foreign portfolio outflows,” he said. Over the next three years, execution will be key, he added.
Jio’s shares are expected to list on the National Stock Exchange and the Bombay Stock Exchange on Oct 28, following the finalisation of share allotments on Oct 26.
