articles.title: UK inflation jumps to highest in nearly a year at 3.5% - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: UK inflation jumps to highest in nearly a year at 3.5%  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
By Suban Abdulla
LONDON, Oct 21 (Reuters) - British inflation and borrowing rose more than expected last month, according to data that will add to calls for help for households in finance minister John Healey's first budget next week and the likelihood of a Bank of England interest rate hike.
Consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% after a 3.1% increase in August, the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday.
Economists polled by Reuters had forecast a rise of 3.4% in the 12 months to September as the surge in energy prices caused by the Iran war gathered steam. The BoE had predicted a smaller rise to 3.0% in forecasts it published in July.
Last month's increase, which the ONS said was due to higher petrol and diesel costs, took inflation to its highest since October 2025.
The September inflation rate is traditionally used by the government to set increases for welfare benefits.
Separate figures showed the government borrowed more than forecast and public debt surpassed £3 trillion ($4.01 trillion), fuelled by higher debt costs which are linked to inflation and underlining the constraints facing Healey.
He is expected to offer some further support for households hit hardest by the jump in energy prices, but his options are limited by the government's fiscal rules.
"Rising inflation and record levels of debt illustrate the double dilemma facing the chancellor – how to ease cost-of-living pressures for families while keeping a lid on government borrowing," Greg Thwaites, interim chief economist at the Resolution Foundation, said.
Ruth Gregory, deputy chief economist at Capital Economics, said the higher-than-expected borrowing in recent months "reinforces our view that the chancellor will deliver a cautious budget on October 28 that has little net impact on the economy and leaves the toughest fiscal choices for next year."
UNDERLYING PRICE PRESSURES SPEED UP
Britain relies heavily on imported natural gas and the BoE is watching to see how much the energy price shock feeds into the broader economy.
Services price inflation jumped to 3.7% from 3.4% in August and was slightly higher than economists' forecasts of 3.6%.
Excluding food, energy, alcohol and tobacco, inflation picked up to 2.8% from 2.6% and was also above expectations.
"Inflation moving closer to 4% makes it harder to simply look through the shock," Adam Deasy, economist at PwC UK, said.
"The higher and longer inflation stays elevated, the greater the risk that it starts to influence wage and price-setting behaviour and the riskier it becomes to continue to wait for definitive evidence of those 'second-round' effects."

articles.title: Rougher waters for REITs amid surge in government bond yields - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: Rougher waters for REITs amid surge in government bond yields  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 12, 2026 - October 18, 2026
MALAYSIAN real estate investment trusts (M-REITs) have long been prized for their income-generating qualities. Listed REITs that distribute at least 90% of their total income qualify for a full tax exemption at the trust level, helping make regular distributions a central part of the asset class’ appeal.
But REIT investors are now demanding a higher yield as competition from government bonds has picked up. Government bond yields have surged worldwide on renewed inflation worries, higher policy rates and heavy debt issuance. The 10-year Japanese government bond yielded 3.08% on Oct 8, hovering close to its highest in three decades, while the US 10-year Treasury was about 5.27%, near levels last seen in 2002.
German, French and UK 10-year bonds have sold off, with yields rising significantly by 62, 131 and 97 basis points (bps) respectively this year.
The sell-off has several causes. Higher oil and energy prices from the prolonged Middle East conflict have revived inflation concerns, while resilient growth has made investors less confident that policy rates will fall soon. Heavy government borrowing has added to bond supply and, some analysts say, artificial intelligence-related corporate borrowing is competing with US Treasuries for fixed-income capital.
Central banks have moved too. The US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate by 25bps in September, its first hike since 2023, while the European Central Bank has raised rates twice this year. The Bank of Japan has lifted its policy rate twice in 2026 to 1.25%, while India’s central bank joined the tightening cycle on Oct 7 with a 25bps hike to 5.5%.
Bank Negara Malaysia has yet to follow. It held the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) at 2.75% on Sept 3 — the seventh straight meeting without a change — and said it would remain vigilant. Governor Datuk Seri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said the central bank’s response would depend on what is driving prices: monetary policy is not an effective tool if inflation is driven solely by cost pressures, but has a role if inflation is driven by demand.
For M-REIT investors however, the OPR tells only part of the story. The OPR affects REIT earnings more directly through higher borrowing costs, particularly for trusts with floating-rate debt. The more immediate valuation benchmark is the rising Malaysian Government Securities (MGS) yield, which stood at 3.96% on Oct 8, some 45bps higher year to date (YTD).
The MGS acts as a domestic risk-free benchmark against which investors judge the return offered by longer duration income assets.
Simply put, an investor may be willing to accept a 5%-6% REIT distribution yield when government bonds yield considerably less. But as the risk-free yield approaches 4%, the extra return demanded for accepting property risk, leverage and volatile unit prices also rises.
Research houses are split on where the OPR rate will head next year. Hong Leong Investment Bank (HLIB) expects a hike in the first half of 2027, while RHB expects the OPR to remain at 2.75% into the first half. MBSB meanwhile sees a possible 25bps hike in 2027. CGS International assumes no OPR increases in 2026.
Bursa Malaysia’s REIT Index has taken a hit this year, falling 7.7% compared with the FBM KLCI’s 4.7% decline YTD. AmInvestment Bank said on Sept 10 that the sector was already about 5% lower since end-July, as the 10-year MGS approached 4%. HLIB subsequently put the decline from the late July second-half high at 5.6%.
The weakness has been broad, although not uniform. Bloomberg data shows 15 of the 20 REIT and stapled-property counters tracked were lower YTD as at Oct 8, with the median trust down about 5.1%. Sentral REIT (KL:SENTRAL) was the worst performer, falling 20.8%, followed by Pavilion REIT (KL:PAVREIT) at 14.9% and Paradigm REIT (KL:PARADIGM) at 13.7%. At the other end, Al-Salam REIT (KL:ALSREIT) and AmanahRaya REIT (KL:ARREIT) have gained 18.4% and 17.9% YTD.
Underlying operations have not deteriorated to the same degree. RHB said all eight REITs under its coverage met expectations in 2Q2026, with market-cap-weighted revenue and earnings rising 14.5% and 15.6% year on year (y-o-y), respectively, though acquisitions assisted the growth. Occupancy remained broadly stable while rental reversions were positive. Axis REIT was the exception, with first-half core earnings down 4.9% on vacancies, a rental suspension and one-off maintenance costs, RHB said. AmInvestment Bank, meanwhile, puts underlying distributable income growth across Sunway REIT (KL:SUNREIT), IGB REIT (KL:IGBREIT) and Pavilion REIT at 6% excluding acquisitions.
The higher-rate environment is only one reason M-REITs have performed poorly this year. The preferential 10% final withholding-tax treatment for several categories of REIT investors expired from the Year of Assessment 2026. Resident individuals now generally include the distributions in taxable income at their prevailing tax rates, while the treatment also changed for foreign institutional investors.
The Malaysian REIT Managers Association has been lobbying for the 10% rate to return and hopes Budget 2027 will restore it. The government had signalled in February that the sector may no longer need the concession.
Jessica Low, a REITs analyst at MBSB, says the tax change has so far done more damage than higher bond yields. “Tax changes had a greater impact on M-REITs, with the KL REIT Index declining 9% from its February peak to its March low following news of the withholding tax expiry. In comparison, the KL REIT Index has fallen 7% from August to date due to higher bond yields.”
HLIB’s numbers point the same way, with a 10.4% slide for the tax against 5.6% from the late July high as at Sept 23. The comparison is not clean, however. The sell-off began on Feb 19, a month before the Inland Revenue Board’s notice, and AmInvestment Bank also lists the Middle East conflict, which flared in late February, among the factors that have weighed on the sector.
CGS estimates that reinstatement of the old preferential rate would remove a roughly 50bps to 100bps drag on post-tax yields.
The fall in REIT prices has pushed their distribution yields higher, reopening the question of whether the sector has now fallen far enough to compensate investors for the higher risk-free rate.
With the KL REIT Index providing a trailing-12-month dividend yield of 6.26%, and the 10-year MGS yielding 3.96%, the spread is currently 2.3 percentage points, according to Bloomberg data.
That spread is the additional headline yield investors receive for taking on property, leverage and equity market risk rather than holding Malaysian government debt.
To some analysts, that makes M-REITs look attractive. Low puts the spread at 220bps, which she says is “significantly higher than its eight-year average spread of 163bps and the 150bps spread recorded in July 2026”.
“We believe the weakness in M-REITs is excessive,” she says. “The wider-than-average yield spread makes M-REITs attractive from a valuation perspective.”
RHB Research’s average since 2018 is 1.71 percentage points, and HLIB notes the spread averaged 77bps from the second to the fourth quarter of 2022, the last stretch of sustained high MGS yields.
But the benchmark comparison matters. CGS International’s 10-year mean is 3.2 percentage points, which puts today’s level well below it, and another analyst, who asked not to be named, puts the historical trend at two to 2.5 points. The houses also measure the spread differently, with HLIB using trailing yields and AmInvestment Bank forward yields.
A gross spread also overstates what some holders keep. On a simplified calculation that assumes the whole distribution is taxed at the stated rate, and that MGS interest is tax free for non-residents, a non-resident individual taxed at 30% would net about 4.4% from a 6.26% gross yield, about 40bps above the MGS. Under the old 10% rate, the cushion was about 170bps.
The other pressure is on earnings, but analysts say it is limited unless the OPR rises. “If there is no change in the OPR, the impact on REIT fundamentals should be limited as rental income is largely fixed while the impact on borrowing costs is also relatively small,” Low says.
If rates did rise, she says Al-‘Aqar Healthcare REIT (KL:ALAQAR) would be the most affected, as all its borrowings are on floating rates, while Sunway REIT and Axis REIT (KL:AXREIT) “may also see some impact”, with approximately 40% of their debt exposed to floating interest rates.
Other houses put the exposure of the larger names higher. RHB Research estimates floating-rate debt at 77% of Pavilion REIT’s borrowings, 61% of Sunway REIT’s and 53% of Axis REIT’s, against 9% at IGB REIT. articles.summary: Global Monetary Tightening and Central Banks’ Policy Dilemma  https://www.usthadian.com/
articles.full_text:
Why Is Global Monetary Policy Under Pressure
Global Monetary Tightening and Central Banks’ Policy Dilemma: Central banks worldwide face a difficult balancing act as persistent inflation, elevated crude oil prices and geopolitical tensions restrict their policy choices. The prolonged conflict in West Asia, rising US Treasury yields and uncertainty over global trade have complicated decisions on interest rates.
Policymakers must control inflation without excessively weakening economic growth, investment and employment. Cutting rates too early could revive inflationary pressures, while keeping them high for too long could slow economic activity.
How the Current Cycle Differs from 2022
During 2022, major central banks, including the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank (ECB), began tightening monetary policy from exceptionally low or negative interest rates. India’s repo rate stood at 4% at the beginning of its tightening cycle.
In the current situation described in the supplied report, borrowing costs in many economies are already restrictive. Consequently, further rate increases could impose greater pressure on households and businesses, while inflationary risks may limit the scope for rate cuts.
Static GK fact: The repo rate is the rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends short-term funds to eligible banks against securities under the applicable framework.
Global Economic Outlook
Despite earlier supply-chain disruptions and higher energy costs, the global economy has shown resilience. However, prolonged geopolitical tensions, unpredictable tariff policies, rising public debt and heavy investment in artificial intelligence are creating additional uncertainty.
According to the World Bank projection cited in the supplied report, global economic growth is expected to slow to 2.6% in 2026, compared with 2.9% in 2025.
Crude Oil and Inflationary Pressures
Brent crude reportedly rose to approximately $105 per barrel, compared with around $70 or lower before the US–Iran conflict began in February 2026, according to the supplied article.
Higher oil prices increase transportation, manufacturing and production costs. Businesses may pass these costs on to consumers, contributing to inflation and reducing household purchasing power.
For India, which depends substantially on imported crude oil, higher prices can increase the import bill, widen the current account deficit and put downward pressure on the rupee. Currency depreciation further raises the domestic cost of dollar-priced energy imports.
Static GK Tip: The current account records international transactions involving goods, services, primary income and secondary income, including remittances.
Rising US Treasury Yields
The supplied report states that the US 10-year Treasury yield reached 5.34% and the 30-year yield reached 5.69%. Inflation concerns, higher government borrowing and expectations of interest rates remaining elevated are among the factors contributing to rising yields.
Heavy investment in AI infrastructure, including data centres, can also increase demand for capital. Higher US yields may make dollar-denominated assets more attractive, encouraging capital to move away from emerging markets.
For India, such movements can pressure the rupee and increase imported inflation. These developments may complicate the RBI’s decisions on interest rates and liquidity.
Developed and Emerging Economies
Both developed and emerging economies must balance inflation control with growth. However, emerging markets such as India can be more exposed to imported energy costs, exchange-rate fluctuations and volatile international capital flows.
Developed economies also face inflation and borrowing-cost pressures, but their exposure to external financing and currency movements differs according to their economic structures.
Way Forward
Central banks need to assess inflation expectations, energy prices, growth and financial stability before changing policy rates. Clear communication and data-dependent decisions can help reduce uncertainty.
India can strengthen its resilience through energy-source diversification, improved domestic energy capacity, prudent fiscal management and deeper domestic capital markets. Maintaining credible inflation control while supporting sustainable growth will remain central to the RBI’s policy choices.

articles.title: Regulators Challenge Solidigm's Nasdaq IPO, Fueling SK hynix Shareholder Backlash - Businesskorea
articles.summary: Regulators Challenge Solidigm's Nasdaq IPO, Fueling SK hynix Shareholder Backlash  Businesskorea
articles.full_text:
FSS Flags Potential Duplicate Listing, Raising Concerns Over Parent Company's Valuation and Investor Protection
South Korea's financial regulators have said that SK hynix's plan to list its U.S. subsidiary Solidigm on the Nasdaq raises concerns over duplicate listing rules. The remarks mark the first time a senior financial regulator has publicly identified potential duplicate-listing concerns involving a foreign subsidiary seeking a direct listing on an overseas exchange, with implications for how South Korean companies approach overseas listings of their subsidiaries.
Lee Chan-jin, governor of the Financial Supervisory Service, said at a parliamentary audit by the National Assembly's Political Affairs Committee on Oct. 19 that the Financial Services Commission and the FSS both viewed Solidigm's proposed listing as potentially conflicting with duplicate-listing rules. Regulators are reviewing whether Solidigm would be required to file a securities registration statement in South Korea and plan to convey their concerns to SK hynix through appropriate channels.
According to investment banking sources and foreign media reports, Solidigm has selected Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley as lead underwriters and is preparing for a potential U.S. listing next year. Market estimates put its valuation at up to $150 billion, or approximately 200 trillion won, while the proposed offering is reportedly expected to raise $10 billion to $15 billion. Solidigm has also stepped up preparations by hiring a government affairs specialist formerly with Qualcomm and engaging local lobbying firms.
The main issue is corporate governance. A Solidigm listing would add another publicly traded entity to an ownership chain extending from SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won through SK Inc., SK Square, SK hynix and AI Company to Solidigm. The Korea Corporate Governance Forum has described the structure as an unprecedented five-tier case of duplicate listing and urged the board to halt the plan. Critics warn that separately listing Solidigm's enterprise solid-state drive business, or eSSD, could lead investors to discount SK hynix's valuation, creating a so-called double-counting problem.
Political opposition has also grown. Rep. Ahn Cheol-soo of the opposition People Power Party said the National Pension Service, SK hynix's second-largest shareholder, should publicly declare its intention to vote against the Solidigm listing. Rep. Kim Hyun-jung of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea warned that the case could set a precedent for other conglomerates and deepen the Korea discount. SK hynix shares have also come under pressure, falling more than 30% in October.
Others argue that the listing could be a practical way to secure funding for major investments. Solidigm is considering building a NAND flash memory production facility in New York state. Supporters of the plan say proceeds from a U.S. listing could help fund the project, reduce reliance on production facilities in China and mitigate geopolitical risks. Kim Yeong-geon, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities, said the move should be viewed not as simply spinning off a subsidiary, but as a way to monetize an acquisition and secure capital for further investment.
Although South Korean financial regulators cannot directly block a listing on a foreign exchange, scrutiny is expected to focus on whether SK hynix's board fulfills its shareholder-protection obligations under duplicate-listing guidelines introduced in August. The KOSPI Market Listing Rules require parent-company boards to meet five obligations in duplicate-listing cases, including assessing the impact on shareholders and establishing protection measures. The effectiveness of the rules remains in question, however, given that the maximum penalty for violations is reportedly capped at 2 billion won.
Attention is now turning to SK hynix's third-quarter earnings announcement, scheduled for Oct. 28. The company has said it is reviewing various options to strengthen its business competitiveness but that no decision has been finalized. It has also reiterated that long-term corporate and shareholder value will be its top priorities. Whether the company offers a fuller explanation of the Solidigm listing plan or announces additional shareholder-return measures alongside its earnings could influence the stock's next move.

articles.title: French riots may bring ECB bond-buying closer - OMFIF
articles.summary: French riots may bring ECB bond-buying closer  OMFIF
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank has been stoutly – and legitimately – resisting any suggestion of using its four-year-old bond-purchase contingency programme to help counter France’s fiscal upsets. But French riots and insurrection may bring closer attempts by France and other countries to draw on the ECB’s so far unused July 2022 ‘transmission protection instrument’ to quell capital market unrest.
The ECB is highly reluctant to make bond purchases to help mitigate France’s punishment by the capital markets for a self-inflicted infringement: insufficient attention to reducing its budget deficit.
Whether or not the ECB intervenes in coming weeks depends on a politically charged judgement by the bank’s governing council. The 27-person body would need to decide whether rising French ‘spreads’ compared with ‘safe haven’ German bonds are deemed warranted or unwarranted based on economic fundamentals.
Impending presidential election
Inevitably, if it wields the TPI, the governing council would be drawn into the political fray months before the presidential election in April 2027 – raising doubts about a dilution of its vaunted independence. Marine Le Pen, the leader of the right-wing National Rally party, the probable next French president according to opinion polls, speaks of the ECB helping the ‘harmonious development of European economies’.
She voices desire for the ECB to take a technocratic lead in promoting investment projects, similar to the original vision of François Mitterrand. The French president in 1981-95, together with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, drove the decision to set up economic and monetary union after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
The mechanism for decision-making on the TPI has been kept deliberately cloudy. In view of the political sensitivities, the ECB prefers to keep details obscure – and, if possible, not even mention the TPI, let alone deploy it. Calls have been brushed aside for a ‘user manual’ to codify the functioning of the TPI and its links with other programmes such as ‘outright monetary transactions’ unveiled in 2012. So have doubts, voiced for example by Nout Wellink, former president of De Nederlandsche Bank, on the legality of the TPI. Its use would almost certainly be contested by lawsuits at the German constitutional court.
Intrinsic dilemmas and contagion
The ECB’s decisions on introducing the TPI are designed to be guided by pre-determined economic criteria, including, crucially, the credibility and sustainability of governments’ deficit-reduction measures. The intrinsic dilemmas become still more complex if other European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) members countries are affected by ‘contagion’ triggered by capital market disturbance spreading from one particular jurisdiction.
Worries about possible politicisation of the ECB coincide with further deterioration in the long-running governance and monetary policy struggle at the National Bank of Poland – a leading shareholder in the ECB although not a member of the euro. Adam Glapinski, the NBP president, has hit back against Polish government allegations of irregularities, in a dispute that could end up paralysing Poland’s monetary decision-making.
The French flare-up has erupted when the ECB has been preoccupied by tussling over top jobs at the central bank. Three or even possibly four board posts (out of six) are due to be switched by January as a result of the early departure of Christine Lagarde, the president. An additional distraction stems from Lagarde’s decision, not disclosed to ECB board members until early September, to write her memoirs (scheduled for publication on 4 February) while still in office.
‘Asymmetric’ use of the TPI
The ECB might see a case for supporting ‘innocent bystanders’ through bond purchasing action. ‘Asymmetric’ use of the TPI – assisting the bystanders, while leaving the country at the source of the unrest unprotected – would appear to be in line with the ECB’s guiding statute outlawing monetary financing of deficits. But this would infect the offending country with an unacceptable economic and political stigma, worsening rather than alleviating overall instability.
As a sign that higher interest rates are spreading through the euro area at an uneven pace, over the last month the spread over Bunds has risen 2.4 basis points to 10 for the Netherlands, 4.5 points to 14 for Ireland, 25 points to 90 for Belgium, 18 points to 94 for Greece, 10 points to 49.3 for Portugal, 15.6 points to 62 for Spain and 41 points to 145 for France. French spreads have almost doubled since Jacques de Larosiere, former Banque de France governor, opined in an OMFIF article in September 2026 that French bonds were too expensively priced.
Another indication of concerns about dislocation has come from Lorenzo Bini Smaghi, former ECB board member and chairman of French bank Société Générale. With long-term rates rising sharply, he has called upon the ECB to put on hold the gradual reduction in its balance sheet and start purchasing bonds again as they mature.
The ECB has roundly rejected this advice up to now, saying that this would be inconsistent with its desire to maintain tight money to counter the fresh rise in integration. But if the risk of turbulence grows, the ECB may have to modify his approach and start thinking of increasing its balance sheet. In view of the fragile politics of the euro area, rather than promoting more cohesion, such a move might end up undermining it.
David Marsh is Chairman of OMFIF.

A resolution that misses the moment: our take on the EU Parliament's draft report on the ECB
This year’s European Parliament draft resolution on the ECB overlooks key threats to price stability, from Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels to growing climate risks. We look at what’s missing and how Parliament could push the ECB to better address these challenges while strengthening its democratic accountability.
Every year, one moment keeps us busy at Positive Money Europe: the European Parliament's resolution on the ECB annual report. It isn't legislation, but it matters. It's one of the few times the only directly elected EU institution gets to scrutinise a powerful, technocratic body like the European Central Bank (ECB) and say what it expects of it.
This year's draft, led by MEP Georgios Aftias from the centre-right European People's Party, has some good elements - but it feels detached from what many people across Europe are living through, and in many places are protesting about: a high cost of living that is driven largely by energy and fuel prices, and supply chains shaken by climate-related extreme events.
What the draft says, and what it leaves out
The text puts weight on the ECB’s mandate to maintain price stability - which is right and very relevant with inflation rising again. However, the ECB's secondary mandate is missing entirely. Beyond price stability, and without compromising it, the ECB is also required to support the EU's general economic policies, including sustainable development, full employment, social progress and the green transition.
The draft expresses concern about the cost of living for low-income households, as food and energy prices have climbed since the crisis in the Middle East. We share that concern, of course - but we are also concerned that the draft stops at just describing the problem.
It mentions geopolitical uncertainty and energy security risks, but it doesn’t name what links them: Europe's dependence on imported fossil fuels. As long as Europe relies on fuels priced on global markets, wars and conflicts driven by decisions in other capitals will keep feeding straight into energy bills and supermarket prices. People have gone from one price shock to the next since 2022, and by now these shocks should be predictable - and a report on price stability should say so.
The draft also says little about what renewables could do to keep prices stable over the long term. Producing more energy at home makes prices less dependent on global fuel markets, so renewables are a price stability issue as well as a climate one. That is exactly the kind of long-term view we would expect in a report on the ECB's mandate.
Sadly, in this year’s resolution there is also a renewed mention of market neutrality - the idea that the ECB should mirror the existing composition of financial markets when buying assets or accepting collateral, rather than favouring certain sectors or activities. The draft insists the ECB respect it "in all of its monetary operations at all times". It is a principle the ECB itself has said isn't in the Treaties, and one it no longer follows in practice, as its climate factor on collateral shows. The ECB's own legal analysis is clear: an open market economy does not commit the ECB to an "absolute operational concept" of market neutrality. ECB Board member Isabel Schnabel has also addressed the question in a speech.
On a more positive note, the draft backs the digital euro as essential for Europe's monetary sovereignty, stresses that cash must stay, and welcomes Pontes, the Eurosystem's first step towards making central bank money fit for a tokenised future. We welcome all of this.
Where the report should go further
The good news is that the text can still be improved.
Everything we're asking for starts from the same place: the energy shock. Inflation has been rising again in the euro area since April. Eurostat has since confirmed that it reached 3.8% in September, with energy prices up 18.8% on the year. As the ECB itself has acknowledged, this comes from Middle East-related shocks to oil, petroleum products and gas. Almost 60% of the EU's energy needs are met through imports of these fuels, so global price spikes land directly on European households and businesses. We saw the same thing in 2022. ECB Executive Board member Frank Elderson has warned that repeated energy shocks can turn temporary price rises into lasting ones. We think MEPs should say this clearly: imported fossil fuels are the main driver of current inflation and a structural threat to price stability.
Climate adds to the picture. The ECB expects food inflation to keep rising throughout 2027, partly because of this summer's heatwaves and the ongoing El Niño. Extreme weather is becoming more frequent, and research shows global warming could make El Niño more intense. Nature loss, such as soil depletion and water scarcity, still makes food production more fragile. A report about price stability should recognise that climate and nature-related risks are part of the story.
If fossil fuel dependence is the problem, renewables are part of the solution, and the evidence is there.
Research commissioned by the European Parliament itself finds a strong link between how much a country relies on fossil fuels and how much its inflation rises when fuel prices spike. Our own analysis finds that renewables cut wholesale electricity prices in Europe by an average of 24.4% between 2023 and 2025, compared to a scenario without them.
This is where monetary policy comes in. Clean energy needs large upfront investment, so it is far more sensitive to interest rates than gas-fired generation, where fuel costs matter more. In our analysis, raising rates from 2% to 6% pushes up the cost of electricity from solar with battery storage by 33%, against just 3.7% for natural gas. Across-the-board rate hikes can therefore make the clean investments that would protect us from future shocks more expensive, and prolong our exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets. That is bad news for price stability in the long run. We would like the Parliament to ask the ECB to assess how its decisions affect energy resilience, and to look at tools like green refinancing operations - meaning targeted lending operations tied to banks' lending to renewables and green transition projects. These could protect energy transition investments from higher financing costs, and would serve both the ECB's primary and secondary mandates.
There are two other important points.
On the digital euro, years of delay are enough. The legislation should move forward quickly so Europeans can benefit from a public digital means of payment that complements cash and reduces dependence on private, non-European payment providers.
The draft rightly calls the digital euro essential for Europe's monetary sovereignty, and this is now even more urgent: to preserve the EU's strategic autonomy, and the financial autonomy of its institutions and citizens, in the face of sanctions imposed by foreign powers. The US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) show what is at stake: European banks, caught between Washington's penalties and their own clients, can end up putting foreign sanctions compliance ahead of EU rules and interests.
On ECB leadership, the draft is silent, despite important changes ahead. The terms of three of the ECB's six Executive Board members expire in 2027, opening the way for a significant reshaping of the institution's leadership. These appointments are decided by EU governments, with Parliament consulted but having no power to block a candidate. Its hearings are therefore among the few opportunities for public scrutiny of a selection process that remains largely behind closed doors. Parliament should use this moment to call for a more transparent and open process, and for a Board that better reflects Europe's diversity in gender, education and professional background. That would strengthen both the ECB's legitimacy and its accountability to the public.
What's next
This draft is a starting point, and there is still time to improve it. Positive Money Europe will continue to work with MEPs as the report moves through Parliament, and we hope the final resolution will reflect what people are facing today: energy-driven prices, a changing climate, and a central bank whose decisions affect some people and businesses far more than others.

articles.title: Bank of Japan may raise inflation forecast, stand pat on rates, sources say - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: Bank of Japan may raise inflation forecast, stand pat on rates, sources say  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
By Leika Kihara and Takahiko Wada
TOKYO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - The Bank of Japan may raise its inflation outlook for the next fiscal year in forecasts due this month, as rising oil prices exert longer-than-expected price pressures on the economy, four sources familiar with the central bank's thinking said.
Having just raised interest rates last month, the BOJ is expected to keep rates steady at the two-day policy meeting ending on October 30, unless the yen renews its slide that lifts import costs and broader inflation, the sources said.
But the central bank will likely maintain its focus on mounting inflationary risks in a quarterly report due after the meeting, the sources said, leaving scope for another rate hike as soon as December.
"Consumer price growth may stay elevated for longer than expected, though there's no big change in underlying inflation," said one of the sources, a view echoed by two other sources.
"Inflation pressures exist but haven't jumped, so there's little reason to rush," another source said on the timing of the next rate hike. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to speak publicly. The BOJ was not immediately available for comment.
In forecasts made in July, the BOJ projected core consumer inflation hitting 2.5% in the current fiscal year ending in March 2027, before slowing to 2.4% the following year. The projections assumed that the pass-through of the initial spike in fuel costs would moderate from the latter half of next year.
In new forecasts due this month, the board may slightly revise up its core inflation forecast for fiscal 2027 to reflect the pass-through from the recent, renewed spike in crude oil prices, the sources said.
Any revisions will be minor with little sign that dangerous second-round effects, in which the energy shock triggers a spiral of sharp wage and price rises, are becoming embedded in the economy, they said.
The board is likely to roughly maintain its economic forecasts projecting growth of 0.6% in fiscal 2026 and 0.8% in 2027, with robust exports of AI-related goods offsetting soft consumption, the sources said.
The BOJ is unlikely to incorporate the expected impact of a two-year cut to a consumption tax on food items scheduled from April next year, as a bill to put the move into effect has yet to pass parliament, they said.
FINANCIAL CONDITIONS KEY
The BOJ raised its key rate to a 31-year high of 1.25% last month, signalling its entry into a phase focused on preventing underlying inflation from overshooting its target and raising the prospect of tighter policy.

articles.title: The informal market in Cuba closes: The dollar and the euro rise at the end of the day - CiberCuba
articles.summary: The informal market in Cuba closes: The dollar and the euro rise at the end of the day  CiberCuba
articles.full_text:
At 8:00 PM, Cuban local time, the informal currency market in Cuba ends the day this Wednesday, October 21, 2026, with the dollar and the euro rising.
The US dollar ends the day at 823 Cuban pesos, while the euro rises to 912 pesos.
The MLC, for its part, registers a reference value that should be taken with caution due to the low volume of transactions during this time period. You can check the complete evolution in the .
The United States dollar
The U.S. dollar is quoted at 823 Cuban pesos (CUP) at the close of this trading day. This represents an increase of 5 pesos compared to the previous day, when it closed at 818 CUP.
In the weekly perspective, the currency has accumulated an increase of 27.5 pesos compared to the 795 CUP recorded seven days ago, which corresponds to a rise of 3.5%.
Exchange Rate Evolution
In the past month, the dollar has climbed from 718 CUP, although it's worth noting that part of this variation may reflect methodological adjustments to the index rather than just market movement.
The highest recorded in the last 30 days is exactly today's value: 823 CUP. It continues to reflect the pulse of the informal market in a context of structural currency scarcity.
The euro
The euro rises to 912 Cuban pesos by the close of this Wednesday, compared to 908 CUP the previous day, marking an increase of 4 pesos.
In the last week, the European currency has gained 21.5 pesos compared to the 890 CUP from seven days ago, an increase of 2.4%.
The value today also represents the highest point in the last 30 days, a period during which the exchange rate started from 818 CUP. It is affirmed as the most expensive currency in the Cuban black market, exceeding the dollar by 89 pesos and consolidating its dominant position.
The MLC
The MLC records an indicative average value of 733 Cuban pesos at the end of the trading session, although the available data is limited during this time frame and the figure should be interpreted with caution.
Regarding the previous session, where it was at 587 CUP, the variation is significant, but the low volume of transactions limits the reliability of this reading.
Without a physical existence, its use is limited to state-owned businesses that accept it, which restricts its circulation compared to cash currencies.
Summary of exchange rates
- Exchange rate of the dollar USD to CUP: 823 CUP.
- Exchange rate of the euro EUR to CUP: 912 CUP.
- Exchange rate from MLC to CUP: 733 CUP (indicative value, limited data).
The official exchange rate of the Central Bank of Cuba (Segment III), at 729 CUP per dollar and 819 CUP per euro, remains well below the values that prevail in everyday practice in the informal currency market.
Although Segment III was introduced as a more flexible currency exchange mechanism, its official rate remains far from that of the informal market and fails to meet the real demand for foreign currency among the population.
In the past month, the official dollar has risen from 669 to 729 CUP, and the official euro from 767 to 819 CUP, a rising trend that, however, does not close the gap with the parallel market: today that difference is 94 pesos for the dollar and 93 pesos for the euro.
In a scenario of sustained inflation, low state wages, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy, every fluctuation in the informal market directly impacts internal prices and the purchasing power of Cubans.
The Exchange Rate of CiberCuba is an index of the informal Cuban market created through the automated analysis of thousands of currency trading posts in Telegram and Facebook groups.
The calculation dismisses atypical offers and spam messages, weighs each operation based on its age, and consolidates a representative value that is updated several times a day.

articles.title: French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets
articles.summary: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protestsFrance’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone. Continue ...
articles.full_text:
France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets.
With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat), issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%.
The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks.
Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living.
Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics, sparking riots in many towns and cities. Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges.
No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called a snap election in 2024. The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending.
France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action.
International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans.
Matthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at the currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies.
“The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said. “It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.”

articles.title: Philip R. Lane: Euro liquidity lines and the international monetary system
articles.full_text:
- SPEECH
Euro liquidity lines and the international monetary system
Remarks by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the CF40-Euro50 luncheon “Monetary System Beyond the Dollar”
Shanghai, 21 October 2026
The provision of liquidity is a basic task for a central bank.[1]
The ECB injects liquidity through its refinancing operations (currently the main refinancing operations and the longer-term refinancing operations, with very long-term refinancing operations and targeted longer-term refinancing operations deployed in the past) and asset portfolios (previously built up under the asset purchase programme and the pandemic emergency purchase programme).[2]
Since the ECB only has domestic counterparties in its refinancing operations, it is essential to complement the domestic liquidity framework with international liquidity lines. These lines, which consist of both repo and swap lines, mitigate adverse spillovers in the event of increased demand for euro liquidity abroad and/or impairment in cross-border euro liquidity flows. In the absence of international liquidity provision, such shocks might exert upward pressure on euro money market rates or disrupt the functioning of securities markets and the banking system, and thereby impair monetary policy transmission.
In recent years, the world economy has undergone profound structural shifts related to geopolitics and changes in the international financial system. These shifts have altered the dynamics of global trade and financial integration and suggest that the macroeconomic and financial environment will remain uncertain and potentially more volatile. More frequent financial disruptions and possible knock-on effects on euro area financial markets have the potential to hamper the smooth transmission of monetary policy.
Given their backstop pricing, international liquidity lines are designed to be drawn down only in response to shocks and in crisis situations. However, their mere existence – even without being drawn upon – can help to prevent adverse market dynamics from arising in the first place. Empirical evidence suggests that the ECB’s liquidity lines have been effective in reducing financial pressures on euro funding markets.[3]
This year, the ECB decided to enhance the Eurosystem repo facility for central banks (EUREP) to make it more flexible and effective in supporting the smooth transmission of euro area monetary policy.[4] Under EUREP, the Eurosystem provides backstop euro liquidity to non-euro area central banks against high-quality euro-denominated collateral, with appropriate risk mitigants. The updated framework introduces standing access, in principle, for all central banks, unless excluded on the grounds of, in particular, money laundering, terrorist financing or international sanctions. The framework will enable central banks in jurisdictions outside the euro area to swiftly address risks of euro liquidity shortages. These changes aim to make the facility more flexible, broader in terms of its geographical reach, and more relevant for global holders of euro securities.
Central banks onboarded to EUREP will receive euro liquidity in the form of loans against high-quality euro-denominated collateral, priced at the main refinancing operations (MRO) rate plus a spread set by the Governing Council to preserve the backstop character of the facility. The maturity of a single transaction will range from one day to one week and may be extended. The maximum line size per individual central bank is €50 billion. Onboarded central banks can use EUREP funds flexibly, without ex ante restrictions. After completing the onboarding process, central banks will be able to draw from the facility as of the fourth quarter of 2026. Appropriate risk mitigants are in place to adequately protect the Eurosystem. More than thirty central banks have expressed interest in EUREP in the past six months and the onboarding of first foreign central banks to the enhanced facility was completed at the beginning of October.
EUREP can be expected to exert a strong positive impact on the euro-denominated bond market, boosting the savings and investments union initiative. In particular, EUREP encourages the holding of euro-denominated debt securities by foreign central banks, which are price-insensitive investors. It also encourages the holdings of longer-duration bonds, since it enhances the liquidity of these bonds: the liquidity enhancement is considerable as EUREP offers same day liquidity of up to €50 billion off-market in a single transaction. Since reserve managers would be able to hold bonds from all euro area countries rather than just the most liquid bonds, EUREP also enhances the playing field between more liquid and less liquid euro area sovereign bonds, contributing to better integration of the euro area bond market. Importantly, this argument extends to Eurosystem-recognised supranational bonds (e.g. European Commission bonds) which suffer from lower liquidity than large sovereigns.
Swap lines complement EUREP from a monetary policy perspective, strengthening the overall international liquidity lines framework. EUREP lends against euro-denominated collateral, which enables breadth of access. However, the collateral constraint limits its role: a country may have extensive euro liabilities and excessive self-insurance (by matching euro liabilities with euro assets) would be an undesirable equilibrium, whereas the availability of swap lines can facilitate more efficient liquidity risk management.
Swap lines can be deployed against local-currency collateral, such that combined swap and EUREP access offers stronger overall support than EUREP alone. In particular, swaps are not contingent on having euro-denominated collateral. Thus, swaps have stronger signalling effects than EUREP alone in terms of access to liquidity, which helps to reduce the likelihood of escalating crises abroad and limits adverse spillovers to the euro area. In particular, provided fundamentals are sufficiently strong, the existence of swap lines can reduce the risk of adverse confidence shocks abroad becoming self-fulfilling.
There are some differences in the transmission channels of swap and repo lines, which enhances their complementarity. In particular, swap lines work more directly through the bank credit channel, as recipient foreign central banks lend euro cash to their domestic banks, which then lend to the financial system. This is consistent with the theoretical literature showing that central-bank lending programmes reduce ex-post financing risk and encourage ex-ante investment through global banks operating across integrated financial markets.
In this way, swap lines can provide deep, targeted euro liquidity support to the domestic banking system of selected partners, even if the lines are expected to be used only in times of crisis, while EUREP is mainly focused on supporting the functioning of euro-denominated debt securities markets at the global level. This is consistent with the empirical evidence that access to swap lines is associated with stronger cross-border bank credit flows, while repo-type access is closely tied to developments in securities holdings.[5]
Since swap lines entail greater risks than EUREP, it is appropriate to provide them only to foreign central banks that are clearly capable of repaying their euro debt in due course, requiring the backing of a highly-rated sovereign. Careful calibration and assessment are also needed to mitigate potential overreliance and moral hazard.[6]
From a European perspective, it is also sensible to restrict swap lines to jurisdictions where the impact on the euro area from defaults on euro-denominated debt or fire-sales of assets – including via indirect or network effects operating through the global financial system – have the potential to impair monetary policy transmission. Global trade, financial and supply chain linkages mean that seemingly isolated idiosyncratic shocks in one country or region – especially if the economy is large, a major financial centre or closely tied to the euro area – may transmit rapidly and unpredictably, escalate through network effects and pose a threat to monetary policy transmission.
The monetary policy case for liquidity lines is reinforced by their dynamic interaction with other policy areas. In particular, liquidity lines can boost the international role of the euro, which further supports the ability of the ECB to achieve its monetary policy objectives.[7] Liquidity lines bolster confidence in the currency and reduce the associated risks, supporting its wider usage in trade invoicing and settlements. Liquidity lines also support expanded issuance of euro-denominated debt. Such an expansion can entail two dimensions: (i) an increase in the volume of (new) euro-denominated credit as a swap line would encourage foreign counterparts to borrow in euro, either through loans or market-based debt instruments; and (ii) currency switching, whereby some FX loans previously extended by European lenders (including through their global subsidiaries) in foreign currency might – if a currency backstop exists – be made in euro. Both of these channels strengthen the effectiveness of ECB monetary policy transmission.[8]
Greater use of the euro internationally, in turn, supports the ability of the ECB to achieve price stability by increasing the international impact of euro area monetary policy and thereby influencing foreign demand as well as domestic demand. For example, a tightening of euro area monetary policy makes it more expensive for foreign entities to source euro denominated funding, which weighs on demand in economies that use the euro, particularly for debt issuance, as well as for trade invoicing and funding of working capital. articles.title: ‘Hunted like animals’: inside Trump’s war on the people who build America
articles.summary: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was a house framer before he was killed by ICE agents. Countless other Latino builders in Texas live in fear of a similar fateEvery morning long before dawn, while America sleeps, legions of Texas construction workers grab their fluorescent vests and hard hats, sling ladders and tools into their trucks, and head down the highway for another day of grueling labour under the blistering sun.Elsewhere, before the first flush of daylight settles over Texas’s concrete sprawl, a ...
articles.full_text:
Every morning long before dawn, while America sleeps, legions of Texas construction workers grab their fluorescent vests and hard hats, sling ladders and tools into their trucks, and head down the highway for another day of grueling labour under the blistering sun.
Elsewhere, before the first flush of daylight settles over Texas’s concrete sprawl, a separate army gets on the move in a fleet of shiny unmarked SUVs. They hover at gas stations, prowl around bodegas, pounce on the highways.
They’re on their way to work too. But the federal agents who form this second army are on a different mission.
Unlike the builders, they are not forging the US’s future one new starter home at a time. Their job is to pursue those who do the building: they follow the framers, track down the roofers, chase the cement masons and concrete finishers.
They are hunters.
“In Texas, you go deer hunting in the early morning,” said Jacob Monty, an immigration lawyer in Houston. “That’s what they are doing. They are hunting for construction workers, early in the morning, like you would an animal.”
Texas and its construction workforce are the ground zero of Donald Trump’s latest mass deportation effort, dubbed ICE 2.0. As the US president has pivoted from last year’s militarized “invasions” of Los Angeles and Minneapolis to this year’s less visible but no less devastating stop-and-search tactics, he has found rich pickings in Texas.
Texas is seeing by far the greatest number of ICE arrests in the country. More than 12,000 in July alone, almost double the number in the next most affected states, Florida and California.
Many of the detainees are Hispanic builders. Of every 10 construction workers in Texas, four are foreign born, most of whom are Hispanic and undocumented.
“This is low-hanging fruit,” Monty said. “If you target Texas Hispanics in trucks, you have a good chance of nabbing an undocumented person, and feeding the mass deportation machine.”
But there is a price to pay for ICE casting its dragnet through Texas barrios and building sites as it seeks to meet its new target of 3,000 immigration arrests daily. The street-level apprehensions are roiling the state, distorting its economy, forcing up house prices and the cost of groceries.
Hispanic families are also being torn apart. Hardworking people are being pushed into the shadows, others disappearing as they flee the country or are deported. The foundations of new homes are lying unfinished, building sites empty.
With the midterm elections just days away, and hugely consequential congressional races as well as the gubernatorial contest hanging in the balance, there are also political costs. Trump appears to be digging a hole for himself with Texas’s Hispanic voters.
Latino Texans who were born in the US or have naturalised, and thus can vote, are increasingly angry and confused. Many of them voted for Trump two years ago, attracted by his promise of a stronger economy and a fortified border that would keep out “criminal” immigrants.
They delivered Trump a historic victory, even in majority-Hispanic districts that had been Democratic strongholds for more than a century – voters like Sergio Benavides, 44, the owner of a home-building construction company in the Texas borderlands of the Rio Grande valley.
A naturalised US citizen, he voted for Trump in 2024. He liked his campaign promises that he would lower prices and secure the border. When people warned him it would turn sour, he didn’t listen.
He’s listening now. The prices of homes, food and gas have all gone up. Workers have to be paid more because so many have been deported. One of his subcontractors and his wife have disappeared, picked up by ICE, leaving behind three US-citizen children.
“That makes me sad,” he said. “We are here to protect our families, send our kids to college, to learn and grow. This is not what I thought when I voted for Trump.”
Benavides is part of a backlash that is showing up in the polls. Latino voters are turning against the president on the very issues that drew them to him – the cost of living, and immigration enforcement.
A poll last month from Equis Research found that disapproval of Trump had risen to 63% among Texas Latinos. In the critical US Senate race, which could determine which party holds the upper chamber during Trump’s final two years in office, 58% of likely Latino voters intend to back the Democratic candidate James Talarico, while only 33% support the scandal-ridden Republican, Ken Paxton. This, in a state that last returned a Democrat to the US Senate in 1988.
Latinos make up a third of Texas’s registered voters, the second-highest number in the country. And they know it.
Construction workers among them.
Marco Antonio Osorio’s day begins at 5am. Same routine, six days a week.
A member of his crew comes to pick him up at his house in Houston. They drive around in their shared white truck gathering other crew, then head off to the site of a new apartment complex where they spend the next 10 hours laying TV and wifi fiber optic cables.
It’s their speciality. They are good at it, and in demand. If only they were left to get on with it.
Around the beginning of the year Osorio, 50, noticed a surge in ICE street activity. “There were so many more sheriff’s vehicles, state troopers, ICE on the highways weaving between cars checking plates.”
As an undocumented Mexican who came to the US in 1993, aged 17, he knew he was vulnerable. But he thought he had some cover. His US-born daughter Gabriela is serving as a marine at Camp Pendleton in California. She has helped him apply for residency, and the paperwork is being processed.
Still, he wasn’t taking chances. He changed his habits. No going out of the house unless for essentials. No nights out at the movies. He couldn’t stop working, or else how would he pay the bills? But now he wears a button-down shirt on the drive to the site rather than his fluorescent yellow vest. No point advertising himself as a construction worker with ICE on the hunt.
He told his company he didn’t want to work outside Houston any more. The freeways to Austin and San Antonio were crawling with cop cars. “The company told me there weren’t any jobs here – either go out of town, or you don’t work.”
So he took a job in Austin. On 10 June, as he was returning home after another 10-hour shift, a sheriff’s car did a U-turn on the freeway and pulled him over. The officer said it was because his truck had a faulty rear light, but Osorio asked himself how they could have known that as they were traveling in opposite directions. More likely, he thought, was that his vehicle has a clear front screen. “They could see we were Hispanic.”
Within two minutes of the traffic stop, ICE SUVs blocked him in, front and back. The speed with which they appeared, Osorio realised, meant it had to be coordinated.
He told them his daughter was a US marine. He showed the officers the receipt for his residency application. An ICE officer replied: “Oh, that doesn’t count.” They took him to a freezing cell, the notorious las hieleras, and from there to an immigration detention facility near the border. He spent 40 days in the wilderness of ICE custody, until Monty got him released for lack of due process.
As he awaits his appeal, Osorio continues to work. Those bills keep coming, his children need feeding. On drives to work sites in Houston, he thinks about his daughter serving the country whose government wants him gone. He worries about his youngest child, an autistic boy, and what will become of him. He imagines returning to Mexico, a place he hasn’t known for 33 years.
As he drives, he spots apartment blocks all over the city that he helped put up. And he’s proud. “See those – I worked there 10 years ago. Or those – we built them 15 years ago.”
He thinks to himself: “This is my home.”
Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, a Mexican national, had been in the US for 35 years, two longer than Osorio. A house framer, the skilled worker who puts up the wooden skeleton of new houses, he carried out his days with an identical drill. Out the door at 5am, pick up the crew, 10 hours of hard graft, then relax on the balcony of his self-built Houston home listening to tierra caliente music with Ñoño, his beloved dog whom he named after a podgy 1970s Mexican sitcom character.
When ICE began to crank up its street arrests in February, Salgado spotted an opportunity. Many workers were too scared to leave the house, and new homes were standing half finished. A fearless entrepreneur, Salgado began accepting jobs that other undocumented framers like him would not contemplate.
He took precautions. He swapped his construction vest for a suit jacket while driving to work. He removed the jumble of blueprints, invoices and receipts from the dashboard of his white van. It was like his mobile office on wheels, but it branded him as a building professional, so he cleaned it off.
As time passed, and the ICE presence grew more oppressive, his three sons grew concerned. They are all American-born US citizens, and Salgado had high aspirations for them. They weren’t going to be builders like him – they were going to be educated, fulfill their own American dream. Ronaldo Salgado, the eldest, is a history teacher; Lorenzo Salgado Jr studied at the prestigious Tufts University and is now an engineer in Washington DC; and the youngest is at college, also studying engineering.
The sons got together and prepared a plan for their dad. They gave him a phone number that he should call if ever he were stopped, and they made sure he carried a “know your rights” card in his wallet. They made him swear that he would never sign any ICE form, as they feared he would be hoodwinked into self-deporting.
